Key economic indicators in Wisconsin during Scott Walker’s tenure (overall nonfarm employment growth and a falling unemployment rate) do not support the broad assertion that the economy 'tanked,' and the cited figure of 6,685 layoffs in 2015 exceeding all of 2014 appears to be misleading or taken out of context rather than reflecting statewide net job losses.

claim: Says a photo shows a white man smiling while holding a black man with a bloody face.
rationale: There is no image, source, or provenance provided to verify this description, and claims about photographs on social media are often miscaptioned, staged, or digitally altered. Without the original photo, metadata, or reliable reporting confirming the subjects' identities, expressions, and injuries, the assertion cannot be confirmed and should be treated as unverified.

claim: Alaska Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Mark Begich "vote as much as 80 percent of the time together."
rationale: The statement is misleading because vote-agreement percentages depend heavily on which votes and what time period are counted, and public roll-call analyses of Murkowski and Begich show varying rates well below a reliable, consistent 80% across their shared Senate tenure. Without a specified timeframe or methodology the 80% figure cannot be confirmed and is likely an overstatement.

claim: U.S. Rep. Connie Mack "voted to raise his own pay several times."
rationale: I cannot verify a clear record that Representative Connie Mack repeatedly voted to raise his own pay; the claim is vague about which Connie Mack (III or IV) and which votes are meant. Without specific bills or dates it is not possible to confirm the assertion that he voted 'several times' for pay raises.

claim: "Tim Kaine doubled down in his support of devastating defense cuts, saying the ‘the deal was the right thing to do.’"
rationale: There is no clear, attributable record of Sen. Tim Kaine saying the quoted line or explicitly ‘doubling down’ in support of ‘devastating defense cuts.’ The claim appears to be a partisan paraphrase without a verifiable source or context; while Kaine has at times supported budget deals that included spending changes, this particular quote and characterization are not substantiated.

claim: "On my last trip to New Hampshire, I think I met the guy who founded the first and only bank since Dodd-Frank passed, since the financial crisis. One bank in the country."
rationale: The claim that only one bank was founded in the country since Dodd‑Frank (after the financial crisis) is incorrect. Multiple de novo banks and state-chartered banks have been created since 2010, and federal and state banking regulators’ records show more than a single new charter in that period.

claim: Polling shows that nearly 74 percent of National Rifle Association members "support requiring background checks for all gun sales."
rationale: I cannot verify a specific, reputable poll that reports 'nearly 74%' of National Rifle Association members back requiring background checks for all gun sales. While many national polls show very high support for universal background checks among the general public (and some show a majority even among NRA supporters), estimates for self-identified NRA members vary by poll, question wording, and sample, and no single consistent figure of ~74% is established.

claim: "In (Sen. Marco) Rubio's state of Florida alone, Social Security lifts more than -- count it -- a million people out of poverty."
rationale: The claim overstates the state-level impact. While Social Security does lift millions nationally out of poverty, state-by-state analyses and Social Security Administration/Census-based estimates show Florida’s count of people lifted is substantially less than 1 million in typical years; the national figures are often misquoted as state totals.

claim: Says Donald Trump indicted Amy Coney Barrett.
rationale: The claim is false. A U.S. president does not have the power to issue criminal indictments—those are brought by prosecutors or grand juries—and there have been no credible reports that Amy Coney Barrett was indicted. Donald Trump has not indicted her.

claim: "The race will tighten, just because that's what happens at the end of campaigns. They always have."
rationale: This is an overbroad generalization. While some campaigns do tighten late as undecided voters break and events shift opinion, many races remain stable or even widen toward one candidate, so it is not true that races always tighten at the end of campaigns.

claim: Says unsuccessful Texas abortion legislation "was supported by a majority of" Texans.
rationale: The claim asserts a majority of Texans supported an unspecified unsuccessful Texas abortion bill, but it provides no bill or timeframe and available polling on Texas shows mixed opinions that vary by wording and exceptions. Without a specific piece of legislation and contemporaneous polling showing a clear majority in favor, the assertion cannot be verified and is unlikely to be reliably true.

claim: Says "every school will be negatively impacted" if Education Stability Fund is not tapped.
rationale: The claim is an absolute universal statement that every school would be negatively impacted if the Education Stability Fund is not tapped; such categorical effects are unlikely. School funding and budgets vary widely by state, district, and school, and some schools may be insulated by other revenue sources or emergency measures. Without specific jurisdictional details and analysis showing universal harm, the blanket assertion is unsupported.

claim: "Klein did not hold a single town hall meeting (on health care) where the general public was invited to ask questions or present their views."
rationale: The claim is absolute and unlikely to be true; the Klein government conducted public consultations and at least some public Q&A/town-hall–style events around health-care changes according to contemporary reporting. It is implausible to assert he held zero such meetings without exhaustive evidence to support that absolute statement.

claim: "We have 25 million Americans out of work."
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or definition and is therefore misleading as a standalone fact. At the peak of the COVID-19 job shock (spring 2020) BLS data showed roughly 23 million people classified as unemployed, while cumulative unemployment insurance claims at times approached 25 million — these are different measures. Without specifying date and which metric is meant, the blanket statement is inaccurate.

claim: "We raised the minimum wage to $15 first in city government. Now, working together with people in Albany, it's the law of the state."
rationale: The claim that the city government was the first to raise the minimum wage to $15 is inaccurate: several U.S. cities (notably Seattle and San Francisco) enacted $15 minimum wage ordinances in 2014 before many other localities. It is true, however, that New York State later passed a statewide law (in 2016) implementing $15 on a phased schedule for New York City and larger employers, but the "first"-to-$15 assertion is incorrect or at least misleading without naming the city and the specific wage type (municipal employees vs. citywide minimum).

claim: Before COVID-19, "Iowa had one of the lowest unemployment rates in the country, and many employers were scrambling to find qualified employees to fill their job openings."
rationale: In the months before COVID-19 (late 2019–early 2020) Iowa’s unemployment rate was at or below the national average and among the lower state rates, and state employers across manufacturing, healthcare, and services reported difficulty filling open positions. Numerous BLS state-level labor reports and local business and workforce agencies documented a tight labor market and employer complaints about a shortage of qualified applicants.

claim: "Obama certificate a fake."
rationale: The claim that Obama’s birth certificate is fake is incorrect. The State of Hawaii’s Department of Health and the governor have confirmed his birth in Honolulu, the White House released a scanned long-form birth certificate, and independent fact-checkers and contemporaneous local birth announcements corroborate his Hawaiian birth.

claim: Video shows helicopters in Ukraine "being picked off in ambush - Short range air-to-air missile"
rationale: There is no independent verification provided that the clip shows Ukrainian helicopters being 'picked off' specifically by a short-range air-to-air missile. Short clips from conflict zones are often misattributed, and visual evidence alone seldom permits reliable identification of the exact weapon (it could be MANPADS, ground fire, anti-aircraft guns, or other munitions). Without geolocation, timestamp, corroborating sources, or expert munitions analysis the claim is unproven.

claim: "Wayfair CEO steps down."
rationale: The claim is vague and, as of mid-2024, there were no widely reported announcements or regulatory filings indicating that Wayfair’s CEO had stepped down. Major business news sources did not report a CEO resignation for Wayfair during that period, so the statement is unverified and likely false without further context.

claim: "We have the highest per-pupil cost in the country."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it fails to identify who 'we' refers to and which year or spending definition is meant. Per-pupil spending varies widely across states and districts and changes annually; multiple jurisdictions have reported higher per-pupil costs in different datasets and years, so the blanket statement cannot be supported without specific context.

claim: President Barack Obama’s health care reform "slashed $500 billion from Medicare."
rationale: This claim is misleading. The Affordable Care Act included provisions that reduced projected Medicare spending by roughly $500 billion over about a decade, but those were primarily reductions in payments to providers and Medicare Advantage plans and slowing future spending growth — not across-the-board cuts to core Medicare benefits for beneficiaries.

claim: The media has "a lower approval rate than Congress."
rationale: The statement is too general to be true as written: approval/trust ratings for “the media” and for Congress vary substantially by country, polling organization, and time period. In some U.S. polls Congress ranks lower than the media, while in others media trust is lower; there is no stable universal ordering. Without a specific country, poll, and date the claim is unsupported.

claim: The streetcar project planned by Mayor Tom Barrett would be a "1900s style trolley."
rationale: The streetcar project associated with Mayor Tom Barrett (Milwaukee’s modern streetcar, "The Hop") was planned and built using contemporary low-floor, ADA-accessible streetcar vehicles and modern infrastructure, not antique 1900s-era trolleys. Promotional materials sometimes evoked historic streetcar heritage, but the vehicles and technology are modern rather than turn-of-the-century trolleys.

claim: "There's only four senators senior to me ... there's still 44 older than me."
rationale: This statement is context-dependent and cannot be verified as a general fact without knowing which senator is speaking, the date, and whether 'senior' means greater tenure or greater age. Numerically it could be true in a particular circumstance, but as presented it is an unverifiable, ambiguous claim. Because the necessary identifying details are missing, it cannot be confirmed.

claim: "If every house in Florida had a solar-heated water tank, that would eliminate consumption by 17 percent."
rationale: The claim is vague and likely overstated. While water heating is commonly cited as roughly 15–20% of residential energy use, saying that installing solar-heated water tanks on every Florida house would 'eliminate consumption by 17 percent' is misleading: solar water heaters would reduce but not fully eliminate that share because of backup heating, variable solar resource, maintenance, and differing fuel mixes. Also the claim does not specify whether it means residential energy, statewide energy, or electricity specifically, so it cannot be taken as a verified fact.

claim: Says Bruce Poliquin "voted to strip 117,000 Mainers of their insurance."
rationale: While Bruce Poliquin did vote for Republican health-care legislation in 2017 that independent analysts said would have reduced coverage nationally and cut Medicaid funding, there is no reliable evidence that his single vote specifically 'stripped 117,000 Mainers of their insurance.' State-level estimates of people who could lose coverage from those bills vary and do not support the precise 117,000 figure as a documented, direct consequence of Poliquin's vote.

claim: "The CDC director just said that 75% of ‘Covid deaths’ occurred in people with at least four comorbidities."
rationale: There is no public record of the CDC director recently stating that 75% of COVID deaths occurred in people with at least four comorbidities. CDC data do show many death certificates list multiple contributing conditions, but that precise figure and attribution to the CDC director appears to be a misstatement or fabrication.

claim: "Women in Oregon are paid 79 cents for every dollar paid to men. If the wage gap was eliminated, a working woman in Oregon would have enough money for 2,877 gallons of gas, 72 more weeks of food for her family or nearly 12 more months of rent."
rationale: The 79¢ figure is a commonly quoted national statistic for women's median earnings versus men's, not definitively Oregon-specific, and state pay ratios vary. The detailed claims about gallons of gas, weeks of food, and months of rent depend on unstated assumptions (which wage measure/year, gas price, family size, rent level) and so cannot be verified as accurate without the original source and date.

claim: "The Democrat controlled House never even asked John Bolton to testify."
rationale: During the 2019 impeachment inquiry House Democrats did seek John Bolton’s testimony and pursued subpoenas; Bolton’s lawyer said he would testify if subpoenaed, but the White House directed him not to and asserted privilege, so he never gave public testimony. The claim that Democrats "never even asked" him is inaccurate.

claim: "Overdoses in Virginia (are) up 35%."
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or specific metric (fatal overdoses, nonfatal suspected overdoses, EMS calls, etc.), so it cannot be verified as stated. Virginia has experienced increases in overdoses in recent years, but the exact percentage change varies by year and data source and is not universally 35%.

claim: "I have returned money every year since taking office."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and lacks essential specifics (who 'I' refers to, what money was returned, and to whom). Without verifiable documentary evidence such as financial disclosures, press reports, or audit records confirming yearly returns, the claim cannot be substantiated and thus is treated as false. If supporting records are provided, the assessment could change.

claim: In Milwaukee, "murder is up an astonishing 57 percent."
rationale: The statement gives no timeframe or baseline, and homicide percentage changes depend entirely on the specific period compared (e.g., month-to-month, year-over-year, or a partial-year window). Without a cited source and exact dates it cannot be verified that Milwaukee murders were up precisely 57%; past reporting has shown large but variable percentage increases in different intervals.

claim: "Last week, the Colorado Supreme Court declared that Boulder’s AR-15 ban was unconstitutional. Today, there was a mass shooting in Boulder."
rationale: I cannot confirm either part of the claim: there is no clear, verifiable record that the Colorado Supreme Court issued a ruling last week declaring Boulder's AR-15 ban unconstitutional, nor is there confirmation of a mass shooting in Boulder 'today.' Both events would be major, widely reported developments; without corroborating contemporary news or an official court announcement the combined claim appears unsubstantiated.

claim: "The Simpsons" predicted Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that The Simpsons explicitly predicted Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine; viral clips and images claiming this are coincidences, taken out of context, or digitally altered. Independent fact-checkers have reviewed the purported scenes and found them to be misleading or unrelated to the actual event.

claim: Says Nelson Mandela "was a communist."
rationale: Calling Nelson Mandela simply 'a communist' is misleading. He collaborated closely with the South African Communist Party, accepted its support and held some left-wing views during the anti-apartheid struggle, but his formal membership is disputed, he denied membership at the Rivonia Trial, and later embraced multi-party democracy rather than adherence to communist ideology.

claim: Says with "Gov. Chris Christie and bipartisan reformers" New Jersey had "the most job growth in 11 years."
rationale: The claim is misleading and likely false because it does not specify an 11-year period or whether it means absolute or percentage job growth. Bureau of Labor Statistics and state labor data show New Jersey recovered jobs after the 2008 recession during Chris Christie’s tenure, but it was not clearly the single leader in job growth across states over any obvious 11-year window; other states posted larger absolute and percentage gains. Without a precise timeframe and metric the assertion that New Jersey had "the most job growth in 11 years" cannot be substantiated.

claim: "If you give guns to gangs, you can get out of jail free, if (California’s Proposition 57) passes. If you do a drive-by shooting, you can get out of jail free, if Proposition 57 passes. If you discharge guns on a school yard, you can get out of jail free."
rationale: The claim is false. California Proposition 57 (2016) did not automatically free people who commit violent crimes; it made people convicted of nonviolent felonies eligible for parole consideration and expanded credit-earning for rehabilitation, while explicitly excluding specified violent and serious felonies. Many gun offenses such as drive-by shootings, discharging a firearm at a school, and weapons trafficking are treated as violent/serious felonies or otherwise ineligible, and Prop 57 never promised an automatic "get out of jail free" outcome.

claim: "#GradInsurance debacle is a DIRECT result of #ObamaCare. #MIZZOU has to break the law to do the right thing."
rationale: The statement asserts a causal chain without evidence: problems with a university graduate-student insurance plan are not automatically a 'DIRECT result' of the Affordable Care Act and instead typically reflect administrative, contractual, or insurer decisions. Likewise, the claim that the University of Missouri must 'break the law to do the right thing' is unsubstantiated—universities generally have legal options (plan changes, waivers, subsidies, negotiations) and there is no demonstrated necessity to violate law to remedy coverage issues.

claim: "In ‘Resident Evil’ the Umbrella Corporation releases a virus that infects the people of Raccoon City. A biological research lab with the exact same logo as the Umbrella Corporation can be found in the city where the coronavirus outbreak originated."
rationale: The first clause is accurate as fictional plot: in the Resident Evil franchise the Umbrella Corporation is responsible for releasing the T-virus that devastates Raccoon City. The second clause is false or misleading: there is no verified evidence that a real-world biological research lab in the city widely reported as the origin of the COVID-19 outbreak uses the exact same Umbrella Corporation logo; viral images and claims have conflated similar-looking commercial or generic umbrella symbols with the fictional logo.

claim: Says 1 in 5 Texans did not have health insurance coverage before the pandemic, and now "nearly 1 in 3 Texans under the age of 65 don’t have access to health care insurance."
rationale: The claim mixes a broadly accurate pre-pandemic fact with a large exaggeration. Texas’ uninsured rate before the pandemic was about 17–18% (roughly 1 in 5), but more recent reliable estimates for nonelderly Texans show uninsured rates well below one-third, not nearly 1 in 3.

claim: Health care reform will not affect veterans' benefits.
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim and is incorrect in general. While veterans’ medical benefits are largely administered and funded separately by the Department of Veterans Affairs, specific health-care reforms can and have had direct or indirect effects on veterans’ coverage, access, eligibility interactions (e.g., Medicaid expansion, insurance marketplaces) and federal budget pressures that affect VA funding. Therefore it is false to assert reforms will not affect veterans’ benefits in all cases.

claim: "1928 was last time Republicans had the White House, the House and the Senate."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: Republicans also simultaneously held the presidency and both chambers of Congress after the 2002 and 2016 elections. For example, Republicans controlled the White House and both the House and Senate from January 2003–January 2007 under President George W. Bush, and again from January 2017–January 2019 under President Donald Trump.

claim: Mehmet Oz "was a spokesman for a group who wanted to defund the police."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Mehmet Oz served as a spokesman for any group advocating to defund the police; his public statements and 2022 campaign positions explicitly opposed defunding police and supported law enforcement. The claim appears to be a fabrication or mischaracterization without supporting reporting.

claim: Says abortion is "the leading cause of death for black Americans and kills as many as 1,000 black children every day."
rationale: Official US mortality statistics list heart disease and cancer as the leading causes of death among Black Americans; abortions are not counted as deaths of living Black Americans in those vital statistics. The frequently‑cited “1,000 black children every day” figure depends on treating fetal abortions as equivalent to deaths of Black Americans and uses high-end aggregation of abortion counts; CDC and researcher estimates of abortions among Black women imply several hundred, not a sustained 1,000, recognized deaths per day and do not change the official ranking of causes of death.

claim: Says a "Pro-Stimulus economist admits it is not working … "
rationale: The statement is an unattributed quotation claiming a 'pro-stimulus economist' admitted 'it is not working' but provides no named person, policy, time, or source to verify. Without specific attribution or context this cannot be confirmed; while some pro-stimulus economists have acknowledged limits of particular measures, that does not validate the blanket, unnamed claim.

claim: "Right to Work states have: faster private sector employment growth"
rationale: The empirical evidence is mixed: some studies find a modest association between right-to-work laws and higher private-sector employment growth, but many other analyses show no robust effect once you control for state characteristics, timing, and industry composition. The claim as stated asserts a general causal truth, which is not supported by consensus research.

claim: "We have one of the most expensive General Assemblies, per capita, in the entire country."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits which state or year and what costs are included. Per-capita costs of state legislatures vary widely and require specific budgetary comparisons (salaries, staff, per diems, operating expenses) to substantiate; without that data the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Congressman Scott DesJarlais "is spending his one year anniversary on vacation -- only working 6 days in all of January."
rationale: This specific claim is not verifiable from the information provided: it gives no year or source and makes a precise assertion about days worked that would require roll-call, official schedule, or credible reporting to confirm. Without those records, the statement should be treated as unproven and likely misleading rather than an established fact.

claim: Says Mitt Romney belittled middle-class tax cuts "as nothing more than 'little Band-Aids.' "
rationale: I could not find a reliably sourced, verbatim instance of Mitt Romney saying middle-class tax cuts were "nothing more than 'little Band-Aids.'" Political opponents and ads often paraphrased or summarized his critiques of incremental measures (calling some measures "band-aids"), but that appears to be a contested paraphrase rather than a documented direct quote targeting middle-class tax cuts specifically.

claim: "This past (legislative) session, we passed out of the Legislature a resolution requiring Congress to pass a balanced-budget amendment to the (U.S.) Constitution."
rationale: No single state legislature can legally 'require' Congress to pass a specific constitutional amendment. States can adopt resolutions urging Congress to act or submit Article V applications to call a convention, but those actions do not compel Congress to pass a balanced-budget amendment.

claim: "The 2008 election was the first election in which voters of color comprised over 25 percent of the electorate, and that number is going up."
rationale: Analyses of U.S. exit polls and Pew Research data show the 2008 electorate was the first presidential electorate in which nonwhite voters exceeded roughly 25% (estimates around 27–28%). Subsequent elections have continued the trend of a growing share of voters of color, so the share has generally been increasing since 2008.

claim: "Wages are on the rise — in fact we were the top small-business wage growth state in the nation."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it omits which state, the time period, and the data source or definition of "small-business wage growth." Without those specifics, there is no reliable way to confirm a top-national ranking; wage-growth rankings vary by dataset (BLS, ADP, state reports) and timeframe. Given the missing details, the claim cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty is endorsed by the Austin American-Statesman.
rationale: There is no widely reported or publicly archived record that the Austin American-Statesman endorsed a candidate named Gerald Daugherty. The newspaper’s endorsements are publicly listed and covered in local media, and Daugherty’s name does not appear among those endorsements as of mid-2024.

claim: Says David Dewhurst skipped nine candidate forums after announcing his U.S. Senate candidacy.
rationale: I cannot find authoritative, consistent evidence that David Dewhurst skipped exactly nine candidate forums after announcing his U.S. Senate run. Counts reported in media and campaign materials vary depending on how a 'forum' is defined and which dates are included, so the specific claim of nine is not reliably supported.

claim: "Florida spends more than $300 million a year just on children repeating pre-K through 3rd grade."
rationale: I cannot find a verifiable, widely accepted estimate showing Florida spends more than $300 million annually specifically on children repeating pre-K through 3rd grade. Costs attributed to grade retention vary widely depending on the accounting method (direct classroom costs, administrative costs, or longer-term societal costs), and public data and independent analyses do not conclusively support the specific >$300M figure as a standalone recurring line item.

claim: "Marco Rubio made it clear: Not only does he think Donald Trump is a con man, he went on to say he doesn't trust Donald Trump with the nuclear codes."
rationale: During the 2016 Republican primary and afterward Marco Rubio publicly criticized Donald Trump, at times calling him a con man or con artist and explicitly saying he would not trust Trump with the nuclear codes in interviews and debates. Those lines appeared in multiple media reports and on-the-record campaign remarks.

claim: Richmond is "the most vegan-friendly city."
rationale: The statement is subjective and not supported by a consistent, authoritative ranking identifying any city named Richmond as the single "most vegan-friendly" globally. Popular, repeatable lists of vegan-friendly cities typically name places like Portland, Berlin, London, and Tel Aviv based on measurable criteria; no consensus elevates a Richmond to the top. Without a specified Richmond or metrics, the claim is unverifiable and therefore treated as false.

claim: "There's been no conclusive or specific report to say" Russia was trying to muddy the election.
rationale: Multiple official U.S. investigations and intelligence assessments have concluded that Russia undertook operations to influence and sow discord around U.S. elections, including the 2016 effort documented by the Mueller report and by U.S. intelligence community and bipartisan Senate Intelligence Committee reports. Those reports described specific methods (social-media disinformation, cyber intrusions, and leaks) and assessed intent to interfere and amplify divisions. Therefore the claim that there has been no conclusive or specific report is incorrect.

claim: Says Measure 3-386 will cost a fortune for elections while Measure 3-388 will cost less.
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify the claim because no jurisdiction, voter pamphlet, or fiscal analysis for Measures 3-386 and 3-388 is provided. Cost impacts of ballot measures depend on their specific provisions and official fiscal notes; without those documents the assertion that one "will cost a fortune" and the other "will cost less" cannot be established. Absent supporting evidence, the claim is unverified and should be treated as likely inaccurate.

claim: "I cut more as a percentage out of government than any state in the country this past decade. And where is Michigan in terms of its economic growth? Cutting did not result in economic growth."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unsupported: the pronoun "I" and the exact decade aren’t identified, and available public budget data do not show Michigan uniquely made the largest percentage cuts of any state over the last decade. Whether spending cuts produced economic growth depends on the time period and metrics used; Michigan experienced a post-recession recovery but its growth performance was mixed and not clearly evidence that cuts universally failed or succeeded.

claim: "Fifty percent of the Ottawa police force have all turned in their resignation."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official confirmation that half of the Ottawa police force submitted resignations. A mass resignation on that scale would have been widely reported by major news outlets and acknowledged by the Ottawa Police Service, but no such reports or statements exist.

claim: Anthony Fauci was on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years and "currently serves on Gates Foundation."
rationale: Public biographies and reporting on Dr. Anthony Fauci list his long government service and numerous advisory roles but do not show he was a member of the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years, nor that he is a board member of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. He has collaborated with and appeared at events with those and other global health organizations, which has been mischaracterized online as formal board membership.

claim: "California is 49th out of 50 in the United States in per capita housing units. Only Utah can lay claim to being lowest in per capita production."
rationale: This statement mixes metrics and appears incorrect: Census and housing-permit data do not consistently show California as 49th in housing units per capita, and Utah is commonly among the leaders in per-capita housing production rather than the lowest. The claim likely confuses different years or definitions (existing housing units vs. recent production/permits).

claim: "McCain opposes repeal of the death tax."
rationale: The claim is too broad and lacks context (which McCain and what time period). Public statements by Senator John McCain on the so-called "death tax" (estate tax) have varied over time and he has not consistently taken a simple categorical position of opposing repeal. Without a specified person and timeframe the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: The Baucus health care bill "would drastically restrict the use of flexible spending accounts (FSAs) in order to help pay for health care reform."
rationale: The Baucus health-care draft included provisions that would limit tax-favored flexible spending accounts (FSAs) by capping allowable pre-tax contributions as a revenue offset. These limits were explicitly proposed as one mechanism to help pay for aspects of the reform, so the claim that the bill would restrict FSAs to help fund reform is accurate, although the term “drastically” is subjective.

claim: "Hidden in the CARES Act was an obscure $135 billion tax break for 43,000 millionaires."
rationale: The CARES Act did include tax-related provisions (temporary NOL carrybacks and payroll tax deferral) that provided liquidity to businesses, but there is no evidence it secretly enacted a targeted $135 billion tax cut specifically for 43,000 millionaires. The $135 billion/43,000 figure appears to come from speculative or model-dependent calculations and misattributes broadly available business tax relief to a narrow group of wealthy individuals.

claim: "They’ve seen employer-supported coverage increase in Massachusetts after this law (Romneycare) was implemented."
rationale: Multiple analyses of Massachusetts’ 2006–2007 health reform found that overall uninsurance fell sharply and employer-sponsored coverage rose modestly after implementation. Massachusetts bucked the national trend at the time, which saw stable or declining employer coverage, so the claim that employer-supported coverage increased there is supported by empirical studies.

claim: "The cost-of-living increase in Social Security is tied to wage inflation."
rationale: The annual Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is calculated from changes in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI‑W), a price-inflation measure, not from wage inflation. Although Social Security uses wage-indexing for initial benefit calculations and some other adjustments, the COLA itself is tied to price inflation, not wage growth.

claim: "Cities in notoriously ‘tough on crime’ states like Texas and Florida saw a more significant increase in violent crime than cities in NYS."
rationale: The claim is an overly broad generalization that isn’t supported without specifying a timeframe, which cities, or which violent-crime measures. Crime trends vary widely by city and year — some cities in Texas and Florida experienced larger increases than some cities in New York State, but many NYS cities saw similar or greater changes and statewide comparisons depend on the period and data source used.

claim: The unemployment rate may be as high as "42 percent."
rationale: The statement is presented without any context (which country, timeframe, or demographic), and as a general claim it is misleading: national unemployment rates rarely reach 42%. While certain subgroups (for example youth unemployment in some countries or localized crises) can exceed that level, the claim as stated lacks the necessary specifics or evidence.

claim: "Al-Qaida operatives, have said, 'Hey, we want you to use this loophole (for purchasing guns despite being on a watch list) to attack and kill Americans.'"
rationale: There is no verifiable public record or credible reporting showing Al-Qaida operatives uttered that exact quote instructing use of a 'loophole' to buy guns while on a watch list. While extremist groups have published guidance encouraging attacks and sometimes discussing weapons acquisition, the specific attributed statement appears unverified and likely a paraphrase or invention. Without a reliable source, the claim cannot be accepted as factual.

claim: "Over 97 percent of the scientific community … believe that humans are contributing to climate change."
rationale: Multiple independent studies of climate scientists and the peer‑reviewed literature (notably Cook et al. 2013 and earlier work by Anderegg et al. and Doran & Zimmerman) find that about 97% of actively publishing climate scientists or climate‑science papers that take a position endorse the view that humans are causing recent climate change. The common caveat is that these studies target climate experts or the climate literature rather than every scientist in all fields.

claim: Democratic U.S. House candidate Julie Lassa pushed for a "Canadian-style government takeover of health care."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Julie Lassa explicitly called for a literal “Canadian-style government takeover” of health care; that phrase was commonly used by opponents as a political attack to describe advocacy for greater public involvement or reform. Without direct quotations or policy proposals from Lassa endorsing full government takeover (single-payer modeled on Canada), the claim overstates and mischaracterizes typical Democratic reform positions.

claim: Says Ben Carson said "illegal immigrants caught voting should be stripped of their citizenship."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable news/fact-check source showing Ben Carson said that illegal immigrants caught voting should be stripped of their citizenship. The claim is also legally incoherent because undocumented immigrants are not U.S. citizens and therefore cannot have citizenship revoked. Carson has criticized illegal voting in general but has not been documented making this specific statement.

claim: "Last year, (Bill McCollum) spent more than $2.2 million dollars to produce and air campaign-style TV ads where you were featured in almost every frame."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it names neither the specific year nor who “you” refers to, and no evidence or sources are provided showing McCollum spent over $2.2 million on ads centering a particular person. Confirming such a precise spending and content claim would require campaign finance filings, media-buy invoices, and the actual ad copies; absent those, the assertion cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "California lawmakers are planning to push free abortion pills on all students across the state as part of a ‘super progressive’ new policy."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that California lawmakers plan to force or universally distribute free abortion pills to 'all students' statewide. California has passed and considered laws to expand access to medication abortion and to fund services (including support for some college health centers and Medi‑Cal coverage), but these are measures to increase voluntary access and funding, not a mandate to push pills on every student.

claim: "The collective net worth of Americans has taken a $5.5 trillion hit ... mainly due to plummeting home values."
rationale: The claim gives a specific $5.5 trillion figure and attributes it mainly to plummeting home values but provides no timeframe or source. Aggregate U.S. household net worth does change, but verification requires a date and data source; in many recent downturns equity market moves, not housing, have been the dominant driver of multi‑trillion dollar shifts. Without a cited period or data, the statement is not reliably supported.

claim: Tim Tebow used to "kneel in prayer and the NFL complained."
rationale: Tim Tebow did frequently kneel in prayer on the field (popularized as 'Tebowing'), but the NFL as an organization did not formally complain or discipline him for that gesture. League officials publicly indicated they would not penalize religious expressions, and any objections came from commentators or fans rather than an official NFL complaint.

claim: "There was never a single shred of evidence presented to anyone" that the attacks in Benghazi, Libya, were "spontaneous, and in fact, the CIA themselves understood that early on."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate: in the immediate aftermath there were public reports and intelligence notes referencing protests tied to an anti‑Islam video and intelligence talking points that mentioned that possibility, so it is false to say there was "never a single shred of evidence" presented that the events could be spontaneous. Subsequent official reviews (State Dept. ARB, Congressional investigations, and FBI/CIA analyses) concluded the attack was a coordinated terrorist operation and show that some CIA analysts assessed it as a terrorist attack relatively early, but agency views were not uniformly identical at the earliest stage.

claim: "I am the only member of Congress that voted for both inquiries -- the Clinton inquiry and now the Trump inquiry."
rationale: The claim is unlikely and not supported without checking roll-call records. Many long-serving members of the House served during both the 1998 Clinton-era actions and the 2019 Trump-era inquiry, so it is implausible that a single member was uniquely the only person to vote for both without specific evidence.

claim: In the 100 days since its passage, the economic stimulus has "saved or created nearly 150,000 jobs."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it omits which stimulus and which source produced the figure; while an administration estimate around 150,000 jobs saved/created was publicly asserted for the early period after the 2009 ARRA, independent economists noted large uncertainty and alternative analyses produced different numbers. Short-term attributions of jobs to a specific stimulus are methodologically fraught, so the blanket claim is misleading without sourcing and caveats.

claim: "As a city, we currently use about 4 percent less electricity today than we used in 1989."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it omits which city and what date 'today' refers to; electricity consumption trends since 1989 vary greatly by city. Without city-specific, weather- and boundary-adjusted utility data (total vs per-capita), a blanket claim of a 4% reduction is unsupported.

claim: Says the Ohio Consumers’ Council office employs 74 lawyers and that the funding them is wasteful duplication.
rationale: The claim that the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel office employs 74 lawyers is inaccurate—this state consumer-advocacy office has a much smaller legal staff. The assertion that funding them is 'wasteful duplication' is a normative judgment; the office is statutorily charged to represent residential utility consumers, so its funding serves a distinct legal advocacy role rather than being an obvious duplicate of other agencies.

claim: "Our income, our GDP per capita, is almost 50 percent higher than (it is for) the average European."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous about which country and which measure (nominal vs PPP) and year are being compared, and blanket claims of "almost 50% higher" usually do not hold across plausible interpretations. Depending on the country and metric the gap to the average European can be much smaller or larger; for example, the U.S. is commonly reported as above the EU average but typically in the ~20–40% range depending on the year and whether PPP or nominal GDP is used, while many other countries are below or near the European average. Without a specified country and metric the claim is misleading.

claim: "27 U.S. Air Force pilots resign over COVID-19 vaccination mandate."
rationale: There is no reliable reporting or official Department of Defense confirmation that exactly 27 U.S. Air Force pilots resigned specifically over the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. Media and official data noted some separations and administrative actions across the military related to vaccine refusal, but the specific claim of 27 Air Force pilots resigning has not been substantiated and appears to have originated on social media.

claim: Under the Hate Crimes bill, "any pastor, preacher, priest, rabbi or imam who gives a sermon out of their moral traditions about sexual practices could be found guilty of a federal crime."
rationale: Federal hate-crimes statutes target violent acts, threats, or attempts to injure or intimidate people because of a protected characteristic, not the content of religious sermons. Ordinary preaching about sexual morality would be protected speech under the First Amendment and would not by itself constitute a federal crime; only speech that crosses into true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, or accompanying criminal conduct could lead to prosecution.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "This country is doomed, not just because of African Americans, but because by 2040 this country is going to be minority white European."
rationale: There is no credible transcript, recording, or reporting from reputable news or fact-checking organizations that shows Joe Biden ever made this statement; the language and framing do not match his recorded public remarks. The quote appears to be fabricated or misattributed, likely circulating as misinformation.

claim: Says "Kurt Schrader supports Obama’s sequester … but won’t cut $1.6 million to fund new video games."
rationale: The statement bundles two specific claims (that Rep. Kurt Schrader supported President Obama’s sequester and that he refused to cut a $1.6 million item to fund video games) for which there is no clear, attributable public record. Democratic members of Congress generally opposed the 2013 sequestration and I find no reliable evidence tying Schrader to an explicit endorsement of Obama’s sequester or to a documented refusal to cut a $1.6 million video-game-related line item.

claim: "We became a net exporter of natural gas in 2017, and until recently, our exports have exceeded our imports."
rationale: For the United States, reliable energy data show the country became a net exporter of natural gas in 2017 (the first time since the 1950s), and annual trade data after 2017 show exports exceeded imports for several subsequent years. The phrasing "until recently" is consistent with continued net-export status through at least the early 2020s.

claim: "We are not producing jobs. We created 80,000 jobs last month. We don't talk about the jobs that we lost. The net of it all is that we lost jobs."
rationale: The statement is internally inconsistent and lacks necessary context. In standard public reporting (e.g., BLS nonfarm payroll releases), saying 'we created 80,000 jobs last month' refers to the net change in payroll employment for that month; if the net was +80,000, that contradicts the claim that 'the net of it all is that we lost jobs' unless the speaker is using a different timeframe or metric. Without specifying the period or distinguishing gross hires from net employment, the claim that net jobs were lost despite a reported +80,000 month is unsupported.

claim: Says Steve Jobs said, "I realize that all my recognition and wealth that I have is meaningless in the face of imminent death."
rationale: That exact sentence is not found in Jobs' documented remarks. It is a paraphrase of sentiments he expressed — notably in his 2005 Stanford commencement address (e.g., "Remembering that I'll be dead soon...") and remarks like "Being the richest man in the cemetery doesn't matter" — but the quoted wording is not a verified direct quote.

claim: "Every day, a black name resume is 50 percent less likely to get responded to than a white name resume."
rationale: A landmark 2003 field experiment found that resumes with African-American–sounding names received about 50% fewer callbacks than identical resumes with White-sounding names, but that was an empirical result in a specific study and context, not a universal daily law. Subsequent research has confirmed racial discrimination in hiring but with varying effect sizes across time, locations, occupations and study methods, so the categorical claim "Every day, a black name resume is 50 percent less likely" is overstated and misleading.

claim: "In Wisconsin, only half of all the adults with serious psychological distress received mental health treatment or medication."
rationale: The claim gives no year or data source and therefore cannot be verified as a general statement about Wisconsin adults; published survey estimates of treatment for serious psychological distress vary by year and by how 'treatment or medication' is defined. Without a specific timeframe and source the assertion that 'only half' received care is unsubstantiated and potentially misleading.

claim: "A rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months. The legislature’s failure to expand Medicaid has brought crisis to many of Missouri’s rural health care providers."
rationale: The precise claim that "a rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months" is not a verifiable ongoing rate and appears overstated without a defined timeframe or source. Also, Missouri voters approved Medicaid expansion in 2020 (Amendment 2) and the legislature subsequently enacted implementation, so it is incorrect to state simply that the legislature has failed to expand Medicaid; while lack of expansion prior to 2020 likely worsened finances for some rural providers, closures have multiple causes.

claim: Says "Joe Biden is absolutely on board with defunding the police."
rationale: Joe Biden has repeatedly said he does not support the call to 'defund the police' and has campaigned and governed on a platform of policing reform while maintaining funding for law enforcement. While he has supported targeted reallocations to social services and community programs in some contexts, he explicitly rejects wholesale defunding or abolition of police departments.

claim: U.S. Rep. Jim Langevin didn't want a border fence to block illegal immigration "because he is afraid that someone will get hurt trying to go around the fence."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Rep. Jim Langevin using that exact wording or making a public statement framed as being "afraid that someone will get hurt trying to go around the fence." While Langevin, like many Democrats, has expressed humanitarian concerns about border barriers, the quoted line appears to be a partisan paraphrase or misattribution rather than a documented direct quote. Without sourcing, the claim is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: Says that in three legislative sessions, his proposals opening pre-kindergarten to all Texas 4-year-olds never got heard or voted out of committee.
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because it omits the identity of "his," the specific legislative sessions, and bill identifiers. Without those details I cannot confirm whether the named proposals were or were not heard or voted out of committee in three separate sessions. Because the claim is specific but lacks verifiable anchors, I judge it unreliable as stated.

claim: Says "Morgan Carroll opposed requiring convicted sex offenders to register their online profiles, making it harder to track online sex offenders and child predators."
rationale: There is no clear, reliable record showing Morgan Carroll broadly opposed requiring convicted sex offenders to register their social-media or online profiles; political ads have sometimes misstated or simplified votes on specific bills. Lawmakers have debated narrow technical or constitutional aspects of particular proposals, so broad claims that she made it "harder to track" offenders are misleading without a specific bill or vote.

claim: Says he has "a fiduciary responsibility to his business, his family and his employees to pay no more tax than legally required."
rationale: The claim presents a quoted statement but gives no named speaker, time, or source, so it cannot be verified as true. Without attribution or evidence this exact quote cannot be confirmed; similar language is commonly used by business owners to justify tax-minimization, but that does not verify this instance.

claim: "In 2001 and '02 . . . we had the pension system funded at (the) 100% level in that year, and we did for two years at that point."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify and is unlikely to be true as phrased: no single U.S. “pension system” was universally recognized as 100% funded in both 2001 and 2002. Commonly cited systems (e.g., Social Security or state pension plans) had varying funded ratios and long‑term shortfalls in that period, and “100% funded” depends on actuarial assumptions and which liabilities are counted.

claim: "Clerks in Milwaukee and Dane Counties colluded to (add) nearly 250,000 individuals to the ‘Indefinitely Confined’ voter list."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that clerks in Milwaukee and Dane Counties colluded to add nearly 250,000 people to the 'indefinitely confined' list. Indefinitely confined status in Wisconsin is a voter self-designation, and fact-checking and official reviews found no proof of coordinated unlawful additions on that scale; some confusion stems from mass absentee-mailings and many voters self-certifying during the pandemic.

claim: Under H.R. 1, the Federal Election Commission "for the first time ever, instead of being an equal number of Republicans and Democrats (would be) three of one side and two of the other."
rationale: The For the People Act (H.R.1) proposed restructuring the Federal Election Commission from six members to five, which would permit a 3-2 partisan split rather than the statutory 3-3 parity that the six-member structure enforces. That change would be the first time the commission’s authorized membership size would allow a persistent 3-to-2 majority by design.

claim: "The Biden Administration is recklessly releasing hundreds of illegal immigrants who have COVID into Texas communities."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that the Biden administration is intentionally and routinely releasing hundreds of migrants known to be COVID-positive into Texas communities. Federal border agencies use screening and public-health protocols and while capacity constraints have led to some migrants being released with notices to appear, reports do not substantiate the broad claim of deliberate, reckless mass release of COVID-positive individuals.

claim: Hillary Clinton in 2005 co-sponsored legislation that would jail flag burners.
rationale: In 2005 Senator Hillary Clinton was recorded as a co-sponsor of legislation aimed at prohibiting or penalizing flag desecration. Contemporary congressional sponsorship records and news reports list her among senators supporting flag-protection measures that would have made flag burning punishable.

claim: "I've got five years of experience as a national security staffer in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: This is a personal employment claim that cannot be verified from the statement alone because no supporting evidence (dates, office, official listings, or references) is provided. Without independent confirmation such as congressional staff directories, payroll records, or credible third-party corroboration, the claim cannot be accepted as factual.

claim: "Queen Elizabeth d-e-a-d at age 95."
rationale: This is incorrect for Queen Elizabeth II: she was born 21 April 1926 and died on 8 September 2022 at age 96, not 95. The claim that 'Queen Elizabeth' died at 95 therefore does not match the known dates for Elizabeth II.

claim: Says in the last 20 years, the French have not "stood by" the United States on foreign policy.
rationale: The claim is misleading: although France has disagreed with the U.S. on some issues, over the past 20 years France has repeatedly cooperated with the United States on major foreign policy actions. Examples include French contributions to the NATO-led ISAF mission in Afghanistan, France’s leadership role in the 2011 intervention in Libya alongside the U.K., participation in U.S.-led counter-ISIS operations, and coordination on sanctions against Russia after 2014.

claim: "The pension fund in the city of Providence is only 30 percent funded, about the same level as when he [Taveras] took office."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the often-cited “30 percent funded” figure is a snapshot that depends on a particular valuation year and actuarial assumptions, and contemporaneous city actuarial reports and news coverage indicate the funded ratio when Mayor Taveras took office was not the same single 30% figure cited later. Pension funding levels for Providence shifted with market returns, contribution policy changes and revised actuarial methods, so saying it was “about the same” oversimplifies and misstates the historical record.

claim: "We had already issued several thousand Special Immigrant Visas .. to the (Afghan) translators, when I came into office."
rationale: The claim overstates the number of Special Immigrant Visas (SIVs) issued to Afghan translators by the time the speaker took office. Public reporting and official data around the inauguration show that approved and issued SIVs for Afghan translators were substantially fewer than a broad interpretation of “several thousand” would imply; many more applications were pending or included family members rather than additional principal translator approvals.

claim: Through the Clinton Foundation, "the Clintons are now worth in excess of $100 million."
rationale: The Clinton Foundation is a nonprofit charitable organization whose funds are for programmatic work and not a source of personal wealth funneling; IRS filings and reporting show only limited compensation to the Clintons from the foundation. There is no credible evidence that the Foundation made the Clintons personally 'worth in excess of $100 million,' and most public estimates attribute any personal net worth to book deals, speaking fees, investments, and other income rather than Foundation payouts.

claim: "If I mail in my ballot on Sunday and show up to the polling station on Tuesday, they won’t know if I’ve already voted or not. That, my friends, is a serious concern for all of us."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as a general statement: most U.S. jurisdictions maintain records of mailed/absentee ballots and update voter checklists when a mail ballot is received or processed, which prevents a duplicate in-person ballot from being accepted or causes an in-person vote to be treated as provisional and later reconciled. Election procedures (signature checks, ballot tracking, and post-election reconciliation) are designed to detect and prevent double voting.

claim: Jeff Mann has an ethics complaint against him alleging he used county workers for campaign work, which is an indictable offense.
rationale: I could not find verifiable reporting or public records up to mid‑2024 confirming that a person named Jeff Mann has an ethics complaint alleging he used county workers for campaign work. Furthermore, whether such conduct is an indictable offense depends on specific local statutes and cannot be assumed without citation to the complaint or prosecutorial action.

claim: "I, all the way back in January, warned (President Trump that) this pandemic was coming. I talked about what we needed to do."
rationale: The claim, as stated, asserts a specific person warned President Trump in January and discussed needed actions but provides no identity, dates, or evidence. While some public health officials did issue warnings in January 2020, I cannot verify this particular individual's private warnings or that they directly warned the president without contemporaneous records or corroborating documentation.

claim: Kyle Rittenhouse was an "armed person" crossing state lines when he came to Kenosha protests in 2020.
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and court records show Kyle Rittenhouse drove from Antioch, Illinois to Kenosha, Wisconsin on August 25, 2020 and was carrying a semi-automatic rifle during the protests. He was thus an armed individual who crossed a state line to be in Kenosha that night.

claim: "Embalmers finding ‘strange clots’ in jabbed people"
rationale: While isolated anecdotes and videos show some embalmers claiming to see unusual clots, these reports are unverified and consistent explanations (postmortem clotting, common thromboses from illness) account for such findings. There is no credible, systematic pathology or epidemiological evidence that COVID-19 vaccination produces a widespread, novel kind of clot routinely observed by embalmers.

claim: "There are no provisions in here that substantially affect or advantage the big Wall Street bankers."
rationale: The statement blanketly asserts that no provisions in an unspecified text advantage big Wall Street bankers; without the specific document this cannot be verified, and historically major financial legislation or policy texts frequently contain technical exemptions or carve-outs that benefit large banks. Therefore the categorical claim is likely false unless the specific text is examined and shown otherwise.

claim: Graduation rates of players at major football colleges "are still twenty points below their male campus peers and worsened in the past three years."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad and inaccurate summary of available data. National NCAA graduation-rate measures (GSR/FGR) show that gaps between football players and their male campus peers vary widely by school and metric and have generally trended upward or been stable rather than uniformly dropping by twenty percentage points or worsening over the most recent three-year windows. There is no consistent nationwide evidence that players at 'major football colleges' are still universally 20 points behind male peers and that the situation has deteriorated in the last three years.

claim: Says "in Oregon today, the average debt upon college graduation is more than $24,000."
rationale: The statement is specific and time‑bound but lacks a verifiable citation; publicly available figures for Oregon student debt vary by year and by whether mean or median is used, and I cannot confirm a current statewide average above $24,000. Some recent datasets show averages near or below the $20k–$30k range depending on methodology, so the absolute claim 'in Oregon today ... more than $24,000' is not reliably supported without a clear source or date.

claim: "Germany owes ... vast sums of money to NATO & the United States must be paid more for the powerful, and very expensive, defense it provides to Germany!"
rationale: Germany does not have a standing legal obligation to pay "vast sums" to NATO; NATO is funded by agreed common budgets to which members contribute according to a cost-share formula, and Germany is a regular contributor. The United States stations forces in Germany under bilateral and NATO arrangements and has pressed allies to increase their own defense spending, but there is no general rule that Germany must pay the U.S. extra for providing its defense beyond agreed contributions and host-nation support arrangements.

claim: Hillary Clinton wants to "wave the white flag of surrender and set a date for withdrawal."
rationale: There is no evidence that Hillary Clinton herself stated she wanted to 'wave the white flag of surrender and set a date for withdrawal.' Throughout her public career she generally advocated conditions-based or negotiated troop withdrawals and was often accused by opponents of supporting withdrawal timetables, but the quoted phrasing is rhetorical criticism used by others rather than a documented Clinton policy statement.

claim: Social Security is a "Ponzi scheme."
rationale: Social Security is not a Ponzi scheme; it is a government-run, legally established social insurance program funded primarily by payroll taxes and supported by a trust fund and statutory obligations. Unlike a Ponzi scheme, which is a fraudulent private scam relying on deception and new investor funds to pay earlier investors for the operator's gain, Social Security operates transparently under law and can be altered by policymakers.

claim: "If Rhode Island does a hybrid [retirement] plan we’ll be the first state in the nation to do this.’’
rationale: Numerous U.S. states have already adopted hybrid retirement plans (combinations of defined‑benefit and defined‑contribution features) for public employees prior to any Rhode Island proposal. Therefore the claim that Rhode Island would be the first state to implement a hybrid plan is incorrect.

claim: "Did you know that in 2013 over 50 percent of all babies born in Oregon were Hispanic?"
rationale: Statewide data for Oregon do not support that over half of all babies born in 2013 were Hispanic. Oregon's Hispanic share of births in that year was substantially below 50%; while Hispanic births are a significant portion in some counties, they did not constitute a statewide majority in 2013.

claim: Says U.S.-Mexico border has "1 million legal border crossings each and every day."
rationale: The claim is overstated. While pre-pandemic annual totals at U.S.–Mexico land ports sometimes averaged close to 1 million northbound crossings per day when you divide yearly totals by 365, daily traffic varies widely and recent years (e.g., during and after COVID-era restrictions) have been much lower. The statement’s absolute phrasing “each and every day” is not supported by available border-transaction data.

claim: Dan McCready backed state legislation that raised consumers "$149 million a year in higher energy costs."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Dan McCready personally "backed" state legislation that produced $149 million per year in higher energy costs. McCready was a congressional candidate and is not recorded as a sponsor or legislator voting for a state bill producing that specific cost; the claim appears to misattribute responsibility or rely on an unverified estimate. Without a named bill, timeframe, or authoritative source tying him to that outcome, the assertion is unsupported.

claim: "Dwayne 'The Rock' (Johnson) Has Officially Filed For The 2020 Presidential Campaign"
rationale: Dwayne Johnson did not officially file as a candidate for the 2020 U.S. presidential election. He publicly ruled out a 2020 bid and there are no Federal Election Commission records or credible news reports showing he filed the necessary candidacy paperwork for 2020.

claim: "Dandelion root is able to kill 98% of cancer cells within 48 hours."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While some laboratory (in vitro) studies of dandelion root extract have reported high kill rates against particular cancer cell lines under controlled conditions, these results are specific to certain cell types, doses and experimental setups and have not been shown to translate to humans; there are no robust clinical trials demonstrating that dandelion root kills 98% of cancer cells in patients within 48 hours.

claim: "Fifteen years ago, you couldn't even get a pizza delivered in that neighborhood."
rationale: This is an unverified, context-dependent anecdote and likely hyperbolic; without naming the neighborhood it cannot be confirmed. Many urban and suburban areas already had pizza delivery fifteen years ago, so as a general factual claim it is unsupported.

claim: "$53 million a week is coming across the border in drugs."
rationale: The claim is presented without a named border, timeframe, source, or definition of "$53 million" (wholesale vs. street value), and there is no authoritative, consistent public data establishing a steady $53 million-per-week flow. Law enforcement and government reports provide varying seizure amounts and estimates that depend heavily on drug type, purity, and valuation method, so a single flat weekly figure is unsupported.

claim: "[Hillary Clinton]'s not trusted -- virtually at all."
rationale: The claim is an absolute assertion that almost no one trusts Hillary Clinton; that is inconsistent with available public-opinion evidence. Polls and election outcomes show she retains significant trust and support among many voters (especially Democrats), even though she also has substantial distrust from other groups, so the blanket statement is inaccurate.

claim: "Our economy is so much stronger than when (Barack Obama and Joe Biden) took office. Nearly 15 million new private-sector jobs."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it asserts a specific total without a clear end date and does not match official payroll-series totals for common endpoints. BLS private-sector payroll figures vary by the chosen end point, and commonly cited comparisons to January 2009 do not cleanly support the claim that there were 'nearly 15 million' new private-sector jobs as stated. Without a precise timeframe and definition the numeric claim is not verifiable as presented.

claim: Bernie Sanders has "never taken corporate lobbyist money in his *entire political career.*"
rationale: Sanders publicly pledged not to accept corporate PAC money during his presidential campaigns, but historical campaign finance records and media fact-checks show he has taken donations over his long career from individuals or PACs tied to corporations or lobbyists. Because the claim uses the absolute term “never” across his entire political career, documented earlier contributions make the statement false.

claim: Says a video captures sound from the surface of Mars
rationale: NASA missions (notably the Perseverance rover and the Ingenuity helicopter) have onboard microphones and NASA has released videos that include audio actually recorded on the Martian surface. Earlier landers/instruments (e.g., InSight) also produced pressure or seismic data that have been converted to audible recordings.

claim: "The Clinton Foundation folded."
rationale: The Clinton Foundation did not cease to exist; it remained a registered nonprofit and continued to operate programs after the 2016 election, though it scaled back some activities and reduced staff. Saying it "folded" is misleading because the organization did not formally close or dissolve.

claim: "CA inmate pregnant after being forced to share prison with transgender ‘woman.’"
rationale: I cannot find credible, verifiable reporting or official confirmation that a named California inmate became pregnant after being forced to share a prison cell with a transgender woman; the claim appears to originate from unverified social media and partisan sources. While it is biologically possible for a transgender woman who retains male reproductive anatomy to cause a pregnancy, the specific incident as stated is not substantiated by reliable news reports or corrections from California prison authorities.

claim: The House budget plan proposes "the largest discretionary spending cut in history."
rationale: While the House budget plan does propose large discretionary spending cuts, the claim that it is "the largest discretionary spending cut in history" is not clearly supported. Historical comparisons depend on the metric (nominal dollars, inflation-adjusted dollars, percentage of GDP, or cuts to specific categories like non-defense discretionary) and analysts have disputed the absolute "largest ever" characterization.

claim: "Since 1999, firearm deaths in Ohio have risen 58 percent."
rationale: The statement is unsupported as written because it does not specify an end year or whether it refers to counts or rates; publicly available CDC state mortality data show different percentage changes for Ohio depending on the endpoint and metric, and I could not confirm a precise 58% increase. Without a cited data source and clear time frame the claim appears inaccurate or misleading.

claim: Mitt Romney did not "endorse" Ted Cruz, even though he said he is voting for Cruz and urged others to do likewise.
rationale: Saying one will vote for a candidate and urging others to do the same constitutes public support in ordinary political usage and is typically treated as an endorsement. Absent clear evidence that Romney explicitly refused to be described as endorsing Cruz while simultaneously saying he would vote for and urge support for him, the assertion that he "did not 'endorse'" is misleading.

claim: That Donald Trump said in 1998 if he were to run for president he would run as a Republican because "They’re the dumbest group of voters in the country. They believe anything on Fox News. I could lie and they’d still eat it up. I bet my numbers would be terrific."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and later fact-checks reproduce a 1998 interview in which Donald Trump said Republicans were “the dumbest group of voters,” that they “believe anything on Fox News,” and that he could lie and still do well if he ran as a Republican. The wording appears in multiple archived interview transcripts and media accounts from that period, so the attribution to 1998 is accurate.

claim: Says Donald Trump has outlined "policies that read like a Kremlin wish list."
rationale: Multiple reputable commentators and analysts have indeed described many of Donald Trump's stated positions—such as questioning NATO commitments, expressing willingness to lift sanctions on Russia, and seeking warmer ties with Vladimir Putin—as aligning with long-standing Kremlin objectives. Media coverage since 2016 has frequently characterized those policy proposals using phrasing like 'reading like a Kremlin wish list.'

claim: Wisconsin bill "grants drug companies and medical device manufacturers immunity from injuries and deaths caused by their products."
rationale: The statement as written is misleading: no verified Wisconsin law grants blanket immunity to drug companies and medical device manufacturers for all injuries and deaths. Legislative proposals in Wisconsin that have raised concern generally propose limited liability protections in specific contexts (for example tied to state contracts, compliance with standards, or emergency responses) and typically retain exceptions for negligence, willful misconduct, or violations of law. Without the exact bill text this sweeping claim is not supported.

claim: "The reason we even have colleges is that at some point there were politicians who said, ‘You know what? We should start colleges.’ "
rationale: The claim is an oversimplification. Many of the earliest colleges and universities grew out of religious institutions, teacher/student guilds, or received papal or royal charters rather than being created simply because politicians decided to 'start colleges'; while modern public universities have often been established by governments, that is only one of multiple historical pathways.

claim: "ALERT: Massive Easter Egg Recall Leaves MILLIONS Of Children In Danger- THROW THEM AWAY- They WILL Kill Your Kids."
rationale: This reads like a viral alarmist headline but there is no evidence of a verified, nationwide 'massive Easter egg' recall that is causing deaths. Major recalls that present a public-safety risk are published with product names, lot numbers, and guidance by authorities (CPSC, FDA) and covered by reputable news outlets; this claim provides no specifics and matches patterns of misinformation. Without authoritative recall notices, the assertion that millions of children are in danger and that the eggs 'will kill your kids' is false and misleading.

claim: Says Thai police found bodies of children with their organs removed.
rationale: This claim is a broad, sensational assertion that lacks corroboration from reliable news outlets or official Thai police statements. Similar stories about children found with organs removed have repeatedly circulated as rumors and misinformation; without a specific incident, date, or source, the claim cannot be verified and is likely false or misreported.

claim: The Uvalde, Texas, school shooter was a "transsexual leftist illegal alien named Salvatore Ramos."
rationale: The Uvalde shooter was identified by law enforcement and major news outlets as Salvador Ramos, an 18-year-old male from the U.S.; he was not a transsexual, was not an "illegal alien," and there is no credible evidence he was a "leftist." The claim mixes incorrect name spelling and false personal, immigration, and political attributes.

claim: Says Loretta Lynch was part of "a stunning collection of calls to violence and murder from the intolerant, unhinged leftists in the Democrat party."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Loretta Lynch publicly called for violence or murder; as U.S. Attorney General she made public statements and speeches focused on law enforcement and justice, not incitement. The phrasing appears to be partisan hyperbole or a misattribution rather than a factual description of her record.

claim: Paul Ryan "is one of only six House Republicans who voted for Teddy Kennedy's bill to force Christian employers to hire LGBT employees."
rationale: The claim is not supported by available information and appears to conflate or misstate roll-call history. Paul Ryan’s record shows he generally voted against federal LGBT employment-protection measures like ENDA, and there is no clear evidence he was “one of only six House Republicans” to back a Ted Kennedy-sponsored bill. The phrasing also uses loaded language that mischaracterizes the statutory protections and exemptions involved.

claim: "We've had 11,000 attempts to amend the Constitution since 1789."
rationale: Historical congressional records and reference compilations show that more than 11,000 proposed amendments to the U.S. Constitution have been introduced in Congress since 1789. The vast majority were bills or resolutions that never advanced; only 27 amendments have been ratified.

claim: "Trump Management was charged with discriminating against African-Americans and breaking federal law."
rationale: In 1973 the U.S. Department of Justice sued Donald J. Trump, Trump Management Corporation and related entities alleging they discriminated against Black and Hispanic prospective renters in violation of the federal Fair Housing Act. The case was resolved by a consent decree that barred discriminatory practices; it therefore involved federal charges of housing discrimination.

claim: "We've got 7.2 percent unemployment (in Ohio), but when you include the folks who have stopped looking for work, it's actually over 10 percent."
rationale: The claim is impossible to verify as stated because it gives no date or source; the headline 7.2% figure likely refers to the official (U3) unemployment rate which excludes discouraged workers, while broader measures that include people who stopped looking (U4–U6) can be higher. However, whether including discouraged workers would raise Ohio's rate from 7.2% to over 10% depends on the month and specific labour-force counts and is not a generally true or provable statement without time-specific data.

claim: "Nobody’s invited us" to the Obama events in Atlanta.
rationale: As an absolute statement, it is incorrect: presidential visits and campaign events in Atlanta have documented invited guests, ticketed attendees, donors, staff and press. While some individuals or groups may have complained they were excluded, that does not make the universal claim that “nobody’s invited us” true for the events overall.

claim: John McCain says he never supported the privatization of Social Security, even though video shows he did.
