Whether Biden’s 100-day rating was unusually low depends on which poll and exact timing is used, but it is not the single lowest in American history.

claim: "In the 2000 Florida election, at least 1,100 eligible voters were wrongly dropped from voting rolls in an attempt to purge a list of felons. Many of those who were dropped showed up to vote and were told they could not."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and subsequent investigations of Florida’s 2000 felon-purge effort found that lists contained numerous errors and at least about 1,100 registered voters (and by many counts several thousand) were wrongly flagged or removed. Many of those whose names were on the purge lists showed up on Election Day and were initially denied the ability to vote or faced challenges before being reinstated in some cases.

claim: "Actor Tom Hanks has passed away age 63."
rationale: This claim is false. Tom Hanks, born July 9, 1956, is alive and there are no credible reports that he died at age 63. Reliable news outlets and public records have not reported his death.

claim: Says Austin Mayor Steve Adler’s transportation plans linked to Proposition 1 on the ballot remove "27+ miles of traffic lanes around the city," replacing "them with lanes dedicated to usage by bicycles" and buses.
rationale: The claim misstates the scope of the Proposition 1–linked proposals. Austin bond and transportation plans associated with Prop 1 funded specific corridor projects, bike lanes and transit improvements and allowed some lane reconfigurations (road diets) on particular streets, but they did not mandate removing more than 27 miles of traffic lanes citywide and wholesale converting them into bicycle- and bus-only lanes.

claim: "In an interview with the Chicago Tribune's Editorial Board, Comptroller Leslie Munger says that in order to balance a budget, the state would have to 'cut social services completely.'"
rationale: I cannot confirm that Leslie Munger used the exact phrase 'cut social services completely' in that Chicago Tribune Editorial Board interview. Contemporary reporting notes she warned that deep cuts to social services might be necessary to balance Illinois's budget, but I find no definitive primary-source evidence of the precise quoted wording.

claim: "Beachgoers trash Florida beaches with 13,000 pounds of litter after beaches reopen."
rationale: I cannot verify a credible, specific statewide figure that beachgoers left exactly 13,000 pounds of litter after Florida beaches reopened. The claim is vague about time period and location and appears to conflate or exaggerate isolated cleanup totals reported in some local news stories. Without a reliable source attributing that exact total to all Florida beaches after reopening, the claim is not supported.

claim: "It was allowed," referring to her email practices.
rationale: If the claim refers to Hillary Clinton’s exclusive use of a private email server for official State Department business, it is misleading to say ‘it was allowed.’ State Department rules required official business to be conducted on government systems and records to be preserved; using a private server without proper approvals violated records-management and security policies. Investigations (State Department Inspector General and the FBI) found the arrangement improper — the FBI called it 'extremely careless' — even though prosecutors declined criminal charges.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "voted against the Brady Bill five times for background checks on people."
rationale: This statement is inaccurate. Public roll-call records and contemporary fact-checking show Sanders did not cast five distinct votes against the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act itself; claims counting multiple related amendments or procedural votes conflate different items to reach the number five.

claim: "During his 18-year Senate career, (Russ Feingold) supported judges who voted to deny your individual Second Amendment right. … (He) promises to protect those rights, but that's not what his record shows."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsubstantiated: while Russ Feingold served in the Senate from 1993–2011 and did vote on many judicial nominations, the statement names no specific judges or confirmation votes showing he supported nominees who explicitly voted to deny an individual Second Amendment right. Second Amendment doctrine also changed with DC v. Heller (2008), so many pre-Heller judicial rulings treated the right differently. Without concrete examples linking Feingold’s votes to particular judges who authored such rulings, the broad accusation cannot be verified.

claim: Every former North Carolina governor opposes "constitutional amendments Raleigh lawmakers put on the ballot this fall."
rationale: The claim asserts unanimous opposition among all former North Carolina governors, which is extremely unlikely and not supported by available evidence. Former governors are a diverse group with differing views, and there is no documented record showing every single former governor opposed those specific constitutional amendments. Without explicit, verifiable statements from every former governor, the universal claim fails.

claim: Rhode Island "charter schools are nationally recognized as outperforming their counterparts across the country."
rationale: There is no broad national consensus that Rhode Island charter schools as a group outperform their counterparts across the country. National research (e.g., large-scale CREDO analyses) finds highly mixed charter results that vary by state, network, and individual school; while some Rhode Island charters have strong local outcomes, that does not support the sweeping claim of national outperformance.

claim: "Our real unemployment is anywhere from 18 to 20 percent. Don't believe the 5.6. Don't believe it."
rationale: The statement overstates commonly used broader measures of unemployment. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports U-3 (official) and U-6 (broader) series; when U-3 was about 5.6, U-6 was roughly around 10–11%, not 18–20%. Only during the acute COVID shock did U-6 exceed 18% (April 2020), so without a specific timeframe or definition the 18–20% claim is unsupported.

claim: There are "49 different federal job training programs that report to eight agencies."
rationale: Counts of federal job-training programs and the number of agencies that oversee them vary by source and over time; while government reviews (e.g., GAO/CRS analyses) have reported similar totals (around the mid-to-high 40s), the precise phrase '49 programs that report to eight agencies' is not a stable, consistently supported fact. Differences arise from how programs are defined, grouped, and from program changes over time.

claim: "You're more likely to be the victim of a violent crime in Milwaukee than in 96 percent of the country."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and likely false as phrased. Milwaukee does have a substantially higher violent-crime rate than the national average and often ranks among the higher-rate large U.S. cities, but whether it exceeds 96% of all U.S. jurisdictions depends on the year, dataset (city vs county vs neighborhood), and methodology; most standard FBI and crime-rate rankings do not consistently place Milwaukee above 96% of all places.

claim: Says that shutdowns are "ineffective" and that we now know that COVID-19 is not commonly spread "by someone going to work."
rationale: Characterizing shutdowns as categorically 'ineffective' contradicts multiple epidemiological studies and meta-analyses showing that timely stay-at-home orders, business closures, and other nonpharmaceutical interventions reduced SARS‑CoV‑2 transmission and deaths, though their effectiveness varied by timing and implementation. Likewise, outbreak investigations and contact-tracing have repeatedly identified workplaces—particularly indoor, crowded, or poorly ventilated settings—as important sites of transmission, so the blanket claim that COVID‑19 is not commonly spread by someone 'going to work' is incorrect.

claim: The FBI lost Hunter Biden’s laptop.
rationale: There is no credible, authoritative evidence that the FBI 'lost' Hunter Biden’s laptop. Reporting and official statements indicate the repair-shop owner provided the device or a copy to the FBI in late 2019 and the bureau retained forensic images and related files; while provenance and chain-of-custody have been contested, no verified source shows the FBI misplaced the physical laptop.

claim: Says Oregon’s highest income tax bracket included anyone making more than $250,000 in 2012 before the state expanded its upper bracket to include "anyone making more than $125,000."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: Oregon’s 2012 top marginal tax thresholds were not a single uniform “over $250,000” cutoff for all filers, and later changes did not simply expand the top bracket to “anyone making more than $125,000” in the way described. State brackets vary by filing status and Oregon’s subsequent tax adjustments introduced new brackets and rates with specific thresholds and timing, so the claim conflates and misstates those figures.

claim: Says Congress gave Wall Street "trillions of dollars of zero interest loans."
rationale: The statement is misleading: Congress did authorize large rescue programs (e.g., TARP in 2008 and CARES-related authorities in 2020) and the Federal Reserve created lending facilities for markets and banks, but it did not give Wall Street 'trillions of dollars of zero interest loans.' The actual programs involved loans with rates, collateral requirements, Treasury backstops or equity injections, and the amounts actually lent were typically less than headline authorizations.

claim: Says Sen. Rand Paul’s 2011 budget "included a big cut in the CDC."
rationale: There is no clear record that Sen. Rand Paul authored a 2011 federal budget that included a large, specific cut to the CDC. He supported broad spending reductions and targeted amendments during that period, but reputable fact-checking and budget records do not support the claim that his 2011 budget proposal included a notable, standalone “big cut” to the CDC.

claim: Kohl’s Department Stores in 2012 "announced the creation of 3,000 new jobs."
rationale: I am not aware of a credible 2012 Kohl’s press release or major news report stating the company announced creation of exactly 3,000 new jobs; retail hiring announcements that year typically referenced different (often larger or seasonal) headcounts or were tied to specific store openings. The claim appears either to misstate the number, the timeframe, or confuses temporary/seasonal positions with permanent jobs.

claim: Says he was the first person to call for invoking the Defense Production Act.
rationale: The claim as written is ambiguous because it does not name who 'he' is or specify a date or context, so it cannot be verified. In most high-profile cases (for example during COVID-19) multiple officials and commentators urged invoking the Defense Production Act and several people have claimed priority, making a blanket 'first' claim unlikely without precise evidence.

claim: "There have been 30 published polls in this election cycle and Harry Reid's been trailing in every single one."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no timeframe, jurisdiction, or source list; polling records for any competitive Senate or other race almost always vary across firms and dates, so an unbroken string of 30 polls all showing Reid trailing is highly unlikely. Without a specific election cycle, date range, or poll roster, the assertion cannot be substantiated.

claim: "Joe Biden just confirmed that he is running for president in 2020 and it has America applauding!"
rationale: The claim is false because Joe Biden did not 'just' confirm a 2020 run; he announced his 2020 presidential campaign in April 2019 and the 2020 election concluded with Biden winning and being inaugurated in January 2021. The added claim that 'it has America applauding' is a subjective, unquantified assertion and not a verifiable factual outcome.

claim: Says Barack Obama "founded ISIS. I would say the co-founder would be crooked Hillary Clinton."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Barack Obama 'founded' ISIS, nor that Hillary Clinton was a co-founder. ISIS traces its roots to al-Qaeda in Iraq, leaders like Abu Musab al‑Zarqawi and later Abu Bakr al‑Baghdadi, and emerged from regional sectarian conflict and post‑2003 destabilization, with its formal rise in 2013–2014.

claim: Says a poll showed Democrat Beto O’Rourke within 2 percentage points of Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.
rationale: During the 2018 Texas Senate campaign several reputable polls at different points showed Beto O’Rourke within a couple of percentage points of Ted Cruz. While results varied by pollster and date, at least one widely reported survey in the closing weeks showed the margin at or around 1–2 points.

claim: "You couldn’t buy a cannon when, in fact, the Second Amendment passed."
rationale: There was no blanket prohibition on purchasing artillery when the Second Amendment was ratified in 1791; militias and some private individuals owned and acquired cannons during and after the Revolutionary era. Cannons were expensive and often controlled by militias or governments, but that is not the same as being impossible to buy.

claim: Says TikTok found Cassie Compton, who has been missing from Arkansas since 2014.
rationale: There is no corroborating reporting from law enforcement or reputable news outlets that TikTok users located Cassie Compton, who was reported missing from Arkansas in 2014. Viral social-media claims of 'finding' missing people frequently circulate without verification, and an official recovery would normally be confirmed by police or major media.

claim: "If a statue of a person in the park on a horse has both front legs in the air, the person died in battle. If the horse has one front leg in the air, the person died as a result of wounds received in battle. If the horse has all four legs on the ground, the person died of natural causes."
rationale: This “hoof-code” is a widely repeated myth, not a consistent rule used by sculptors or monuments. Horse poses are chosen for artistic, structural, or local symbolic reasons and many well-known statues contradict the purported code.

claim: Countries were exporting COVID-19 "diagnostic test instruments" in 2018.
rationale: SARS‑CoV‑2 (the virus that causes COVID‑19) was not identified until late 2019, so instruments labeled specifically as COVID‑19 diagnostic tests could not have been produced and exported in 2018. It is true, however, that general diagnostic instruments (PCR machines, immunoassay analyzers, and test kits for other pathogens) were manufactured and traded before 2019, and mislabeling or retrospective categorization of customs data has caused confusion.

claim: "Since Barack Obama became president of the United States, 95 percent of economic gains have been made by the richest 1 percent."
rationale: The statement is an oversimplification that mixes timeframes and measures. Some analyses of pre-tax income growth during the early part of the recovery (roughly 2009–2012) found that a very large share of income gains accrued to the top 1 percent, but that specific 95% figure depends on the exact years and whether you measure pre-tax market income, after-tax income, or wealth. Over the entirety of Obama’s two terms and using broader measures, the distribution of gains is different and does not conclusively support the blanket 95% claim.

claim: "If you printed a $1 bill for the entirety of the $14.1 trillion national debt, the resulting pile of money would weigh more than 136 aircraft carriers."
rationale: A US bill weighs about 1 gram, so $14.1 trillion in $1 bills would weigh ~14.1 trillion grams (14.1 million metric tonnes). A Nimitz‑class aircraft carrier displaces roughly 100,000–102,000 metric tonnes, so the pile would be on the order of 138–141 carriers, which is greater than 136.

claim: The novel coronavirus was "man-made."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that SARS-CoV-2 was deliberately engineered; multiple genomic analyses find features consistent with natural evolution and zoonotic spillover. Although a lab-accident hypothesis has been investigated by some, investigators and public-health agencies have not produced verifiable evidence that the virus was man-made.

claim: "We had 6,000 oil and gas spills in 2012" with "more oil and gas spreading in the United States than the entire Exxon Valdez spill."
rationale: This specific claim is not verifiable as stated. While thousands of small oil and gas incidents are reported in the U.S. each year, there is no consolidated, authoritative federal tally showing exactly 6,000 spills in 2012 or that their combined volume exceeded the Exxon Valdez spill (~11 million gallons). State reporting practices, definitions of “spill,” and incident volumes vary widely, so the precise numbers in the claim are unsupported without a cited source.

claim: Since 2009, "after-tax incomes are up nearly 14 percent."
rationale: The claim is underspecified — it gives no country, end date, or whether ‘after‑tax incomes’ are measured in nominal or real terms, and whether it refers to mean or median household/individual income. After‑tax income growth since 2009 varies substantially by country, by whether taxes/transfers are included, and by whether values are inflation‑adjusted, so a blanket statement that they are “up nearly 14 percent” cannot be verified and is likely misleading without that context. Because the claim lacks key parameters it cannot be treated as a factual universal statement.

claim: Huckabee "was one of the highest taxing governors that we had in this country and rivaling Bill Clinton in terms of the Cato ratings."
rationale: The claim overstates the case. Cato’s Fiscal Report Card does score governors on taxes and Huckabee received mixed/below‑average scores on fiscal measures, but he was not consistently listed as one of the very highest‑taxing governors nationwide nor clearly “rivaling” Bill Clinton in Cato’s rankings. The statement is vague about timeframe and comparison metrics and exaggerates what the Cato ratings show.

claim: The Department of Homeland Security’s database of legal immigrants has "never" been "bounced against a state’s voter rolls."
rationale: The absolute claim that DHS immigration databases have "never" been checked against state voter rolls is incorrect. State election officials have in multiple instances used federal immigration-verification resources (such as DHS/USCIS verification systems) to screen or investigate voter registrations, so blanket "never" is not supported.

claim: Six states "decided to stop counting" votes as Donald Trump was "headed for a win" on election night.
rationale: No state unilaterally 'decided to stop counting' votes because Donald Trump was ahead; official counting continued under state and local election rules. Some local jurisdictions paused processing overnight (e.g., because polls had closed, staff left, or law restricts when certain ballots can be processed), but these routine pauses are not equivalent to states halting counts to affect outcomes.

claim: On financial reform, there is "a million dollars being spent, per congressman, in lobbying expenses on this issue. (The) industry has four lobbyists per member of the House and Senate working on this."
rationale: The claim gives precise per-member figures without a stated timeframe or source. While the financial industry did spend hundreds of millions on lobbying around major financial reform efforts and employed many lobbyists, independent counts and reporting do not consistently support a uniform $1,000,000 spent per member of Congress or exactly four lobbyists per member; totals and ratios vary by year, scope, and counting method and are typically lower when narrowly limited to a single issue.

claim: The Affordable Care Act "will likely go down as the biggest tax increase in history."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did include new taxes and revenue provisions (higher Medicare payroll tax on high earners, a net investment income tax, excise taxes on high-cost plans, and the individual mandate penalty) that raised hundreds of billions over a decade, but independent budget analyses found these were not of the scale of the largest historical U.S. tax increases. Major 20th-century tax changes tied to world wars and broad tax-code overhauls were larger in absolute and GDP-adjusted terms, so the claim that the ACA 'will likely go down as the biggest tax increase in history' is incorrect.

claim: ﻿﻿"Since Mayor Kennedy O’Brien took office Sayreville has issued 22,081 building permits! Now O’Brien is holding secret meetings with big developers."
rationale: The claim combines a very specific numeric assertion about permits and an allegation of undisclosed meetings; neither part is supported by verifiable evidence provided here. Municipal building-permit totals and meetings are public-record matters that should be confirmed from Sayreville’s official permit records or reputable local reporting, and I cannot find those sources in the claim. Absent such evidence the assertion must be treated as unverified and therefore false for fact-check purposes.

claim: Illegal immigration on the U.S.-Mexico border is "the lowest in 17 years."
rationale: The statement is misleading as written because it omits which metric (apprehensions, encounters, net illegal entries) and what exact time period is meant. Official U.S. Customs and Border Protection data and independent analyses show large year-to-year fluctuations and very high encounter counts in 2021–2022; claims that levels are the "lowest in 17 years" typically cherry-pick a particular short window or metric and do not match broad historical trends. Without specifying the measure and span, the blanket claim is not supported by the available data.

claim: "Drunk" Nancy Pelosi "was removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans."
rationale: There are no credible reports that Nancy Pelosi was intoxicated and formally removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans. Viral clips and partisan posts have mischaracterized footage or out-of-context moments, but mainstream reporting and House records show no such removal or official action for drunken behavior.

claim: Says Keene, N.H., requested a "military-grade armored personnel truck," citing their annual Pumpkin Festival as "a possible target" for terrorists.
rationale: Reporting from multiple news outlets and records of surplus-equipment requests show Keene police applied for an armored vehicle (described as military-grade) and in their justification mentioned large public events such as the annual Pumpkin Festival as potential targets. The language in the application or press coverage specifically referenced the festival when explaining the need for the vehicle.

claim: Says his plan to end the toll on Ga. 400 fulfills his campaign promise to commuters.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who “his” refers to or specify the details of the plan; whether a proposal actually fulfills a campaign promise depends on the plan’s concrete actions and outcomes. In Georgia, ending the SR 400 toll has historically required retiring bonds, statutory or contractual changes, and state action rather than a unilateral executive promise, so a mere announcement does not by itself prove the promise was fulfilled.

claim: Says he "earned the highest possible credit ratings as state treasurer."
rationale: The statement cannot be confirmed as presented because it provides no named person, state, timeframe, or which rating agencies awarded the ratings. Credit ratings are agency-specific and can change over time, so claiming someone 'earned the highest possible credit ratings as state treasurer' requires documentary evidence (e.g., AAA/Aaa/AAA from major agencies during their tenure), which is not supplied here.

claim: Elena Kagan "has published five scholarly review articles, mostly on administrative law and the First Amendment. These articles were mostly on technical and procedural issues."
rationale: I cannot confirm the precise count and characterization in the claim. Elena Kagan has authored several law-review pieces on administrative law and related constitutional topics, but the statement that she has published exactly five scholarly review articles and that they were mostly on administrative law and the First Amendment (and mostly technical/procedural) is too specific and not reliably supported by readily available bibliographic summaries. Given uncertainty about the exact number and thematic balance, the claim as stated is likely inaccurate.

claim: "For every $1 spent on mitigation, $4 in post-storm cleanup and rebuilding is saved."
rationale: This is a commonly cited, evidence-based finding: a 2005 independent study (commissioned by FEMA/NIBS) concluded that on average every $1 invested in mitigation saves about $4 in future disaster losses, including post-storm cleanup and rebuilding. However, the exact benefit varies by mitigation type, hazard, location and study methodology, and later analyses have produced different ratios for specific measures.

claim: Patrick Rose "voted to explore a state income tax."
rationale: I cannot verify that Patrick Rose explicitly "voted to explore a state income tax." The claim is vague and appears to conflate different legislative actions (e.g., procedural or study motions) with a clear vote to initiate exploration; without a specific bill, date, or roll-call, the statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: A bill to advance the Keystone XL Pipeline "is an earmark" under House rules.
rationale: Under House rules an "earmark" generally refers to a provision that directs federal funds, targeted tax or tariff benefits, or other specific financial advantages to a named recipient. A typical bill to advance Keystone XL that speeds permitting or authorizes construction does not itself appropriate federal money or confer a discrete spending/tax benefit to a named entity, so it would not meet the common House definition of an earmark.

claim: Says President Donald Trump this week will sign an executive order creating term limits for Congress.
rationale: A U.S. president cannot unilaterally create binding term limits for members of Congress by executive order; imposing term limits on Congress would require a constitutional amendment or lawful statute and cannot be achieved through executive action. Therefore a claim that the president 'will sign an executive order creating term limits for Congress' is misleading or false insofar as it implies such an order could lawfully impose congressional term limits.

claim: Says "an unchecked Democratic Majority in Trenton" is responsible for "years of diversions" from the state’s unemployment insurance trust fund.
rationale: The claim pins “years of diversions” from a state unemployment insurance trust fund solely on an “unchecked Democratic Majority in Trenton,” but public budgeting and audit records show that transfers, loans, or use of UI reserves typically involve specific legislative and executive actions over time and have occurred under both parties and different administrations. Without a defined time period and citation to particular transfers, it is incorrect to attribute multi-year diversions exclusively to a single party majority.

claim: Says House Democrats’ impeachment inquiry of President Donald Trump "doesn’t feature the opposition party, it doesn’t feature cross-examination."
rationale: The claim is misleading as an absolute. Early closed-door depositions in the 2019 inquiry were run by House Democrats and limited direct cross-examination by Republicans, but the overall inquiry did involve the opposition: Republicans had access to transcripts, offered minority views, and Republican members participated in public hearings where they questioned witnesses.

claim: Ninety pounds of cocaine was found on a boat owned by Mitch McConnell's family and that they are "financing his Senate campaigns with their cocaine drug profits."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or law-enforcement reporting that ninety pounds of cocaine were found on a boat owned by Mitch McConnell's family, nor any evidence that his Senate campaigns have been financed with drug profits. The allegation appears to originate from social media/conspiracy claims and has not been substantiated by reputable news outlets or official records.

claim: "Under the federal Controlled Substance Act, marijuana is listed in the same Schedule I as heroin," even though "marijuana is not a killer drug like heroin."
rationale: Under current federal law (the Controlled Substances Act), both marijuana (cannabis) and heroin are listed in Schedule I. Epidemiological and toxicological evidence shows heroin is associated with frequent fatal overdoses, whereas cannabis does not produce the same direct lethal overdose risk, making the comparison about lethality accurate in general terms.

claim: "There's only three countries in the entire world where there's no paid vacation by law, we happen to be one of them."
rationale: The statement that there are exactly three countries with no legally required paid vacation is not supported by reliable global data. While the United States is frequently cited as one of the very few countries without statutory paid annual leave (and is the only OECD country in that position), counts of countries lacking any paid vacation vary by definition and source and do not consistently equal three.

claim: Says Georgia’s secretary of state won’t let the people recounting ballots check the signatures for fraud.
rationale: This is misleading. Georgia law and practice assign signature verification to trained election officials during absentee-ballot processing, and recounts generally retabulate ballots that were already validated rather than redoing signature matching; private individuals or untrained recount teams are not permitted to handle ballots or perform official signature checks for chain-of-custody and legal reasons.

claim: Says the Trump administration’s new policy for legal immigrants on welfare "has been around for a while. This is not a new thing that the president is trying to implement here, that the United States has been this way."
rationale: The broad concept of a "public charge" inadmissibility standard has existed in U.S. immigration law for decades, so saying the idea "has been around for a while" is partly true. However, the Trump administration issued a 2019 rule that materially expanded how public-charge is applied by including many non-cash benefits (like Medicaid, SNAP, and housing assistance) in the assessment — a significant change from prior practice. Therefore the statement that the administration’s policy "is not a new thing" is misleading.

claim: "We have 41,000 people right now on the waitlist for financial-based assistance for our tech colleges and universities," most of them for tech schools.
rationale: The claim gives a precise number (41,000) and scope (financial-based assistance waitlist for tech colleges and universities) but provides no jurisdiction or time frame; I cannot confirm such a specific national or regional figure from general knowledge. Public financial-aid systems and institutions typically publish enrollment and aid statistics, and no widely reported dataset supports this exact claim as stated. Without a named program, region, or source, the assertion is unverified and therefore treated as false.

claim: In the past three years, state legislatures have "enacted more of these restrictions (on abortion) than in the previous 10 years combined."
rationale: Available tracking by policy researchers (e.g., the Guttmacher Institute and state legislative trackers) does not support a clear finding that the most recent three-year period produced more abortion restrictions than the prior ten years combined. While the post‑Dobbs period saw a surge in high-profile bans and new restrictions in many states, the prior decade already produced hundreds of varied restrictions (waiting periods, gestational limits, clinic regulations), and counts depend on definitions. Therefore the blanket comparative claim is not clearly supported.

claim: "Atlanta just lost 75% of its police force"
rationale: There are no credible reports or official records indicating the Atlanta Police Department suddenly lost 75% of its officers; a loss of that magnitude would be widely reported and immediately visible in municipal staffing data. While Atlanta has experienced periods of higher-than-normal attrition and staffing challenges, reported declines have been far smaller than three-quarters of the force.

claim: Says Marilinda Garcia supports "$150 billion in new taxes."
rationale: There is no credible record that Marilinda Garcia publicly endorsed "$150 billion in new taxes." Public statements and her campaign materials emphasize tax cuts and limited government, and instances alleging she backed that specific figure appear to be mischaracterizations or out-of-context claims.

claim: Under Hillary Clinton, State Department "officials were sending official thank-yous to people who gave to the Clinton Foundation."
rationale: Contemporary news investigations and released internal State Department emails show that staff under Secretary Hillary Clinton drafted and sent official thank-you or congratulatory letters to individuals and organizations that had given to the Clinton Foundation. Fact-checkers who reviewed the documents confirmed the existence of such correspondence, though they also noted that the letters were often routine and context around intent and reciprocity is disputed.

claim: Says Sam Houston opposed slavery and as governor said Texas should not leave the union over slavery.
rationale: The claim mixes a true and a false element. Sam Houston did publicly oppose Texas’ secession and as governor resisted leaving the Union in 1861, but he was a slaveholder and was not an abolitionist — his opposition to secession was political/practical rather than a principled anti-slavery stance.

claim: Says a photo shows Adam Schiff and Jeffrey Epstein.
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable photograph showing Rep. Adam Schiff with Jeffrey Epstein; images circulating online have been debunked as misidentifications or manipulations by multiple fact-checkers. Major news organizations and photographic archives have not confirmed any authentic photo of the two together.

claim: Says Pope Francis "was arrested Saturday in connection with an 80-count indictment of charges including possession of child pornography, human trafficking, incest, possession of drug paraphernalia and felony fraud."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Pope Francis was arrested on any such indictment; major international news organizations and fact-checkers have debunked viral posts making this claim. An arrest of the pope on an 80-count indictment would have prompted widespread, verifiable coverage and official statements from the Vatican and law enforcement, which do not exist.
cited_knowledge: General knowledge of international news coverage and fact-checking reports that identified this claim as a hoax; absence of any official Vatican or law-enforcement confirmation.

claim: "If anyone should know irresponsible it should be Senator Buono. She’s the one, her budget left us with a $2 billion budget deficit in fiscal 10 that I had to fix. Her mistakes. And for fiscal year 2011 an $11 billion budget deficit. Her mistakes, along with her partner Jon Corzine."
rationale: The claim misattributes precise deficit figures and sole responsibility to Senator Barbara Buono. New Jersey budget shortfalls around 2009–2011 were primarily tied to actions and revenue shortfalls during Governor Jon Corzine’s administration and the broader fiscal crisis; individual legislators do not unilaterally ‘leave’ a budget deficit. Reported gap figures from that period do not match the claim’s specific $2 billion (FY2010) and $11 billion (FY2011) attributions to Buono alone.

claim: "For every extra year that a girl stays in secondary school, her chance of getting infected with HIV/AIDS decreases by half."
rationale: This claim is an overgeneralization and not supported as a universal law. While multiple studies find that additional years of schooling for girls are associated with lower HIV risk in some settings — and some targeted interventions have produced large reductions — the effect size varies by country, age, program type and study design and is not a consistent halving of infection risk for each extra year of secondary school.

claim: "We don't know anything about Hillary in terms of religion. Now, she's been in the public eye for years and years, and yet there's no — there's nothing out there."
rationale: False — Hillary Clinton's religious background and statements are publicly known. She has identified as a Methodist and has discussed her faith in interviews, speeches, and biographical profiles over many years.

claim: Says he is the "ranking member" of the House select committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol.
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable because it does not identify who “he” is or when the statement was made. Whether someone is the committee’s ranking member depends on formal designation by the House minority and recognition by House leadership; for the Jan. 6 select committee there were disputes over GOP appointments. Without a named individual and date, the assertion cannot be confirmed and should not be treated as fact.

claim: Says Jill McCabe "supports late term abortions. Larger baby parts are more profitable."
rationale: There is no credible evidence, verified transcript, or reputable news report showing Jill McCabe said that. The phrasing resembles a fabricated or misattributed viral claim tied to disinformation about fetal tissue procurement rather than a documented statement by her.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "paid only 14 percent in taxes — probably less than you."
rationale: Romney’s released returns showed an effective federal income tax rate of about 13.9% for 2011, so the “14 percent” figure for federal income tax is essentially correct. However the claim is misleading because it omits payroll and state taxes and presents a bare federal income–tax rate as a total-tax comparison; whether that rate is “probably less than you” depends on one’s income and which taxes are counted. Fact-checkers concluded the ad’s formulation is deceptive without this context.

claim: "Iowa's Republican caucus stopped mattering years ago. It in no way determines the party nominee."
rationale: It is false to say Iowa "in no way" determines the Republican nominee. While Iowa winners do not always become nominee, the Iowa caucus — as the first major contest in many cycles — still provides early momentum, media narrative, fundraising and endorsement effects that can make or break campaigns. Its influence varies by year but it remains an important early test.

claim: Under Gov. Tom Corbett, "Pennsylvania ranks 49th in job creation."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and therefore misleading: rankings for 'job creation' depend on the time window and metric (total jobs, percent change, private-sector jobs), and Pennsylvania’s rank during Tom Corbett’s term varied by source and period. While Pennsylvania generally underperformed many states in job growth during his tenure, it was not universally or consistently ranked exactly 49th across common measures. Without a specified timeframe and metric the blanket statement is false as written.

claim: A video clip from the Notre Dame cathedral fire shows a man walking alone in a tower of the church "dressed in Muslim garb."
rationale: Contemporary fact-checks and video analysis showed the viral clip was miscaptioned and the person was not identifiable as wearing 'Muslim garb.' The footage was misrepresented — the figure appeared to be wearing protective/work clothing and there is no credible evidence the clip depicts a lone person in Muslim dress inside Notre-Dame during the fire.

claim: Insurance companies "have made a fortune with Obamacare."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. While some large insurers did see increased revenue and periods of higher profits after the Affordable Care Act was implemented, others lost money or had mixed results, and ACA rules (like medical loss ratios and subsidies) constrained profit margins. Profitability varied by company, market, and year rather than insurers uniformly “making a fortune.”

claim: Republican challenger Bill Flores "has never once voted in a general election in our district."
rationale: There is no credible evidence to support the absolute claim that Bill Flores "has never once voted in a general election in our district," and it is implausible given his long public profile and tenure as a U.S. representative. Such an absolute assertion would require checking local voter-roll and turnout records for a specified district and timeframe, which are not cited here.

claim: Millennials are "more pro-life than baby boomers and older Americans."
rationale: Major public-opinion polling over the past decade shows younger cohorts (Millennials and Gen Z) are on average more supportive of abortion rights than Baby Boomers and older Americans, not more "pro-life." Surveys from organizations such as Pew Research and Gallup consistently report higher pro-choice attitudes among younger adults compared with older age groups.

claim: Says "city leadership is threatening to lay off police and emergency services personnel to balance the budget."
rationale: The claim is unsourced and provides no identifying details (which city, when, or who in leadership). Without a named municipality and corroborating official statements, budget documents, or reputable news reporting, the assertion cannot be verified as true in its present form.

claim: Gwinnett County government has made "significant cutbacks in staffing."
rationale: I cannot find corroborating evidence in available public records or reputable local reporting up to mid-2024 that Gwinnett County implemented widespread or 'significant' staffing cutbacks. The claim is vague about timeframe and what qualifies as 'significant,' and no major layoffs or systematic reductions were widely reported.

claim: "The United States was energy independent in 2019 for the first time since 1957. In just 10 days we are sent back 50 years."
rationale: The first clause is accurate: U.S. Energy Information Administration data show the United States was a net energy exporter in 2019, the first annual net export since 1957. The second clause—"In just 10 days we are sent back 50 years"—is a vague, subjective political claim with no specified metric, event, or evidence and cannot be verified as factual.

claim: "A third of the budget for the city of Ferguson (Missouri) was being reaped by civil fines."
rationale: Contemporary investigations and reporting found that municipal fines and court fees were a substantial revenue source for Ferguson but did not constitute exactly one‑third of the city’s budget. Official DOJ findings and news analyses around 2013–2015 put the share closer to roughly a fifth to a quarter of revenue, not 33%.

claim: "Recent data showed Nevada ranks 50th in the money received from" the stimulus bill.
rationale: The claim is too vague and cannot be confirmed as stated: it does not specify which stimulus bill, which metric (total dollars vs. per‑capita), or the data source. Rankings for states vary greatly depending on whether you measure total allocations, per‑capita receipts, or specific programs within CARES or later relief packages, and I am not aware of authoritative data showing Nevada dead last (50th) across a recent stimulus measure. Without a clear bill and metric, the assertion that 'recent data showed Nevada ranks 50th' is unsupported.

claim: "President Biden says he wants to ban handguns."
rationale: President Biden has repeatedly called for stricter gun controls such as banning assault-style weapons, high-capacity magazines, universal background checks, and other measures, but he has not said he wants to ban handguns generally. Claims that he has called for a blanket handgun ban mischaracterize his stated policy priorities and public remarks.

claim: "The (health care) law does not demand that all of these cancellations go out."
rationale: While the Affordable Care Act did not literally include a line instructing insurers to mail cancellation notices, it imposed new minimum benefit and coverage standards and narrowed which plans could be 'grandfathered.' Plans that failed to meet 2014 requirements could not be sold or renewed, so many had to be discontinued — effectively forcing widespread cancellations even if the law did not use the word 'cancel.'

claim: "Congress files charges against Nancy Pelosi."
rationale: Congress as a body does not file criminal charges; criminal charges are brought by prosecutors (state or federal). The House can approve articles of impeachment for removable federal officers and can vote to expel its own members, but those are not the same as criminal charges. There is no established record of Congress having filed criminal charges against Nancy Pelosi.

claim: "Breaking: Trump fires deputy attorney general Rod Rosenstein, raising questions over Mueller’s fate."
rationale: This specific claim is inaccurate: Donald Trump did not fire Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein. Rosenstein was not removed in a sudden "breaking" action; he later left the Justice Department via resignation in 2019, and earlier reports that Trump planned to fire him were widely reported as unfulfilled rumors. While Rosenstein’s status did prompt discussion about the future of Special Counsel Mueller’s probe, the asserted immediate firing did not occur as stated.

claim: "Nationally, the unemployment rate for veterans is far greater than the national unemployment rate," and Wisconsin is "one of those rare examples where unemployment is actually lower for veterans than it is for the population as a whole and certainly lower than it is nationally."
rationale: The statement is too broad and unsupported as phrased. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show veteran unemployment rates fluctuate year to year and by state and are often similar to — not uniformly 'far greater than' — the national unemployment rate; some years veterans have slightly higher rates, other years similar or lower. While Wisconsin has in some recent months/years shown veteran unemployment lower than its non‑veteran rate or lower than the national veteran rate, that is not a persistent, rare exception as the claim implies without specifying a timeframe.

claim: Says Adam Schiff used taxpayer money to "reach a sexual harassment settlement with a 19-year-old male."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence or congressional record showing Adam Schiff used taxpayer funds to reach a sexual-harassment settlement with a 19-year-old male. Reporting and fact-checking on similar viral claims found no substantiation that taxpayer money was used for such a settlement involving Schiff.

claim: U.S. Senate candidate Todd Akin was "partly right" that a woman's body has a way of shutting down so that a pregnancy doesn't occur if she's raped.
rationale: Medical and reproductive biology do not support a physiological mechanism that automatically 'shuts down' a woman’s body to prevent pregnancy after rape. Documented cases and research show pregnancies can and do result from rape, and acute stress does not reliably prevent ovulation, fertilization, or implantation.

claim: "Richard Nixon was the last president to be impeached."
rationale: False. Richard Nixon resigned in August 1974 before the full House of Representatives voted to impeach him (the House Judiciary Committee had approved articles, but the full House never did). Later presidents have been formally impeached by the House, most recently Donald Trump (impeached in 2019 and again in 2021).

claim: The Fair Tax proposal encourages innovation and investment "level the playing field" for American companies to compete globally.
rationale: This is a contested, predictive claim without consensus evidence. Supporters of the Fair Tax argue that replacing income and payroll taxes with a national consumption tax would remove double taxation on savings, exempt exports, and thereby encourage investment and competitiveness; however many economists dispute the magnitude and direction of these effects and point to regressive impacts and uncertain behavioral responses. There is no clear empirical proof that the proposal would reliably 'level the playing field' for U.S. companies globally.

claim: "Coolmath Games is being taken down cause it was run by the Mexican drug cartel?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Coolmath Games was owned or run by a Mexican drug cartel or that it is being taken down for that reason. Public reporting, domain/ownership information, and technology news outlets have not reported any criminal cartel ties; the claim appears to be a rumor or disinformation.

claim: "Texas now has the second-highest high school graduation rate in the country. And it has the highest graduation rate for African Americans and Hispanics."
rationale: The claim lacks a year or data source and is not supported by national graduation-rate reports. Recent U.S. Department of Education and state-level data show Texas has improved graduation rates, but states like New Jersey and Massachusetts typically rank above Texas overall, and subgroup rankings (Black and Hispanic students) vary by year and dataset rather than showing Texas consistently highest.

claim: Members of Congress "have not reduced their salaries ... since the Great Depression," meaning they've gone "eight decades without a pay cut."
rationale: This claim is misleading. While Congress rarely cuts the statutory nominal base salary, there have been instances since the 1930s where raises were blocked, cost-of-living adjustments withheld, or pay effectively reduced through legislative measures and freezes — so it is incorrect to say members have gone eight straight decades without any pay cut or reduction in take-home pay.

claim: Says Pennsylvania chemical plant and Louisiana liquified natural gas plant "could never have happened" without his administration.
rationale: The absolute claim that those plants "could never have happened" under any other administration is not supported. Large chemical and LNG facilities are typically driven by private investment decisions, multi-year planning, state and local permitting, and market demand; while a federal administration can influence policy and approvals, it is unlikely to be the sole necessary condition for such projects.

claim: Says Obama opposes offshore drilling and a gas tax holiday.
rationale: Barack Obama has publicly opposed opening many new offshore areas to drilling (particularly near coasts and protected areas) and has criticized federal 'gas tax holiday' proposals, calling them short-term gimmicks that would not sustainably lower prices. These positions were stated repeatedly during his campaigns and presidency.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton’s energy agenda "will cost the U.S. economy over $5 trillion"
rationale: There is no broadly accepted, nonpartisan economic analysis showing Hillary Clinton’s energy agenda would unambiguously 'cost the U.S. economy over $5 trillion.' Numbers of that magnitude have appeared in partisan or model-dependent studies that rely on disputed assumptions about regulations, timelines, and indirect effects. Independent fact-checkers and mainstream economic analyses did not endorse a single, definitive $5 trillion loss.

claim: The impeachment process against Donald Trump "provides fewer due process protections and fewer protections for minority rights than what we have seen in previous impeachment efforts."
rationale: The claim is a broad, comparative assertion that is not demonstrably true as stated because impeachment procedures vary by chamber, by specific case, and by which protections are counted. While Trump’s second impeachment was conducted on an accelerated timeline with fewer hearings and limited witness testimony compared with some prior high-profile impeachments (e.g., Nixon/Clinton inquiries), impeachment is a political process and procedural protections differ across instances, so a blanket statement that it provides fewer due process and minority-rights protections than all previous efforts is not verifiable.

claim: The typical anglerfish is seven feet long.
rationale: Most anglerfish species are much smaller than seven feet; deep-sea anglerfish are typically only a few inches to at most under a meter in body length, and while some related species (like monkfish/goosefish) can be larger, a seven‑foot 'typical' anglerfish is not accurate.

claim: "Prescription drug companies are charging Americans prices that are on average 4x higher than what's charged in other countries."
rationale: U.S. prescription drug prices are well documented to be substantially higher than in many other countries, but the precise multiple varies with the drug sample, countries compared, and whether list or net (rebated) prices are used. Most broad analyses and OECD/KFF summaries find typical U.S. prices around 2–3 times higher, while some studies of selected brand-name or top-selling drugs report differences approaching 3–4×; a blanket "on average 4x" claim overstates the consensus.

claim: This year’s state budget and my spending proposal for Fiscal Year 2016 represent an infusion of more than $1 billion in additional money for K-12 education.
rationale: The claim names a specific dollar amount for K-12 education tied to 'this year’s state budget' and 'my spending proposal for Fiscal Year 2016' but gives no state, speaker, or source documents. Without identifying which state's enacted budget and which proposal are meant and without reconciled budget documents showing an incremental $1+ billion, the assertion cannot be verified. Because budget totals and whether amounts are 'additional' depend on baselines, transfers, and timing, the claim as stated is not verifiable.

claim: A 13-year-old girl "is now in critical care in the hospital here in Halifax because her heart stopped right after she had a vaccine."
rationale: This specific claim is unverified: there are no confirmed public reports or official statements that a 13-year-old in Halifax is in critical care because her heart stopped immediately after vaccination. Temporal proximity alone does not establish causation, and such individual medical events require confirmation from hospitals or public health authorities before being presented as fact.

claim: Says Brett Kavanaugh "refused to uphold key patient protections in the past."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute assertion but is vague about which 'key patient protections' and which actions are meant. While Kavanaugh has faced criticism during confirmation for certain rulings and prior government work that critics said could limit health-care protections, there is no clear, documented record that he broadly 'refused to uphold' core patient-protection laws without specifying particular cases. Verifying the claim requires naming specific protections and actions.

claim: "The media ... sort of made it sound like I had a feud with the intelligence community."
rationale: The claim is a subjective statement about how unspecified media portrayed an unspecified person; without identifying the speaker, timeframe, or which outlets, it cannot be independently verified. Media coverage varies widely and some outlets may have framed tensions with the intelligence community while others did not, so the broad assertion is unprovable as stated.

claim: Columbia, Mo., is "one of the fastest growing cities in the region, the only city in the state to grow jobs faster than the nation as a whole."
rationale: The claim is precise and absolute but gives no timeframe or definition of “region,” making it unlikely to be strictly true. Job-growth rankings change by period and data source, and other Missouri cities and metros have had periods when job growth exceeded the U.S. rate, so calling Columbia the only city in the state to do so is not supported without a specific year and data source.

claim: Says "Harry Reid, when asked about the Republican field, said the Republican he likes the best is Donald Trump, and he said, because I can work with him. He'll cut deals."
rationale: There is no credible record of former Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid praising Donald Trump as his favorite Republican and saying he could work with him and that Trump would 'cut deals.' Reid was publicly critical of Trump on multiple occasions, and major news outlets and fact-checkers do not corroborate this quote, suggesting it is misattributed or fabricated.

claim: Says science shows the physiological effects of wearing masks include hypoxemia, hypercapnia, shortness of breath, toxicity and increased muscle tension.
rationale: High-quality studies and public-health guidance show that routine use of surgical or cloth masks does not cause hypoxemia or clinically significant hypercapnia in healthy people; measurable oxygen and CO2 levels remain within normal ranges. Some people report subjective shortness of breath, discomfort, or increased perceived work of breathing (especially with tight-fitting respirators during exertion), but claims of generalized 'toxicity' or widespread physiologic harm are not supported by the evidence.

claim: "We are now, for the first time ever, energy independent."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate because it lacks definition and context: "energy independent" can mean different things (net exporter, no imports of any fuels, or energy self-sufficiency across all forms). While some countries (notably the U.S.) have recently been net exporters of certain energy categories in some years, that does not equate to complete or permanent energy independence, and historically the situation has varied by fuel and timeframe.

claim: Says "if current trends continue, by 2040, one out of three Texas workers will not have a high school diploma."
rationale: Long-term data and projections show high-school completion rates have generally risen, not fallen, so it is unlikely Texas workers would reach a 1-in-3 rate lacking a diploma by 2040 under continuation of current trends. Achieving one-third without a high school diploma would require a major reversal of multi-decade improvements in educational attainment and documented workforce projections.

claim: Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson "gave child porn offenders sentences below the guidelines and below what the prosecutors were requesting," showing she is "soft on child pornography offenders."
rationale: This statement is misleading. While Ketanji Brown Jackson did impose sentences below the advisory federal guideline range and below prosecutors' recommendations in some individual child pornography cases as a district judge, that was not uniformly true across her docket and sentencing decisions were presented as case-specific exercises of judicial discretion. The claim lumps select examples into a categorical judgment that she is broadly "soft," which is an opinion rather than a demonstrated universal fact.

claim: No openly gay man has ever been elected to the Georgia Legislature.
rationale: This claim is false. In 2016 Sam Park, an openly gay man, was elected to the Georgia House of Representatives (District 101), becoming the first openly gay man elected to the Georgia General Assembly; other openly gay men have been public members since then.

claim: Keystone Pipeline was blocked by Obama on Warren Buffett’s behalf.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Obama blocked the Keystone XL pipeline as a favor to Warren Buffett. The Obama administration’s decision followed a lengthy State Department environmental and climate review and was publicly justified on environmental and legal grounds. Although Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway owns BNSF, a railroad that hauls oil by rail, that economic connection is circumstantial and not proof of coordination or a quid pro quo.

claim: Under Mayor Angel Taveras "Providence’s bond rating was downgraded from A to BBB, two steps above junk-bond status."
rationale: While Providence’s credit rating was cut during Angel Taveras’s tenure, the specific phrasing is misleading: different agencies applied different notches and the city’s ratings were not cleanly described as “from A to BBB, two steps above junk.” Rating agencies use multiple notches (e.g., A, A-, BBB+, BBB) and some downgrades were to BBB+ or equivalent levels, so the claim’s exact numbers and the ‘two steps above junk’ characterization are inaccurate or oversimplified.

claim: "There was a raid on the Biden residence yesterday by the military!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting (through my last update) that the U.S. military conducted a raid on President Biden’s residence, and such an operation would be unprecedented and legally constrained. An action of that scale would prompt immediate, widespread national and international coverage and official statements.

claim: "There's no negative advertising in my campaign at all."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that no negative advertising occurred in the campaign, but that cannot be verified from the information given. Political campaigns and independent groups frequently run negative ads across many channels, and without comprehensive ad-tracking or disclosure records one cannot reliably assert the complete absence of negative advertising.

claim: Says the California congressional district he represents "has a higher GDP than Russia."
rationale: No California congressional district produces anywhere near the total economic output of an entire country like Russia. Russia's GDP is on the order of trillions of dollars, while even the largest U.S. congressional districts (which cover major metro economies) generate at most a few hundred billion dollars in regional GDP, far below Russia's national total.

claim: "Economic inequality in Multnomah County has a face -- and a name. It has 90,000 faces and names -- the number of county residents who are still unemployed, or underemployed, in the wake of the 2008 Wall Street crash."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific, current tally (90,000) of Multnomah County residents "still unemployed or underemployed" because of the 2008 crash; that precise figure and causal claim are not supported by available labor statistics and are ambiguous in time and definition. Multnomah County's population and typical unemployment/underemployment rates make such a large, persistent single-source number unlikely without a cited study. The claim appears rhetorical and unverifiable as stated.

claim: Jason Carter supports using Georgia tax dollars to promote Obamacare
rationale: The claim mischaracterizes Jason Carter’s position. During his 2014 gubernatorial campaign he backed accepting Medicaid expansion and supported enrollment outreach under the Affordable Care Act, but he did not propose using Georgia general tax dollars to run promotional advertising for Obamacare. Fact-checks at the time found ads saying he would use state tax money to promote Obamacare were misleading or false.

claim: Says U.S. Senate rival Tommy Thompson ran Medicare "into the ground" and "nine years closer to bankruptcy."
rationale: The statement is a partisan exaggeration and lacks evidence tying Tommy Thompson personally to driving Medicare “into the ground” or shifting insolvency by exactly nine years. As HHS Secretary (2001–2005) he was involved in the 2003 Medicare Modernization Act (Part D), but Medicare trust-fund solvency projections are affected by many laws, demographic trends, and economic factors and are not attributed to a single individual. No authoritative sources credit Thompson alone with moving a Medicare bankruptcy date by nine years.

claim: "The American economy is continuing its longest monthly streak of job growth in history, with 3.9 million jobs added since President Trump was elected."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the uninterrupted monthly job-growth streak in the U.S. began after the Great Recession (around 2010) and therefore predates President Trump’s election, and the cited "3.9 million" jobs figure does not match official payroll-series totals for clearly defined endpoints. Whether the cumulative gain since the November 2016 election is 3.9 million depends on which months and which survey are used, but standard BLS nonfarm payroll totals for the period commonly referenced are different, so the phrasing is inaccurate.

claim: "95 percent of the income gains in the last few years have gone to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The statement is too sweeping and lacks a defined country and timeframe. While specific analyses of U.S. data (notably Saez/Piketty) found that roughly 95% of income gains during the 2009–2012 recovery went to the top 1%, that result applies to a particular short period and income definition; broader or more recent periods and other measures do not support a universal 95% figure.

claim: Al Sharpton went to Ferguson, Mo., and is "declaring as a matter of fact that ... Michael Brown didn't use any deadly force or posed no deadly threat to the officer."
rationale: Al Sharpton traveled to Ferguson after Michael Brown’s shooting and publicly argued that Brown was unarmed and that the shooting was unjustified. Sharpton repeatedly characterized Brown as not posing a deadly threat and criticized the officer’s use of force, which aligns with the paraphrased claim that he declared Brown did not use deadly force or pose a deadly threat.

claim: "PEDOPHILIA is now LEGAL in CALIFORNIA. Now a 21 year old can have sex with an 11 year old, and not be listed on the sex registry as a sex offender."
rationale: California has not legalized sexual activity between adults and prepubescent children; the state's age of consent is 18 and sexual activity with an 11-year-old would be a serious felony (statutory rape/child molestation) and typically triggers mandatory sex-offender registration if convicted. No recent lawful change permits a 21-year-old to legally have sex with an 11-year-old or to avoid registry for such conduct. The claim misrepresents or wildly exaggerates any legislative proposals or changes.

claim: "An April study found that about 70 percent of ads in this election cycle have been negative [due to SuperPACs], up from only 9 percent through the same period in 2008."
rationale: The precise claim (70% negative this cycle vs. 9% through the same period in 2008 caused by SuperPACs) does not match figures reported by major ad-tracking organizations. Groups like the Wesleyan Media Project and independent fact-checkers reported higher shares of negative ads in 2008 than 9% and attribute increases to a mix of campaign and outside-group spending, not solely SuperPACs. The statement appears to misstate or oversimplify the available data and causal attribution.

claim: Says Bill O’Reilly spoke 40 percent of the words in an interview with President Barack Obama.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or transcript-backed analysis showing Bill O’Reilly spoke 40% of the words in any interview with President Obama. Available transcripts and reporting from independent fact-checkers do not support that specific 40% figure and generally show the president speaking more than the interviewer in those televised segments.

claim: A proposed San Antonio ordinance will allow men into women’s restrooms in the city.
rationale: This claim misstates typical nondiscrimination proposals. Such ordinances usually prohibit denying access to restrooms based on gender identity, which means transgender women could use women's restrooms consistent with their identity, but they do not broadly permit cisgender men to enter women’s restrooms or remove existing safety/privacy rules.

claim: Tapping the Strategic Petroleum Reserve would immediately lower gasoline prices
rationale: Releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve increases crude supply and can put downward pressure on wholesale crude prices, but retail gasoline prices reflect refinery runs, inventory levels, distribution, taxes, and local market factors. Those downstream adjustments typically take days to weeks and a small or uncoordinated SPR release often has only modest or temporary effects on pump prices, so an immediate drop at the gas station is not guaranteed.

claim: Says he could be "the first president in modern history to be outspent."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and likely false because many U.S. presidents and major candidates in the modern era have been outspent by opponents at various points; therefore someone now saying they would be the "first" is incorrect without a precise definition of "modern history". The statement is also ambiguous about whether it refers to campaign spending, overall political spending, or time period, which undermines the absolutist claim.

claim: "Science says that being single will kill you faster than obesity."
rationale: Research shows that poor social relationships, loneliness, and social isolation are associated with higher mortality, but equating that to simply being 'single' and claiming it kills faster than obesity overstates and misrepresents the evidence. Some meta-analyses have found social isolation is a risk comparable to other major risk factors in certain contexts, but outcomes depend on how 'single', loneliness, and obesity are defined and controlled for; obesity independently increases mortality risk as well.

claim: "When I go on Letterman" the "ratings go up."
rationale: The claim asserts a consistent causal effect without providing data or a clear timeframe. Television ratings fluctuate for many reasons (guests, guests' newsworthiness, competing programming, promotion), and there is no broadly accepted evidence that any single person's appearances on Letterman reliably produced higher ratings every time. Without episode-by-episode ratings and controls for confounders, the universal claim is unsupported.

claim: "The job [of correctional officer] lowers your life expectancy . . . Metropolitan did a study in, I believe it was 1998, and the life expectancy was 58."
rationale: While multiple occupational-health studies report that correctional officers face elevated stress, higher rates of cardiovascular disease and suicide, and increased mortality risk, I can find no verifiable evidence that a 1998 “Metropolitan” study established a general life expectancy of 58 for correctional officers. The specific 58-year figure appears to be an unverified or misattributed statistic that has circulated anecdotally. The broader claim that the job can shorten lifespan is plausible in some cohorts, but the cited study and precise number are not supported.

claim: "McDonald’s (makes) you all sign noncompete contracts that you cannot go across town to try to get a job at Burger King."
rationale: McDonald’s does not universally require all employees to sign noncompete agreements barring them from working at competitors like Burger King. Whether a noncompete is used depends on the franchise owner, the employee’s role (more common for managers or higher-level staff), and state law, many of which restrict or ban noncompetes for low-wage workers.

claim: There are twice as many gun shops as McDonald’s in the United States.
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported as stated. There are roughly 13–14 thousand McDonald’s restaurants in the U.S., and while the number of licensed firearm dealers (FFLs) is often reported to exceed that figure, many FFLs are not dedicated retail 'gun shops' (they include pawnbrokers, private dealers, and occasional sellers). Because the term 'gun shops' is ambiguous and available counts mix different categories, the blanket statement that there are twice as many gun shops as McDonald’s is not reliably supported.

claim: Says James Clapper "and virtually everyone else" said "there is no collusion" in the Russia investigation findings.
rationale: The claim overstates consensus. While some officials (notably Attorney General Barr in his public summary) said the Mueller report did not establish collusion, the Mueller report itself used more nuanced language—finding insufficient evidence to establish conspiracy/coordination and explicitly declining to exonerate the president—and many analysts and officials highlighted those nuances. Saying James Clapper and "virtually everyone else" said there was "no collusion" is therefore inaccurate.

claim: "More than 32,000 Americans lose their lives to gun violence each year."
rationale: Recent U.S. mortality data show total firearm deaths exceed 32,000 per year; for example, CDC counts were roughly 45,000–48,000 firearm deaths in 2020–2021. These totals include suicides, homicides, accidental shootings, legal intervention, and undetermined intent.

claim: Donald Trump’s "golf course on the island defaulted, like so many of his other failed business schemes. The failure left Puerto Rican taxpayers with a nearly $33 million bill."
rationale: While Trump’s golf course in Puerto Rico did experience financial troubles and was tied to government-backed bonds, the assertion that it directly "left Puerto Rican taxpayers with a nearly $33 million bill" is misleading. Reporting on the project shows complex bond guarantees, restructurings, and differing accounting of exposure; the exact taxpayer liability is disputed and not a simple nearly $33 million direct bill.

claim: "Bad math (is) driving Wisconsin’s exploding positive test rate."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that a mathematical error is the primary cause of Wisconsin’s rising test positivity; positivity rates rise mainly because more infections are being detected and because who gets tested and how many tests are done can change the percentage. While differences in calculation methods (tests vs. people tested) or reporting delays can alter the reported rate, those methodological details do not generally create an "exploding" rate absent a true increase in positives.

claim: A bill to eliminate Delta Air Lines’ jet fuel tax breaks "violates federal law and puts the state at risk of losing critical funding from the Federal Aviation Administration."
rationale: The claim overstates the legal certainty. While state actions that single out an airline or conflict with federal grant assurances or nondiscrimination requirements can raise federal-law problems and could put federal airport grant funding at risk, whether a particular bill "violates federal law" and would cause the FAA to pull funding depends on the bill’s precise text and legal analysis rather than being automatic.

claim: "Obama secretly gave citizenship to 2,500 Iranians as part of nuke deal."
rationale: There is no evidence that the Obama administration secretly granted U.S. citizenship to 2,500 Iranians as part of the Iran nuclear deal. U.S. citizenship is granted through defined immigration and naturalization processes administered by USCIS and cannot be conferred en masse by an international agreement; major fact‑checking organizations investigated and found the claim baseless. The JCPOA (nuclear deal) contained no provisions about granting U.S. citizenship.

claim: The significant drop in Florida’s unemployment rate is a good economic sign.
rationale: A significant drop in the unemployment rate can indicate a strengthening labor market, but it is not automatically a clear 'good' sign. The rate can fall because people leave the labor force (discouraged workers), because of seasonal or statistical effects, or because jobs added are part-time or low quality; without examining participation, payrolls, and wages the drop alone is ambiguous.

claim: "There's a loophole where you can sell guns without a background check … 40 percent of guns are sold that way" at gun shows and over the Internet.
rationale: It is true that federal law generally requires licensed dealers to run background checks while many private sales at gun shows or online may not trigger a federal check, but the precise claim that '40 percent of guns are sold that way' is not reliably supported. Estimates of the share of privately sold guns without checks vary widely depending on the study, year, and definitions used, and no contemporary, authoritative data consistently shows a 40% figure.

claim: In Sauk City, Wisconsin, "the ID office" that provides identification for voting "is only open on the fifth Wednesday of every month" -- a total of four days in 2016.
rationale: While 2016 did have four 'fifth Wednesdays', there is no basis to conclude a municipal ID provider in Sauk City would restrict in-person ID issuance to only those rare days. Local clerks and DMV offices generally maintain regular, posted hours; the claim appears to conflate a calendrical curiosity with actual office scheduling and is not supported by typical municipal practice or available descriptions of clerk/DMV services.

claim: Obama "voted for ... $3-million for an overhead projector at a planetarium in Chicago."
rationale: There is no credible record that Barack Obama voted to spend $3 million specifically for an 'overhead projector' at a Chicago planetarium. Independent fact-checkers and official roll-call records found no appropriation or specific vote matching that description; the claim appears to be a distorted or fabricated smear combining unrelated spending items.

claim: "Senator Cryin’ Chuck Schumer fought hard against the Bad Iran Deal, even going at it with President Obama, & then Voted AGAINST it! Now he says I should not have terminated the deal"
rationale: Senator Chuck Schumer publicly announced in 2015 that he opposed the Iran nuclear agreement and had a high-profile disagreement with President Obama over it. He subsequently voted against the deal in congressional consideration, and after President Trump withdrew from the JCPOA in 2018 Schumer publicly said he disagreed with the administration’s decision to terminate the agreement.

claim: A campaign poster for New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern with the slogan, "No jab. No job, no refunds."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Jacinda Ardern or the New Zealand Labour Party produced a campaign poster reading "No jab. No job, no refunds." Investigations of official campaign materials and mainstream reporting show this slogan circulated as a doctored image/meme on social media rather than an authentic poster.

claim: Twenty-seven percent of Californians, almost 11 million, "were born in a foreign land."
rationale: Recent U.S. Census Bureau / American Community Survey estimates show California’s foreign‑born population is roughly 10.6–11.0 million, which is about 27% of the state’s ~39–40 million residents. Thus the statement that 27% of Californians — almost 11 million — were born in a foreign land is consistent with those official estimates for recent years.

claim: Oregon’s "three largest employers, and 13 of the top 25, are health care providers."
rationale: This claim overstates the dominance of health care in Oregon employer rankings.
