rationale: In 1976 John McCain was an active-duty U.S. Navy officer assigned as the Navy’s liaison to the U.S. Senate, which was an official military/government posting representing the Navy. That role was not a civilian lobbyist position; McCain did not begin his Washington career as a private-sector lobbyist.

claim: Since he took office as Milwaukee County executive, "we have never raised" bus fares and "this year there’ll be a million route-miles more than there were five years ago."
rationale: The statement makes two specific, verifiable claims about fare history and a large service-mile increase, but I could not corroborate both claims from available public records. Transit fare changes and annual route-mile (service-mile) totals are documented by Milwaukee County/MCTS and local reporting; without those records confirming no fare increases and a net +1,000,000 route-miles versus five years prior, the combined claim is unsupported and likely incorrect.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "just gave a speech a few weeks ago" and said "we should still have troops in Iraq."
rationale: The claim as written is unverified because it provides no date or source — "just a few weeks ago" is ambiguous. While Mitt Romney has at various times supported continued U.S. engagement in Iraq or a continued U.S. role in the region, I cannot confirm he gave a speech a few weeks ago containing the exact line "we should still have troops in Iraq" without more context or a specific reference.

claim: "Exit polls indicate that Democrats get over 70 percent of LGBT votes in federal elections."
rationale: While LGBT voters have tended to favor Democrats by large margins in many recent federal elections, exit-poll estimates and surveys vary by year and methodology and do not universally show Democrats receiving over 70% of the LGBT vote. Some elections and some polls have reported >70%, but others report lower shares and many exit polls historically did not consistently or reliably measure sexual orientation.

claim: "Scott Walker has a plan to privatize state lands" and "wants to sell our deer to the highest bidder."
rationale: There is no documented policy proposal from Scott Walker calling for wholesale privatization of state lands or for literally "selling our deer to the highest bidder." Criticisms and attack ads have used hyperbolic language about his land-management and hunting-permit positions, but those do not constitute a plan to privatize all state land or auction wildlife itself.

claim: "Kids in cages" in border facilities are "at 700% capacity."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the widely cited '700% capacity' figure referred to certain Border Patrol short-term holding facilities at a particular time (and to overall occupancy), not that child-specific detention sites with 'kids in cages' were universally at 700% capacity. Capacity calculations also vary (design vs. rated vs. temporary surge capacity) and adult and child populations are tracked differently, so the statement as written is not accurate.

claim: Under Rick Scott, there has been a "historic $20 billion in funds for education."
rationale: The statement is misleading: while Florida’s total education budget reached about $20 billion in certain fiscal years during Rick Scott’s governorship, that figure represents total annual funding, not a newly created or additional $20 billion 'historic' increase attributable to him. Scott did preside over budget increases for K–12 and higher education, but the claim as phrased implies a $20 billion increase or new allocation, which is not supported by budget records.

claim: "Surveys show that many of our citizens think we devote a full quarter or even a third of our federal budget to foreign aid."
rationale: Multiple public-opinion polls have repeatedly found that many people (particularly in the United States) vastly overestimate the share of the federal budget spent on foreign aid, often giving figures around 20–30%. These survey results contrast with actual spending on foreign assistance, which is typically about 1% or less of the U.S. federal budget, confirming the claim that many respondents believe it is a quarter or a third.

claim: Says critics who say he cut Medicaid are wrong; his budget added $1.2 billion to the program
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits who "he" is, which jurisdiction and fiscal year, and whether the $1.2 billion was net new, ongoing, nominal or adjusted for baseline growth. Even a headline increase of $1.2 billion can coincide with overall cuts once compared to projected growth, inflation, federal matching changes, or re‑classifications, so the claim cannot be accepted without those details.

claim: Says "FBI and Texas State Police are both confirming that Raymond Peter Littleberry, the man accused of shooting up a Texas church, was an avid atheist on the payroll of the Democrat National Committee."
rationale: There is no credible public record or official statement from the FBI or Texas law enforcement confirming that a person named Raymond Peter Littleberry was an atheist employed by the Democratic National Committee and accused of a church shooting. Major news outlets and law-enforcement releases typically report identifying information and motive when confirmed; this specific, detailed claim appears to be unsubstantiated and consistent with disinformation patterns.

claim: "Hurricane Irma could be a Category 6 by the time it hits East Coast."
rationale: There is no official "Category 6" on the Saffir–Simpson hurricane wind scale; it currently tops out at Category 5 for storms with sustained winds of 157 mph (252 km/h) or greater. A storm stronger than that would still be described as Category 5, so saying Irma "could be a Category 6" is inaccurate in formal meteorological terms.

claim: "The forest fires were so grotesque last year that we had the worst air in the world in Washington."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not verifiable as stated: it does not specify which 'Washington' or the exact year. While wildfire smoke has produced episodes of extremely poor air in Washington (for example parts of Washington state in 2020 and smoke impacts in 2023), saying 'we had the worst air in the world' for 'last year' is not supported without date-specific AQI rankings. Temporary daily spikes have placed some Washington locations among the worst globally on particular days, but that does not validate the broad, year-long assertion.

claim: Says Gov. Tony Evers "tried to make us pay even more at the pump by hiking the gas tax."
rationale: Governor Tony Evers has repeatedly proposed raising Wisconsin's gas (and diesel) taxes in budget and transportation funding proposals to generate revenue for roads and transit. Characterizing those proposals as attempts to 'make us pay more at the pump by hiking the gas tax' accurately reflects his policy initiatives.

claim: As Massachusetts governor, Mitt Romney used a line-item veto to cut "millions of dollars for firefighting equipment," including firefighters' "coats, pants, helmets and boots."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and later fact-checks show Governor Romney used his line-item veto to remove multi-million-dollar legislative earmarks for local projects, including appropriations designated for firefighter protective clothing (turnout gear such as coats, pants, helmets and boots). The vetoes took out several million dollars in those specific line items during his tenure.

claim: Black cats in Vietnam are being killed and consumed as a COVID-19 cure.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence of a widespread campaign in Vietnam to kill and eat black cats specifically as a COVID-19 cure. Viral videos and social-media claims were often misattributed, isolated, or dated, and Vietnamese authorities and fact-checkers reported no substantiation for a systematic practice of killing pets as a cure.

claim: In Texas, "the No. 1 name for new male babies — many of whom will vote one day — is Jose."
rationale: Statewide baby-name rankings from sources like the Social Security Administration and Texas vital statistics in recent years show names such as Liam, Noah, and Mateo at or near the top for boys; Jose has not been the overall #1 male baby name in Texas. The claim likely overgeneralizes: Jose is common within Hispanic communities and may top lists in some counties or demographic subsets, but is not the statewide No. 1.

claim: "Here are the facts: there is no massive wave of migrants pouring into California. Overall immigrant apprehensions on the border last year were as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years (and 85 percent of the apprehensions occurred outside of California)."
rationale: The claim mixes a partly accurate point (California accounts for a relatively small share of total Southwest border apprehensions) with a false one: overall border apprehensions in recent years have been very high, not “as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years.” U.S. Customs and Border Protection encounter totals in the past few fiscal years reached levels well above historic lows. The 85% figure depends on the specific year and whether one counts apprehensions versus total encounters, so it is not reliably supported as stated.

claim: "In the last several months, the Biden administration has released over 7,000 illegal aliens who were COVID positive just in one Texas city." Biden's border policies are "endangering not just the people of Texas, but people all across the country."
rationale: There is no credible, corroborated evidence that the Biden administration released over 7,000 COVID‑positive migrants in a single Texas city in the past several months. Federal and local health and immigration agencies have protocols for isolating and handling known COVID cases, and reporting of such a large, specific number in one city has not been substantiated by reliable sources. The additional claim that the administration's border policies are "endangering" people is a partisan opinion rather than a verifiable factual statement.

claim: "Before this law was passed, Americans were told they could keep their current health care plans. After it became law, the administration issued regulations stating nearly half of Americans would lose their current plan."
rationale: President Obama did repeatedly say "if you like your plan, you can keep it," and HHS later issued rules about grandfathering that meant many non‑compliant plans in the individual and small‑group markets would not meet new standards. However, the administration did not say "nearly half of Americans" would lose their plans; the estimates cited applied to portions of the individual market (not the entire U.S. population) and the number of Americans overall affected was much smaller. The claim conflates limited market‑segment estimates with the whole population.

claim: Photo shows Barack Obama and George Clooney in a compromising situation with a child.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream reporting that Barack Obama and George Clooney appear together in a compromising photo with a child. Images alleging such scenarios are commonly fabricated, manipulated, or miscaptioned, and a genuine photo of that nature involving high-profile figures would have been widely documented and verified.

claim: Says Steph Curry decided to split with Nike because the company wouldn’t allow him to write Bible scriptures in his shoes.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Steph Curry split from a shoe partner because the company refused to allow Bible scriptures on his shoes. Curry's long-term shoe partner historically has been Under Armour (not Nike), he has previously displayed Bible references on his gear, and reporting about endorsement changes attributes them to contractual and business reasons rather than a ban on religious text.

claim: "Ohio companies export more goods and services globally than 41 other states."
rationale: The statement implies Ohio ranks higher than 41 other states (i.e., among the top nine) in combined goods-and-services exports, but federal state export rankings vary by year and by whether 'goods' or 'goods and services' are counted. In recent federal data Ohio has often ranked in the mid-to-high single digits for goods exports but not consistently above 41 other states when services are included, and the claim provides no year or data source, so it is misleading.

claim: "Colorado school forces students to wear hijabs."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a Colorado public school system or a specific widely-known Colorado school is forcing students to wear hijabs. Public schools compelling students to adopt religious clothing would likely violate the U.S. Constitution; while private religious schools may have dress codes, the broad claim as stated is unsupported by reliable reporting.

claim: Teachers "are working their third consecutive year -- some longer than that -- without salary increases."
rationale: The claim lacks any specified jurisdiction or time frame, and teacher pay outcomes vary widely by state, district, and contract cycle. While some teachers in particular states or districts have gone multiple years without raises, many others have received increases or cost-of-living adjustments during the period in question, so the blanket statement about 'teachers' generally is not supportable as a universal fact.

claim: Says of Gov. Tony Evers and 2020 violence in Kenosha after the police shooting of Jacob Blake: "It took the loss of lives before help finally came."
rationale: The claim asserts that no help arrived until after lives were lost. While Governor Evers was criticized for a delayed, larger National Guard deployment, state and local law enforcement resources were active during the unrest and the Guard was mobilized around Aug 25–26; the two killings occurred the night of Aug 25. Because the timing and what counts as “help” are nuanced, the categorical statement is inaccurate.

claim: Says that in Texas, it’s "already illegal to enter a bathroom to harm someone."
rationale: Texas law already criminalizes assaults, attempted assaults, sexual offenses, voyeurism, and related harms; entering a bathroom with the intent to harm or to commit one of those offenses would therefore be unlawful. Prosecutors can charge conduct such as assault, attempted assault, indecent exposure, or criminal trespass when someone enters a restroom to injure, harass, or sexually exploit another person.

claim: The polls "show over half of Americans identify themselves as being pro-life."
rationale: The statement is too sweeping and misleading: national survey results vary by poll, question wording, and timing, and in many recent reputable polls (e.g., Pew, Gallup) a plurality or majority have identified as pro-choice rather than pro-life. While some individual polls or subgroup samples at certain times may report over half identifying as pro-life, there is no consistent consensus across major national polls that a majority of Americans identify as pro-life.

claim: Says George Patton said, "Politicians are the lowest form of life on earth. Liberal Democrats are the lower form of politicians."
rationale: There is no reliable primary-source evidence that General George S. Patton said this full remark. While a terse jab like "politicians are the lowest form of life" is sometimes misattributed to Patton, the specific second sentence referencing "Liberal Democrats" is anachronistic and not documented in Patton's speeches or writings.

claim: "Only Reuters" reported that the doctor who detected the omicron variant said its symptoms are "very mild."
rationale: Multiple major news organizations besides Reuters reported Dr. Angelique Coetzee’s comments that the Omicron cases she saw were mild or 'very mild.' Reuters was not the only outlet to publish or quote her observations; broadcasters and newspapers around the world picked up the story within hours.

claim: "7 out of 10 Oregon families living in poverty have at least one parent who works."
rationale: I cannot confirm the precise figure as stated because the claim gives no source or year; while many families in poverty do include at least one working parent, the exact proportion for Oregon varies by year and by how "family", "parent", and "works" are defined. Without a cited dataset, the specific "7 out of 10" (70%) number cannot be verified and may be inaccurate or out of date.

claim: Of six Rhode Island tax-credit programs worth about $35 million, "three companies got 90 percent of that -- CVS and two companies not even located in the state of Rhode Island."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim from publicly available summaries of Rhode Island tax-credit awards; state tax-credit programs and annual reports typically list multiple recipients and do not show three companies receiving 90% of a $35 million package without naming the programs, year, or recipients. CVS is headquartered in Rhode Island (Woonsocket), which makes the phrasing about out-of-state recipients ambiguous, and I found no corroborating breakdown that matches the exact figures and wording given.

claim: Says Aaron Rodgers "is not the highest tax rate payer" in Wisconsin, it's "the single mom getting 24 grand in benefits with two kids who will lose 80 cents on the dollar if she goes and takes a job."
rationale: I could not verify that Aaron Rodgers made that exact statement and no reliable contemporary reporting or direct transcript corroborates the quoted wording. The numeric claim about a single mom receiving $24,000 in benefits and 'losing 80 cents on the dollar' if she takes a job is an oversimplification — effective marginal benefit/tax rates vary by program and household and cannot be universally stated without detailed modelling.

claim: "The U.S. spends more money on its military than the 16 biggest military budgets in the world" combined.
rationale: Reliable sources that compile national defence spending (e.g., SIPRI and national budgets) show the United States spends more than the next several largest spenders combined (commonly quoted as the next 10), but the combined totals of the next 16 largest military budgets exceed U.S. spending. In other words, U.S. spending does not surpass the sum of the 16 next-biggest national military budgets in typical recent years.

claim: "Flip Flop! After opposing term limits for decades, Adam Putnam adopts Donald Trump and Ron DeSantis’ position."
rationale: The claim overstates and mischaracterizes Adam Putnam’s record. Public statements and actions through 2024 do not show a clear, decades-long opposition to a specific term‑limits policy nor a documented, singular switch to adopt an explicit Trump/DeSantis term‑limits proposal; available records are mixed and context‑dependent.

claim: Proposition 2 on November’s Texas ballot "does not cost state taxpayers any money."
rationale: The blanket claim that “Proposition 2 … does not cost state taxpayers any money” is unlikely to be accurate without reference to the official fiscal note. Texas constitutional amendments often have direct or indirect fiscal effects (on state aid, school funding, or local revenue) and official estimates from the Texas Comptroller or Legislative Budget Board are needed to verify a no-cost determination. Absent that specific, authoritative fiscal analysis, the absolute statement is not supportable.

claim: RNC version of a Hillary Clinton valentine: "Roses are red, violets are blue, I'll raise your taxes and there is nothing you can do."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that the Republican National Committee officially produced or distributed a Hillary Clinton Valentine with that exact wording. Similar anti-Clinton 'valentine' images circulated online during campaign periods, but they appear to be grassroots or meme creations rather than an RNC-issued piece.

claim: "A Florida judge ruled parts of Obamacare unconstitutional."
rationale: In 2011 U.S. District Judge Roger Vinson in the Northern District of Florida ruled that the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate (and, in his view, related provisions) was unconstitutional and invalidated the law. That decision was part of early federal litigation over the ACA and was subsequently appealed.

claim: "Ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary."
rationale: I cannot find corroborating evidence that ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary; an incident of that size and specificity would have been widely reported and is not supported by well-known news accounts. It is more likely the claim confuses or exaggerates a small, local voter-challenge story from a different place or year.

claim: "Biden says he doesn’t need voters to get elected."
rationale: There is no credible record of President Biden declaring he does not need voters to get elected; his public campaign and statements consistently seek voter support. The claim appears to be a misquote, out-of-context paraphrase, or false attribution rather than a true direct quote.

claim: Says Rick Scott "didn’t even come to his own education summit. But he did take time to go to the tea party convention the same week."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim as stated: it alleges Rick Scott skipped an education summit he organized while attending a Tea Party convention the same week, but my knowledge does not confirm those simultaneous events or his attendance pattern. Without a clear date, summit name, or convention reference this assertion is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: Ninety percent of the job growth in Virginia has been in the private sector.
rationale: The claim gives a precise figure but provides no timeframe or source, and state employment data vary by period. While most net job growth in Virginia typically occurs in the private sector, the share fluctuates year-to-year and is not reliably or universally 90% without a specified period and data source. Because the statement is unqualified and unverifiable as written, it cannot be accepted as factual.

claim: "My opponent, in 2008, had contributions investigated by the federal government."
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable and therefore treated as false because it fails to identify who "my opponent" is or provide details about the alleged 2008 investigation. Assertions that someone was the subject of a federal probe should be supported by named individuals and public records (DOJ, FEC, court filings, or contemporary reporting); without that, there is no basis to confirm the claim. Absent a specific, documented allegation, the statement cannot be substantiated.

claim: "The majority of my contributions have been from private individuals" giving $125 on average, "not from PACs, not from groups."
rationale: The statement makes a concrete quantitative claim about the source and average size of contributions, but there is no supporting public data here to verify it. Confirmation would require examination of the campaign’s finance disclosures (FEC or relevant state filings) showing donor types, counts, and amounts for the stated period, so the claim cannot be treated as fact based on the information provided.

claim: "Individuals and small businesses will be hit by increases in health insurance premiums as high as 39 percent."
rationale: The claim is presented as a general certainty but lacks context (timeframe, location, whether it's an average or a maximum). Health insurance premium changes vary widely by state, insurer, plan type and year; while isolated reports have documented near-39% increases for specific plans or markets, that is not a general rule that all individuals and small businesses "will be hit" with such increases.

claim: Says Kurt Schrader voted to cut $500 billion from Medicare, threatening "thousands of Oregon seniors and their access to their current coverage."
rationale: There is no clear record of Kurt Schrader casting a floor vote that directly 'cut $500 billion from Medicare.' Attack ads often compress or mischaracterize budget resolutions or deficit-reduction plans as direct benefit cuts; Schrader did not vote for a standalone bill that immediately cut Medicare benefits by $500 billion. Without a specific bill and timeframe this assertion is misleading and not supported by a direct vote record.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "wants higher standards for toy guns than real guns."
rationale: There is no evidence Bernie Sanders has advocated for imposing stricter standards on toy guns than on real firearms; his public gun-control positions focus on tighter regulation of real guns (background checks, bans on assault-style weapons and high-capacity magazines). The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or a satirical/misleading framing rather than a documented policy stance.

claim: "Obama administration kept illegal Mexican kids in detention camps as ‘experiment’"
rationale: While the Obama administration did detain undocumented children and families—expanding family detention and processing large numbers of Central American and Mexican minors—there is no credible evidence that those children were held as part of an intentional "experiment." Reported actions were immigration enforcement responses, pilot alternatives-to-detention programs, and legal/practical constraints (e.g., the Flores settlement), not ethically sanctioned experiments on children.

claim: "The pope and Donald Trump and Tammy Baldwin all agree" on eliminating the "carried-interest" tax break.
rationale: Sen. Tammy Baldwin has publicly supported ending the carried‑interest tax preference, but Pope Francis has only spoken broadly against tax avoidance and inequality and has not specifically called for eliminating the technical “carried interest” provision. Donald Trump’s statements on carried interest have been mixed and not a clear, enduring public endorsement of full elimination. Because the three have not all explicitly agreed on that specific tax change, the blanket claim is false.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Duffy is among seven "Tea Party freshmen" who "spent an average of $15,000 on cars for themselves."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While some 2010 freshmen Republicans used campaign funds to buy or reimburse vehicles, available reporting does not support a clear, accurate statement that Rep. Sean Duffy was specifically one of seven 'Tea Party freshmen' who 'spent an average of $15,000 on cars for themselves.' The characterization conflates purchases made for campaign use or reimbursed expenses with purely personal car purchases and overstates a uniform average.

claim: "We do not have an overcrowding problem. As a matter of fact, Rhode Island has one of the lowest incarceration rates in the country."
rationale: The claim mixes two different assertions: it is true that Rhode Island has generally ranked among states with lower incarceration rates per capita compared with many U.S. states, but that does not by itself prove there is no overcrowding. Overcrowding is a facility-level, time-dependent issue (depends on capacity, jail vs prison populations, pretrial detention, etc.) and cannot be ruled out by a low statewide incarceration rate alone.

claim: The EPA "wants to hire 230,000 new government regulators that will cost the taxpayer $21 billion."
rationale: The EPA has not proposed hiring 230,000 new regulators costing $21 billion; that number far exceeds the agency’s current federal workforce (roughly in the low tens of thousands) and typical annual budget requests. The claim appears to misinterpret or inflate other figures (such as estimates of jobs affected, cumulative costs over time, or state/local roles) rather than a concrete EPA hiring plan.

claim: Says in "our region," 2011 was worst drought year ever recorded.
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it refers to an unspecified "our region" and an absolute claim ("worst ever recorded") that depends on local records and metrics. While 2011 was a historically severe drought in some places (for example parts of the U.S. and East Africa), it was not universally the worst drought on record across all regions.

claim: If you paid rent in March or April, "they got to give" you your money back.
rationale: The statement is an overbroad universal claim that is not true in general: there is no blanket rule that anyone who paid rent in March or April must be refunded. Whether rent must be returned depends on jurisdiction, specific emergency orders or relief programs in effect at the time, and the terms of the lease or landlord-tenant agreement.

claim: "If there is a firearm available, it is 17 times more likely to be used either for suicide or for assaulting a friend, relative, an acquaintance than it is to be used in fending off an intruder."
rationale: The claim gives a precise 17× ratio without a cited source; while multiple studies show that firearms in the home are associated with higher risks of suicide and domestic homicide than with successful defensive use, the estimated multipliers vary widely across studies and depend on definitions and methods. No stable, widely accepted finding uniquely supports the specific 17-times figure as a general rule.

claim: "People are less likely to just vote for party now. … They’re looking at the personalities."
rationale: The claim presents a broad, universal trend that voters have moved away from party loyalty toward personality-focused voting; empirical evidence is mixed and context-dependent. While candidate-centered campaigns and the appeal of personalities can matter in some elections, party identification and partisan polarization remain strong predictors of vote choice in many democracies.

claim: Says New Jersey has "the highest unemployment rate in the region" and "stagnant job growth."
rationale: The statement is unverified and misleading because it gives no timeframe or definition of “the region.” New Jersey’s unemployment rate and job growth have varied over time and are not consistently the highest or uniformly “stagnant” compared with neighboring states; such claims require specific dates and comparator jurisdictions to be supported. Without that context, the blanket assertion is false as presented.

claim: "Obama has proposed 442 tax hikes since taking office."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The 442 figure comes from an advocacy group's expansive tally that counted many disparate items (regulatory fee changes, budget line items, expirations, and proposals) as separate "tax hikes," whereas independent fact-checkers found this methodology inflates the count and many items were not new tax increases or required congressional action.

claim: Says John F. Kennedy "smoked cannabis in the White House, while president, because he suffered from severe back pain and Addison's disease."
rationale: There is no credible contemporary evidence that President John F. Kennedy smoked cannabis in the White House. While JFK did suffer severe chronic back pain and was treated with many prescription drugs (and some sources discuss an adrenal disorder), reputable biographies and declassified medical material do not document presidential cannabis use.

claim: Miami-Dade County is the "No. 1 donor county in the state."
rationale: The statement as written is ambiguous and cannot be verified: it does not specify what kind of donations (political contributions, charitable giving, organ donors, tax revenue, etc.) or the time period. Miami-Dade is Florida’s most populous county and often ranks near the top for several donation categories, but that does not make it universally the “No. 1 donor county in the state.” Without a defined metric and timeframe the claim is unsupported.

claim: "I've created over 40,000 jobs."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits who 'I' refers to, the time period, and how 'created' is defined; without independent documentation (payroll, filings, third‑party reporting) it cannot be confirmed. While some entrepreneurs or officials have plausibly created 40,000+ jobs, this specific claim lacks the necessary evidence and context to be treated as true.

claim: "Under Rick Scott, homeowners are paying higher (home insurance) premiums for less coverage."
rationale: The claim asserts a causal link that under Rick Scott homeowners are paying higher premiums for less coverage, but it’s imprecise and not supported as a general fact. Major premium increases and coverage contractions in Florida largely occurred after Scott left the governor’s office in 2019 and are driven by broader factors (hurricane losses, reinsurance costs, insurer insolvencies and market exits) as well as legislative and regulatory actions by the state, so attributing the trend directly to Scott is misleading.

claim: "Lauren Boebert received a PPP loan for her restaurant."
rationale: Publicly released SBA PPP recipient data and contemporaneous news reporting show Shooters Grill, the restaurant owned by Lauren Boebert, was awarded a Paycheck Protection Program loan in 2020. Multiple media outlets reported the restaurant as a listed recipient.

claim: Tide gauges measuring sea level in Rhode Island since 1930 have risen "maybe about 10 inches since that time."
rationale: NOAA tide-gauge records for Rhode Island (e.g., Providence/Newport area) show roughly on the order of 8–11 inches (20–28 cm) of relative sea-level rise from about 1930 to recent years, so “maybe about 10 inches” is a reasonable, approximate statement. Exact amounts vary by station and the precise start/end years, but the magnitude claimed matches observed tide-gauge trends.

claim: "I got a letter from 20 people who said they wanted their money back, 14 never gave me a penny."
rationale: This is a private, anecdotal claim about specific communications and payments that cannot be independently verified from the information given. Without supporting evidence (copies of the letter, names, or financial records) there is no reliable basis to accept the precise counts stated. Therefore the claim should be treated as unproven and not factual.

claim: "From 1990 to 2015 under (Democratic) control, W. Va. teacher pay rank plummeted from 30th in the nation to 48th."
rationale: The statement combines a specific numeric rank change and an assertion of continuous Democratic control, neither of which is reliably supported. While West Virginia did decline in teacher-pay rankings relative to other states over recent decades, published rankings depend on the data source and methods and do not consistently show 1990=30th and 2015=48th. Additionally, West Virginia was not continuously under Democratic control from 1990–2015 (there was a Republican governor from 1997–2001 and Republicans made legislative gains by 2014), so the claim’s political attribution is misleading.

claim: "We’re at the point of reaching 2 million deportations ... this is a historic level, more than any other president of the United States."
rationale: The claim is misleading: official DHS statistics distinguish between formal removals and returns, and no recent single presidential term reliably produced 2 million formal deportations. The largest totals in the modern era came under the Obama administration when combined removals+returns across two terms exceeded 2 million, while formal removals alone were substantially lower, so saying a current president has done "more than any other" is inaccurate without clarifying definitions or timeframe.

claim: The man in a mugshot is "responsible for lighting 32 of the wildfires" on the West Coast.
rationale: The claim provides no identifying details and there is no widespread, credible reporting or official law-enforcement confirmation that a single individual shown in a mugshot started 32 separate West Coast wildfires. Large-scale attributions like this would be documented in official charges and major news coverage, and viral posts frequently misattribute mugshots to unrelated crimes.

claim: "Coroner saying George Floyd died of drug overdose, not police brutality."
rationale: The Hennepin County Medical Examiner determined George Floyd's manner of death was homicide, finding cardiopulmonary arrest complicating law enforcement subdual, restraint, and neck compression. While toxicology showed fentanyl and methamphetamine in his system and other doctors noted those findings, the official autopsy did not attribute death to a drug overdose alone.

claim: "When they say Mexico can't pay for the wall, I say of course they can. We have a trade deficit with Mexico that's unbelievably big. ... It's billions and billions of dollars -- far more than what we're talking about for the wall."
rationale: It is true the U.S. runs a goods trade deficit with Mexico measured in the tens of billions of dollars annually, but the claim conflates that deficit with Mexico’s ability or obligation to "pay for the wall." Whether the deficit exceeds a particular wall cost depends on which cost estimate is used, and trade deficits represent the value of goods exchanged, not funds Mexico would transfer to the U.S. government to finance a border wall.

claim: Marijuana today is "genetically modified," with THC levels that "far surpass the marijuana" of the 1970s.
rationale: The claim mixes a true fact with a misleading label: average THC concentrations in cannabis have risen markedly since the 1970s due to selective breeding, cloning and modern cultivation techniques, but the vast majority of today’s cannabis is not 'genetically modified' in the sense of laboratory transgenic or gene-edited plants. Describing modern marijuana as genetically modified is inaccurate; higher potency is the result of conventional breeding and production methods.

claim: Says Donald Trump's claim that "there was insufficient evidence and therefore, in our country, a person is innocent" directly contradicts Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s statement.
rationale: Special Counsel Robert Mueller explicitly said his team "did not exonerate" the president and that "if we had had confidence that the President clearly did not commit a crime, we would have said that." That statement directly contradicts the claim that lack of sufficient evidence should be interpreted as a declaration of innocence. Mueller refused to equate the absence of charges in the report with an affirmative finding of innocence.

claim: Military spending cuts, known as the sequester, were President Barack Obama’s idea.
rationale: The automatic across-the-board cuts known as the 2013 sequester were created by the 2011 Budget Control Act as an enforcement mechanism after a congressional 'supercommittee' failed to reach a deal; they were part of a negotiated compromise during the debt-ceiling talks, not an original idea proposed by President Obama. Obama signed the law and agreed to the deal, but the sequester mechanism has legislative origins and precedents predating his administration.

claim: Says five studies show his tax plan can cut rates and still bring the same revenue without raising taxes on the middle class.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify the plan or the five studies, and independent budget analyses typically find tax cuts do not fully pay for themselves without offsetting revenue or large, optimistic growth assumptions. When analysts do find revenue neutrality for tax cuts, it usually rests on narrow assumptions or selective citations; without seeing the specific studies and their methodologies the assertion is misleading.

claim: The federal health care law raises taxes and cuts Medicare.
rationale: The 2010 federal health care law (Affordable Care Act) included revenue-raising provisions—such as the net investment income tax, an additional Medicare payroll tax for high earners, and other excise taxes—and also enacted reductions in Medicare spending (for example lower payments to Medicare Advantage plans and slower payment updates). Those measures were intended to help finance coverage expansions. It did not, however, cut guaranteed traditional Medicare benefits for current enrollees; many of the "cuts" were reductions in future payment rates or transfers within the Medicare program.

claim: "We have one of the lowest mortality rates in the world" from COVID-19.
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it does not identify which country or time period “we” refers to and which mortality metric is meant. COVID-19 mortality comparisons depend on the metric used (case-fatality rate vs deaths per 100,000 population), reporting practices, and the specific timeframe; many countries have both higher and lower rates at different times. Without a specific country and period, the blanket statement that “we have one of the lowest mortality rates in the world” is not supportable.

claim: "Sixty percent of New Jersey doctors do not accept Medicaid patients."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific statewide percentage but there is no consistent, authoritative evidence that 60% of New Jersey doctors refuse Medicaid patients. Medicaid acceptance varies widely by specialty, practice setting, and time period, and available surveys and state reports do not support a single, current 60% refusal rate for all physicians in New Jersey. Without a clear source and breakdown, the precise 60% figure is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Masks will kill quite a few people, it’s well known that they reduce blood oxygen levels and those with respiratory and cardiac disorders will die."
rationale: Clinical studies and public-health guidance show that cloth and surgical masks do not significantly reduce blood oxygen saturation or cause dangerous CO2 retention in the general public or in most people with chronic heart or lung disease. Serious breathing compromise from routine mask use is rare; individuals with acute or severe respiratory failure should follow clinician advice, but the blanket claim that masks will "kill quite a few people" is not supported by evidence.

claim: More than 500,000 mail in ballots in Virginia and 200,000 in Nevada were sent to dead people or pets
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and state election officials found no evidence that Virginia sent over 500,000 mail ballots to dead people or that Nevada sent 200,000 to dead people or pets. The viral numbers conflated different datasets — such as inactive or duplicate registration records and mass mailings of ballot applications — with ballots actually mailed to confirmed-deceased registrants. Officials note that ballots are not routinely issued to removed or confirmed-deceased registrations and that safeguards (like signature checks and registration updates) reduce the risk of such mass mailings to ineligible recipients.

claim: Says the "South African Government is now seizing land from white farmers" and alleges a "large scale killing of farmers" in the country.
rationale: While South Africa has ongoing land‑reform debates and has pursued legal mechanisms (including proposals for expropriation without compensation), there is no evidence the government is conducting systematic mass seizures of land specifically from white farmers. Farm attacks and murders do occur and are a serious concern, but available crime data do not show a coordinated, large‑scale campaign to kill farmers; farm murders are a small portion of national homicide figures.

claim: "There have been some estimates that if you deported everybody who is in Texas illegally," it "would create an economic recession for the state."
rationale: Multiple economic studies and analyses by economists and policy groups have produced estimates that mass deportation of all undocumented immigrants from Texas would lead to substantial GDP losses, large job declines, and could push the state into an economic recession. Media coverage and academic work have reported such estimates, though magnitudes vary by methodology and assumptions.

claim: Says there’s "no wait list" for private school vouchers
rationale: The blanket statement that there is "no wait list" for private school vouchers is unsupported. Voucher programs are established at state or local level and many have funding caps, enrollment limits, or application cycles that create wait lists; some programs may have no wait list but others do, so the universal claim is false or at least misleading.

claim: "If we went back to the obesity rates that existed back in the 1980s, the Medicare system over several years could save as much as a trillion dollars."
rationale: The claim gives a precise large savings figure without a cited timeframe or source; peer-reviewed and government estimates do show obesity drives substantial Medicare costs but do not support a well‑established, consensus figure that returning to 1980s obesity rates would cut Medicare spending by as much as $1 trillion over just “several years.” Estimates of potential savings vary widely depending on assumptions and tend to be much smaller or calculated over different populations/time horizons. Because the claim is specific and undocumented, it is not supported as stated.

claim: "In this country, we have a 25 percent dropout rate."
rationale: The claim gives no country, year, educational level, or definition of 'dropout rate', so it cannot be verified as stated. Dropout rates vary widely across countries and by how they are measured, and international datasets show many different values rather than a universal 25 percent.

claim: Coca-Cola, Ben & Jerry’s and other companies support rioting.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Coca‑Cola, Ben & Jerry’s, or similar mainstream companies explicitly endorse or fund rioting. These companies have issued public statements in support of racial justice or made donations to nonprofits and advocacy groups, which is often conflated on social media with endorsing violence. Public corporate support for causes does not equal support for rioting, and specific claims that they finance riots have been debunked in multiple fact‑checks.

claim: Only "18 percent of jobs are accessible by transit for metro Atlanta residents. 33 percent for those living in the city."
rationale: I cannot confirm the exact figures as stated. While multiple transit-accessibility studies for Atlanta report relatively low percentages of jobs reachable by transit, published estimates vary widely by year, travel-time threshold, and the geographic definitions of “metro” versus “city,” and no authoritative source clearly supports the precise 18% (metro) / 33% (city) claim without additional context.

claim: "The first (state) budget that came out of our Republican leadership slashed funding to Planned Parenthood...It resulted in the reduction of hours, the elimination of days, elimination of access to women in my city and all over my state."
rationale: The claim lacks any specific state, year, or budget text, so it cannot be independently verified as stated. While Republican-led state budgets in some states have cut public funding or redirected funds away from Planned Parenthood and those cuts have in some cases led to reduced services or clinic closures, the broad, unqualified assertion here cannot be confirmed without more context.

claim: "Barbara Buono by the numbers: As a Trenton politician, she voted to raise taxes 154 times. Under her, property taxes up 70 percent. Backed a 16 percent sales tax increase. Utilities, nursing homes, cell phones, parking lots, lottery wins, gyms – She taxed them all. Architect of Corzine’s budget, she drove New Jersey $2 billion into debt. Barbara Buono by the numbers: taking New Jersey backwards."
rationale: The claim bundles several specific numeric allegations that are misleading or unproven. The "154 votes" figure is a campaign attack metric that lacks context (it likely counts many procedural or non-tax measures), property tax growth is a statewide trend caused by many factors and cannot be directly attributed to one legislator, and characterizing Buono as the sole "architect" who "drove" New Jersey $2 billion into debt overstates her individual role in multi-actor budget processes. Other specific tax claims (e.g., a 16% sales tax increase and taxing a long list of items) are either factually incorrect as stated or presented without necessary context.

claim: "This is the slowest job recovery since Hoover."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and misleading. The 2007–2009 job recovery was unusually slow in the post‑World War II era, but comparing it to the Hoover/Great Depression era is not accurate without specifying the metric and dates — the 1930s saw far deeper and longer job losses and recoveries. Many reputable analyses say it was the slowest recovery since World War II, not since Hoover.

claim: "Hidden" in the healthcare.gov code is language that means users "waive any reasonable right to privacy of your personal information."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that healthcare.gov contains a hidden clause that makes users 'waive any reasonable right to privacy of your personal information.' The official site and published privacy policy describe how data are collected, used, and shared for enrollment and administration; a blanket waiver of privacy rights would conflict with federal privacy laws and would be legally dubious. Circulating claims typically misinterpret code comments, analytics/cookie notices, or terms of use language rather than show a binding blanket waiver.

claim: Quotes Winston Churchill as saying "Diplomacy is the art of telling people to go to hell in such a way that they ask for directions."
rationale: No reliable primary-source evidence shows Winston Churchill actually said this line. The quip is widely and repeatedly attributed to Churchill in popular usage, but quote researchers have not found it in his speeches or writings and have identified earlier or alternate attributions. Because the phrase appears in print without a solid original source, the Churchill attribution is considered a misattribution.

claim: "Interior deportations under Obama were down 40 percent and at a nine-year low."
rationale: The statement is misleading because whether interior removals fell '40 percent' and were at a 'nine-year low' depends on the chosen baseline year and the exact DHS/ICE metric used. While interior removals did decline in some years as enforcement priorities shifted under Obama, DHS/ICE annual statistics do not consistently support a blanket 40% drop and a clear nine-year low without specifying the comparison years and whether 'interior deportations' means ICE removals, removals after interior apprehensions, or another subset.

claim: A Marine painted his house red, white and blue after he "was told by his neighbors that he could not fly the American flag in his yard all year long."
rationale: I could not find reliable, verifiable evidence that a Marine painted his house red, white and blue specifically in response to neighbors telling him he could not fly the American flag year-round. This appears to be a recurring unverified viral anecdote about veterans and flag/HOA disputes rather than a documented incident.

claim: "We're No. 46 out of 50 states... we're 46th in terms of percentage of deaths in nursing homes."
rationale: The statement cannot be confirmed as presented because it fails to identify which state, what time period, or whether it refers to COVID-19 deaths versus all-cause deaths; rankings of states by percentage of deaths occurring in nursing homes have varied by source and over time. Because the claim lacks necessary specifics and such rankings are time- and definition-dependent, it is not verifiable and is treated as false.

claim: Says Joe Biden stayed silent about violence at Black Lives Matter protests.
rationale: Joe Biden did not "stay silent" about violence during the Black Lives Matter protests—he issued multiple public statements, speeches, and interviews in 2020 that condemned violence, urged peaceful protest and de‑escalation, and called for accountability and reforms. Critics sometimes argued about the timing or strength of particular responses, but the broad claim that he stayed silent is inaccurate.

claim: Says Jeb Bush "said he would take his pants off and moon everybody ... Nobody reports that."
rationale: There is no credible record in major news outlets, campaign transcripts, or reliable archives of Jeb Bush saying he would 'take his pants off and moon everybody.' The phrase appears to be a misattribution, satire, or fabricated quote rather than a documented public statement. Given the absence of documentation from reliable sources, the claim is false.

claim: Hillary Clinton "has already said she's going to wipe out the Second Amendment. She doesn't believe in the First Amendment. And, she also believes in big government, which flies in the face of the 10th Amendment"
rationale: This statement is a misleading conflation of rhetoric and policy: Hillary Clinton has advocated for stricter gun regulations (e.g., universal background checks, assault-weapons restrictions) but has not stated she would ‘wipe out’ the Second Amendment. She has repeatedly affirmed support for free speech and criticized media practices at times, but has not publicly denied the First Amendment. While she favors an active federal role in many policy areas, characterizing that as a rejection of the Tenth Amendment is a political interpretation rather than a factual quote or clear policy commitment to nullify states’ powers.

claim: "There’s more murders with hammers last year than...shotguns and pistols and AK-47s."
rationale: The claim is unlikely to be true: in the United States and in most countries, firearms (including handguns, shotguns, and rifles) account for a larger share of homicides than blunt instruments such as hammers. National homicide statistics from agencies that track method of killing consistently show firearms as the leading method while blunt objects are a small minority. Because the claim gives no country or year it is unsubstantiated as stated.

claim: "Court orders Obama to pay $400 million in restitution."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or major media reporting that a court has ordered former President Barack Obama to pay $400 million in restitution. A judgment of that size against a former president would be widely documented in court records and news coverage, and none exist. The claim appears to be fabricated or misattributed.

claim: "KXL Radio in Portland reported today that Firefighters are now being shot at by suspected Antifa and BLM members."
rationale: There is no independently verifiable evidence that KXL in Portland reported firefighters are being shot at by suspected Antifa and BLM members. A claim this serious would almost certainly be corroborated by multiple reputable local or national news outlets and official agencies; absent that corroboration, the assertion appears to be an unverified rumor and is likely false.

claim: Aaron Bean voted to give illegal immigrants in-state tuition.
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record that Aaron Bean voted to grant in-state tuition to undocumented (often described as 'illegal') immigrants. Available public roll-call records and contemporary reporting do not show him supporting such a measure, and without a specific bill or date the claim is unsubstantiated. Given the ambiguity about which legislative body or vote is referenced, the assertion is not supported.

claim: "More businesses are closing than opening in Virginia today."
rationale: The statement is a time-specific factual claim for which I have no access to real-time Virginia business opening/closure data, so it cannot be verified. Business openings and closures vary day-to-day and require current official records (state business filings, labor statistics, local reports) to confirm. Absent such evidence, the claim should be treated as unverified and therefore classified as false.

claim: "Years of economic decay are over" because Trump "reversed the failed economic policies of the previous administration."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the U.S. economy was generally recovering from the Great Recession before Trump (falling unemployment, positive GDP growth), so the premise of "years of economic decay" is false. While Trump enacted tax cuts and deregulatory measures that affected growth and corporate profits, independent analyses find mixed effects and do not support the simple causal claim that he "reversed" prior policies and thereby ended long-term decay. Attribution of broad economic recovery to a single administration’s actions without specifying metrics or timeframe is not supported by the evidence.

claim: "We have the lowest corporate tax rate since 1968."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous—'we' and which corporate tax rate (federal vs combined federal+state, statutory vs effective) are not specified. For example, in the United States the federal statutory rate was cut to 21% in 2018, lower than the statutory rates in the decades immediately preceding 2018, but combined or effective corporate tax burdens can differ and may not be the lowest since 1968. Because the statement lacks jurisdiction and a clear rate definition it cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Says Missouri Democratic Senate candidate Jason Kander is "attending fancy dinners all over the country."
rationale: The statement is a vague, hyperbolic assertion and there is no verifiable evidence that Jason Kander was routinely "attending fancy dinners all over the country." While Kander, like many national candidates, participated in fundraising events and appearances outside Missouri during his Senate campaign, the specific claim that he attended fancy dinners nationwide is unsubstantiated and overstated.

claim: "324,000 pregnant people experience domestic violence during their pregnancy."
rationale: The claim gives a precise number but provides no context (country or timeframe). While similar figures near 324,000 have appeared in past U.S. public-health estimates of pregnant women experiencing intimate partner violence annually, the statement as presented is unverified and misleading without specifying scope and source.

claim: "If you’re a single mom, and you’ve two kids in the city of Richmond, you can almost make $50,000 a year on the public dole."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization: typical cash welfare (TANF) and food benefits (SNAP) are modest, and while adding tax credits, housing subsidies and Medicaid's imputed value increases total household support, it is uncommon for a single mother with two children in a U.S. city named Richmond to receive nearly $50,000 a year solely from public benefits. Some combinations of generous local housing vouchers, tax credits, and in-kind benefits could raise total resource value in particular cases, but the blanket statement is misleading. Therefore the claim as phrased is false.

claim: Says Florida Gov. Rick Scott "just signed a bill that could make most of Florida’s beaches private."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Gov. Rick Scott signed a law that would convert most of Florida’s beaches into private property. Florida law and the public trust doctrine preserve public rights to use much of the beach (notably the wet-sand area up to the mean high tide line), and while some legislation can affect shoreline access or property-owner rights in limited ways, it does not wholesale privatize most beaches.

claim: Says Bruce Braley took "tens of thousands from his friends in the health insurance industry" and gave them "special favors" by voting for Obamacare.
rationale: Public records show Bruce Braley voted for the Affordable Care Act and he received some contributions from the broader health sector like many members of Congress, but there is no substantiated evidence that he took specifically “tens of thousands” from friends in the health insurance industry or that he granted them identifiable quid pro quo “special favors” by his vote. The claim combines an imprecise assertion about donors with an unproven allegation of corrupt exchange.

claim: "Disease-ridden" migrants from parts of Africa with Ebola are being "dumped in San Antonio."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official reporting that migrants carrying Ebola from Africa are being transported and abandoned in San Antonio. Public-health agencies, local health departments, and reputable news fact-checkers have not substantiated any mass arrivals of Ebola-infected migrants; Ebola causes severe, recognizable illness and would trigger detection, isolation, and contact-tracing under standard protocols.

claim: Hillary Clinton advocates "a freeze on foreclosures. Barack Obama said no."
rationale: The statement is misleading and lacks context: during the 2008 financial crisis Hillary Clinton supported measures to help homeowners but did not clearly endorse a single, broad "freeze on foreclosures" as a universal policy, and Barack Obama did not issue a simple one-word public refusal of such a proposal. Both candidates publicly backed targeted homeowner relief and interventions rather than an unqualified, across-the-board moratorium, so the binary claim is not supported as stated.

claim: "We are almost halfway to our goal of 1,000 rapes prosecuted!"
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no jurisdiction, timeframe, data source, or definition of what counts as a 'rape prosecuted.' Without those specifics and supporting official statistics, the claim cannot be confirmed and should be treated as false. Prosecution counts vary widely by place and year and require authoritative records to substantiate.

claim: Says opponent Ted Cruz has not led businesses.
rationale: The claim that Ted Cruz 'has not led businesses' is misleading. Cruz’s career includes private-sector leadership roles—he worked in private law practice and served as a partner/lead counsel and as Texas Solicitor General, positions that involve managing teams and business responsibilities—though he has not been the CEO of a major publicly traded company.

claim: When he was Milwaukee County executive, "eight years in a row we pushed through budgets that did not increase the tax levy from the previous year."
rationale: The statement is misleading: while Milwaukee County executives (notably Scott Walker) frequently said they avoided raising the county tax levy in budget votes, independent fact-checkers and reporting found exceptions and technical increases in some years once debt service, accounting shifts, or changes in what counts toward the levy are included. The claim depends on a narrow definition of 'tax levy' and omits years with levy increases or other tax/fee hikes tied to county budgets.

claim: Says 2010 was the "worst year ever for America's doctors" reimbursed by Medicare.
rationale: Calling 2010 the “worst year ever” for doctors reimbursed by Medicare is a subjective claim and is not supported by objective, consistent evidence. Medicare payment history across the SGR era included multiple years with large threatened cuts and stopgap patches, and there is no clear metric showing 2010 uniquely worse than other years.

claim: A Fox News affiliate reported on a shooting before it happened.
rationale: The claim is vague and unsubstantiated as stated; there is no verified, widely accepted example showing a Fox News affiliate reliably reported a shooting before it occurred. Apparent instances usually stem from timestamp issues, time zone differences, wire-service updates, or post-publication edits rather than true pre-reporting.

claim: "When Rachel Zenzinger was on the Arvada City Council, she voted to spend taxpayer funds for a junket to China."
rationale: I could not find clear public records or reputable contemporaneous reporting showing that Rachel Zenzinger, while serving on the Arvada City Council, voted to authorize taxpayer-funded travel described as a 'junket' to China. Allegations of this sort require specific council meeting minutes or local news documentation, which are not evident in the available information.

claim: The administration has issued rules for "$1 abortions in ObamaCare" and "requires all persons enrolled in insurance plans that include elective abortion coverage to pay" an abortion premium.
rationale: The administration did issue rules requiring insurers offering elective abortion coverage on ACA exchanges to account for and collect a separate abortion premium so federal subsidies are not used for elective abortions, but there was no rule creating a '$1 abortion' price — that figure arose from misinterpretation and marketing examples. Also, only people who enroll in plans that include elective abortion coverage would pay that separate premium, not 'all persons' generally.

claim: Bill McCollum "backed Jim Greer's effort to hide financial irregularities."
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence that Bill McCollum actively backed an effort by Jim Greer to hide financial irregularities. Jim Greer faced internal party disputes and later legal trouble over party funds, but mainstream reporting does not show McCollum supporting a cover-up. Allegations tying McCollum to hiding irregularities appear unproven and contested.

claim: Says the Georgia Dome would need up to $350 million in work over the next five to seven years.
rationale: I cannot corroborate a widely reported, authoritative estimate that the Georgia Dome specifically would need up to $350 million in work over the next five to seven years; public discussion at the time focused on replacing the aging Dome with a new stadium rather than committing to a single $350M refurbishment figure. While there were various cost estimates and repair concerns, no clear, well-sourced projection matching that exact amount and timeframe is verifiable from general reporting.

claim: "BREAKING: Trump family donates $1 billion to wall fund."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public disclosure that any member of the Trump family donated $1 billion to a wall fund. Major donations of that magnitude would have been widely reported and reflected in campaign/PAC filings and tax/financial disclosures, but available records and media coverage show no such gift; past fundraising for the wall totaled far less.

claim: Before "our last three presidents, you have to go back to the 1800s, early 1800s to find three presidents in a row being consecutively re-elected."
rationale: This is incorrect. Bill Clinton (re-elected 1996), George W. Bush (re-elected 2004), and Barack Obama (re-elected 2012) are three consecutive presidents who each won re-election, so you do not have to go back to the early 1800s to find such a run. The claim likely misstates timing or which presidents are meant.

claim: Says Conor Lamb "ran on a campaign that said very nice things about me."
rationale: The statement is an unattributed quote and lacks necessary context (who said it, when, and what messaging is referenced). Without a source or evidence that Conor Lamb’s campaign explicitly ran messages praising the unnamed speaker, the claim is unverifiable and cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: Delaware has the "eighth-largest black population in the country"
rationale: By absolute numbers, Delaware’s Black population (roughly a few hundred thousand) is far smaller than those of the largest states (e.g., Texas, Florida, Georgia, New York, California, North Carolina, Illinois, etc.), so it is not the eighth-largest Black population in the U.S. The claim likely confuses rankings by proportion or by a smaller geography, but as stated (absolute statewide Black population) it is incorrect.

claim: "The child tax credit, if we don't do it, there will be no tax relief for working families. How much tax relief working families get under tax reform is entirely dependent on whether or not we put in place an increase to the child tax credit."
rationale: Whether working families receive tax relief does not depend solely on the child tax credit; other parts of tax reform—such as changes to tax rates, brackets, the standard deduction, or expansions of credits like the Earned Income Tax Credit—can provide relief. Saying there would be 'no' tax relief without a child tax credit increase is inaccurate because alternative provisions can and have delivered benefits to working families.

claim: Says the logo of a porn website appeared during a CNN broadcast.
rationale: The claim is vague and I find no widely reported, verifiable evidence that a porn-site logo actually appeared on an official CNN broadcast; many viral clips of this type have been edited or misattributed. Without a date, timestamp, or credible source, the assertion cannot be substantiated and is likely a manipulated or out-of-context video.

claim: Says Ayn Rand said, "The question isn’t who is going to let me; it’s who is going to stop me."
rationale: This pithy line is widely and consistently attributed to Ayn Rand in quotation collections and popular references, reflecting her themes of individualism and determination. Therefore the claim that Ayn Rand said, "The question isn't who is going to let me; it's who is going to stop me," is accurate.

claim: Says Betsy Devos said "only" 0.02% of kids are likely to die when they go back to school.
rationale: I cannot confirm that Betsy DeVos uttered the specific claim that “only 0.02% of kids are likely to die when they go back to school.” While she publicly argued in 2020 that children face a low risk from COVID-19 and cited small mortality figures, fact-checkers reported her use of statistics was misleading or taken out of context rather than a precise, supported statement that 0.02% are "likely to die" on return to school.

claim: When Terry McAuliffe was governor, "Unemployment went down in every single county, including rural Virginia by nearly 50%.
rationale: State and county-level labor statistics for McAuliffe's term (2014–2017) show unemployment fell in most but not literally every Virginia county; a small number of counties/independent cities saw little change or small increases over some months. The claim that rural Virginia unemployment fell "by nearly 50%" is an overstatement when applied uniformly — while some jurisdictions experienced large percentage declines (because their starting rates were high), the median and many rural areas saw much smaller reductions.

claim: Wisconsin was embroiled in a "constitutional crisis" brought on by the Democratic senators fleeing the state for Illinois to block Gov. Scott Walker's budget-repair bill.
rationale: In 2011 fourteen Democratic Wisconsin state senators left the state (many traveling to Illinois) to deny quorum and block consideration of Governor Scott Walker’s budget-repair bill, triggering a major legal and political standoff that many outlets and observers described as a constitutional or governmental crisis. The action directly precipitated the statewide protests and an extended confrontation over quorum, legislative procedure, and executive authority.

claim: "We have a 40 to 50 percent dropout rate in our inner-city schools."
rationale: The claim is a broad, unqualified statement about 'our inner-city schools' with no place or time specified. In the United States and many other countries, overall high school dropout rates have fallen and are far below 40–50% today; while some specific schools or districts (especially historically or in particular local contexts) have experienced very high dropout rates, a 40–50% rate is not a general, current fact for 'inner-city schools' as a whole.

claim: Says "76 percent of all voters in the United States say they want Johnson-Weld, by name, in the presidential debates."
rationale: No reputable national poll supports that 76% of all U.S. voters specifically named 'Johnson-Weld' as wanting them in the presidential debates. Such a high figure is inconsistent with mainstream polling on third‑party debate inclusion and is likely drawn from a non‑representative sample, a push‑poll, or misinterpreted subgroup results.

claim: "The price tag amounted to nearly $4,200 for every man, woman and child in the state."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and lacks the necessary context (which state, what 'price tag', and timeframe), so it cannot be verified as stated. Confirming such a per-capita figure requires the precise total cost and the state's population at the relevant time; without those data the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: Australia is microchipping its public.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Australian government is conducting a program to microchip the general public. Reports of RFID or implant use have been limited to isolated, voluntary private-sector or medical applications and have been seized on by conspiracy theories, not corroborated government policy or mass programs.

claim: "Statistics show one male cat can father 420,000 kittens in five years."
rationale: The figure is implausibly high given cat biology and demographic limits. Female cats have a ~63–65 day gestation, reach sexual maturity several months after birth, and produce only a few litters per year with average litter sizes of 3–5; survival, maternal capacity, and time-to-maturity prevent a single male from fathering 420,000 live kittens in five years. Claims that large numbers arise use unrealistic exponential math that ignores these biological and ecological constraints.

claim: Says that as president, Barack Obama has not gone to the Texas-Mexico border
rationale: Public records and news coverage indicate President Obama visited the U.S.–Mexico border region during his time in office, so the absolute claim that he never went is incorrect. However, whether he specifically set foot on the Texas segment of the border is less clear in summary accounts and requires checking detailed presidential travel logs.

claim: "Hillary ignored multiple requests for security, didn’t respond for 13 hours, & let 4 Americans die in Benghazi. Trump rushed in reinforcements, threatened to destroy Iran, & made sure no lives were lost in Baghdad."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate facts, exaggerations, and unsupported causal attributions. Four Americans did die in the 2012 Benghazi attacks, but multiple official investigations (including the State Department Accountability Review Board and congressional inquiries) found systemic security failures rather than evidence that Hillary Clinton personally ignored repeated requests or sat silent for 13 hours with criminal culpability. Donald Trump did issue aggressive rhetoric toward Iran and authorized military actions (notably the strike that killed Qasem Soleimani), but the specific assertions that he "rushed in reinforcements" to Baghdad and thereby "made sure no lives were lost in Baghdad" are not supported by public records and conflate separate events and outcomes.

claim: "House Bill 6627 also requires the applicant to attest to their eligibility to vote, as is required by the National Voter Registration Act and used by all other states that have (automatic voter registration)."
rationale: While the National Voter Registration Act does require a voter attestation on registration forms and many automatic voter registration (AVR) systems incorporate an eligibility attestation, I cannot confirm that the specific text of 'House Bill 6627' contains that attestation requirement. The claim asserts a specific provision of a particular bill without quoting its language or jurisdiction, so it is not verifiable as stated. Without the bill text or state context, the assertion should not be treated as proven.

claim: Says Ted Cruz "said I was in favor in Libya. I never discussed that subject."
rationale: There is no record in major news reporting or available transcripts of Ted Cruz using the exact phrase quoted here. While Cruz has made public statements about U.S. policy in Libya, this specific line appears to be a garbled or misattributed quote rather than a documented statement he actually made.

claim: "Seventy percent of all Texans are overweight or obese."
rationale: The statement gives no year or age group and is therefore imprecise. Public-health survey data show adult obesity in Texas is in the mid-30% range and combined overweight-plus-obesity estimates depend on the source and age group; while adult combined rates can approach around 70% in some datasets, including children or using different definitions yields lower percentages, so the blanket claim about 'all Texans' is unsupported.

claim: The Democrats’ Green New Deal includes "working towards ending air travel."
rationale: The official Green New Deal resolutions do not call for "ending air travel." They call for achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions and for investments in zero-emission vehicle infrastructure, public transit and high-speed rail, and reducing transportation-sector pollution, but do not mandate banning or eliminating air travel. Sponsors and supporters have also rejected the claim that the resolution seeks to stop flying.

claim: "In Oregon, students are skipping math class to learn about the Bible."
rationale: This is an overbroad claim with no evidence of a statewide pattern in Oregon. Public schools are generally barred from providing religious instruction as curriculum; while isolated incidents, private religious schools, or released-time programs may involve students missing academic classes for Bible study, that does not support the blanket statement that students in Oregon are skipping math class to learn the Bible.

claim: "Over 80 percent of the people want the shot to vote" on whether to approve same-sex marriage, according to polls.
rationale: The claim is overly broad and unsupported: there is no general polling consensus showing that over 80% of people want a public vote on approving same-sex marriage. Poll outcomes vary widely by country, time, and exact question wording, and most national polls ask about support for legalization rather than desire for a referendum.

claim: "Two out of our last three governors in Virginia were investigated by the FBI. One went to jail and one is running for office again in this election."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. Among recent Virginia governors only Bob McDonnell was federally prosecuted (his 2014 conviction was later overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court), and Ralph Northam and Glenn Youngkin were not the subject of FBI criminal investigations; Terry McAuliffe did run again for governor in 2021 but was not known to have been investigated by the FBI. Therefore the statement that two of the last three were investigated, with one jailed and one running again, misstates the facts.

claim: Obama "voted for and even sponsored amendments that were intended to kill the (immigration overhaul) legislation."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Senator Barack Obama voted for or sponsored amendments intended to wreck comprehensive immigration overhaul. Obama’s Senate record and public statements show he generally supported comprehensive immigration reform; while he voted on many procedural and substantive amendments, credible sources do not show he authored measures designed to ‘kill’ the legislation.

claim: "No city in the state can quarantine itself without state approval."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and therefore false: authority to impose quarantines varies by state. Many states delegate public-health powers to local health departments or allow municipal emergency orders, while others preempt local action or require state approval; practices during COVID-19 showed both local independent orders and state preemption depending on jurisdiction.
