claim: "Since 1904, the Ohio victor has won the presidency 25 out of 27 times "
rationale: The statement was true if measured only through the 2008 election (1904–2008: Ohio picked the winner 25 of 27 times), but it is outdated as a general claim. Including later elections (notably 2020, when Ohio voted for the losing candidate) changes the tally and makes the standalone claim incorrect without an end date.

claim: "We have over a million (legal immigrants) a year, more than at any time in the history of this country. We have the largest percentage of immigrants, almost tied now with the historical high as a percentage of immigrants living in this country."
rationale: Recent years have seen roughly one million lawful permanent residents admitted annually, but that level is not clearly the highest in U.S. history and depends on which measure and year are used. The long‑run share of foreign‑born people in the U.S. was higher or comparable in the late 19th/early 20th centuries, so the claim that current admissions and the immigrant percentage are the largest ever is misleading.

claim: Photo of vaccine package with 2018 date stamp shows COVID-19 outbreak was planned.
rationale: A photo of a vaccine package stamped 2018 does not prove the COVID-19 outbreak was planned. SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in late 2019, and package dates can represent manufacture, expiry, lot numbers, or pertain to unrelated vaccines or research stock; a lone image without provenance is insufficient evidence of a coordinated plan.

claim: "The Obama administration has even joined Islamist governments in sponsoring a U.N. resolution that would shred our First Amendment by threatening to make discussion of radical Islamism potentially illegal."
rationale: The claim exaggerates and misstates facts. The Obama administration did engage at the UN on resolutions addressing religious hatred (notably the 2011 HRC effort around combating intolerance), but those UN resolutions are non‑binding, focused on preventing incitement to violence and discrimination, and did not direct the U.S. to outlaw discussion or criticism of radical Islamism or override the First Amendment.

claim: "New Jersey's governor cut $1.6 billion from public education while handing out $2.1 billion in corporate tax breaks, more than the entire previous decade."
rationale: The statement mixes specific dollar figures and a multi-year comparison without a clear timeframe or source. While New Jersey governors in the 2010s did cut some education aid and expanded business tax incentives, the precise claims that $1.6 billion was cut from public education at the same time $2.1 billion in corporate tax breaks were handed out — and that the latter exceeds the entire previous decade — are not verifiable as stated and depend on definitions and accounting choices.

claim: A photo shows a recent White House event was actually filmed at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that a recent White House event photo was filmed at Tyler Perry Studios; official White House events are normally held on White House grounds and prior viral claims that purportedly show otherwise have been debunked by image provenance checks. Absent verifiable metadata or credible reporting tying the image to Tyler Perry Studios, the assertion is not supported.

claim: "At the moment, energy companies spend 0.25 percent on R&D."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and likely incorrect as a blanket statement: R&D spending by "energy companies" varies widely by firm, subsector, country and how spending is measured, so a single figure of 0.25% is unsupported. Many large oil and gas companies historically report R&D intensity that can be below 1% of revenue but not uniformly exactly 0.25%, and some utilities and technology-focused energy firms spend more. Without specifying the denominator (revenue, GDP or something else), time period, region, or which companies are included, the claim is unreliable.

claim: Says Amber Alerts are issued for white kids "but not Black kids in Milwaukee."
rationale: AMBER Alerts are intended to be issued based on objective criteria (confirmed abduction, imminent danger, age, and sufficient descriptive information), not race, and the blanket statement that they are issued for white kids but not Black kids in Milwaukee is an overgeneralization lacking supporting data. While reporting and academic studies have documented disparities in media attention and sometimes in how missing-child cases are handled for children of different races, that does not validate the categorical claim about Milwaukee without case-by-case evidence.

claim: Says opposing the Paycheck Fairness Act is part of the Koch brothers’ agenda.
rationale: Koch-affiliated organizations and the broader Koch network have publicly opposed the Paycheck Fairness Act and lobbied against pay-equity measures, consistent with their longstanding agenda of opposing regulations they view as burdensome to businesses. Reporting and advocacy records show groups linked to the Kochs campaigned against the legislation and supported senators who blocked it.

claim: "In 2011, texting surpassed alcohol as the leading contributing factor in teen driving deaths."
rationale: Contemporary crash-data reports and later fact-checks do not support that texting overtook alcohol in 2011 as the single leading contributing factor in teen driving deaths. Official datasets show alcohol remained a major contributor, and while 'distracted driving' (a category that can include texting) became more prominent, texting specifically was underreported and not clearly established as the top factor that year.

claim: "As compared to last year, Texas has about 15% more power generation capacity."
rationale: A 15% year-over-year jump in Texas generation capacity would equal roughly 10–15 GW given ERCOT’s ~80–100 GW fleet, which is much larger than typical annual commissioned capacity. Recent real-world additions have been on the order of a few gigawatts and many projects in the interconnection queue are not yet operational; official ERCOT/EIA reports show smaller year-over-year growth. The claim therefore likely overstates the actual change.

claim: "Most of the people that work in finance make $70,000, $80,000 a year."
rationale: The finance sector includes a wide range of jobs with very different pay levels; while some professional roles commonly earn in the $70k–$80k range or higher, many common finance occupations (e.g., tellers, clerical/bookkeeping staff, some customer-service roles) earn well below that. Labor statistics show a broad distribution of wages rather than most workers clustering in a narrow $70k–$80k band, so the claim that most people in finance make $70k–$80k is inaccurate.

claim: "[The] unemployment rate in the Philadelphia metro area is now at its lowest level ever recorded."
rationale: The claim gives no date or source and therefore cannot be confirmed. Unemployment for the Philadelphia metro area is reported monthly by statistical agencies and has fluctuated over time; asserting it is at an all-time low requires checking the long-term BLS/local series and specifying whether seasonally adjusted or not. Without that evidence the statement is unverified and likely false.

claim: "Washington, D.C., now has greater population than Wyoming and Vermont, more active duty military than 29 states, more tax revenue than 29 states (and) a larger domestic product than 27 states."
rationale: The first part is correct: Washington, D.C.'s population exceeds those of Wyoming and Vermont based on recent census counts. However, the other numerical claims are unsupported and likely incorrect or misleading: publicly available data do not clearly show D.C. has more active‑duty military personnel than 29 states, nor unambiguously more tax revenue than 29 states or a larger GDP than 27 states without specifying year and definitions. Because the grouped claim mixes a correct population statement with other dubious or context‑dependent assertions, the overall claim is false.

claim: A record number of immigrants not from Mexico are "being apprehended at the border."
rationale: The claim is too vague and lacks a specific timeframe or jurisdiction; without that context it cannot be verified as true. U.S. Customs and Border Protection data do show spikes in encounters of non-Mexican nationals in certain months and years, but saying a blanket 'record number are being apprehended at the border' is unsupported without specifying which border and which period. Terminology (apprehended vs encountered) and changing monthly/yearly trends mean the statement as written is misleading.

claim: Giant companies like Toyota will not locate in a state that has not passed a right-to-work law
rationale: This is not universally true. Large manufacturers like Toyota make location decisions based on a mix of factors (workforce skills, logistics, taxes and incentives, supply chain) and have historically located plants in jurisdictions both with and without right-to-work laws. While some firms may prefer right-to-work states or consider labor-law environment, it is not an absolute rule that they will refuse to locate in non–right-to-work states.

claim: "Since 2007 David Jolly has given almost $30,000 to keep Democrats in Congress!"
rationale: I could not corroborate the assertion that David Jolly has given nearly $30,000 since 2007 specifically 'to keep Democrats in Congress.' Public campaign finance records (FEC/OpenSecrets) are the authoritative source for such donations and do not appear to support that exact figure or characterization without additional context. Absent verifiable FEC data showing that amount and intent, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Eighty percent of the antibiotics in this country are fed to livestock."
rationale: The statement is too general and lacks necessary context (which country and which year). In the United States at certain times a large majority of antibiotic mass sold was destined for food animals (commonly quoted around 70–80% in past FDA reports), but percentages vary by country, year, and by whether one counts all antimicrobials or only those important to human medicine. Because the claim is absolute and context-free it is misleading as stated.

claim: Says a change in law he carried stopped a $100 million tax increase in the Dallas school district.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who “he” is, which law was changed, or when this allegedly stopped a $100 million tax increase for the Dallas school district. Without a named actor, specific statute, and timeframe, there is no way to confirm causation from public records or news reporting; the claim therefore cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: Schools stopped teaching children cursive so they wouldn’t be able to read the U.S. Constitution and other historical documents.
rationale: The decline in cursive instruction is largely attributed to changing curriculum priorities (including emphasis on keyboarding and standardized-tested skills), limited classroom time, and evolving educational standards, not to a coordinated effort to prevent reading historical documents. Many states and school districts never fully abandoned cursive, and several have enacted laws or policies to keep or restore cursive instruction.

claim: "Florida is one of only 10 states that totally prohibit a (firearm) registry."
rationale: The claim that Florida is one of only 10 states that totally prohibit a firearm registry is inaccurate because the number of states that ban registration varies by source and is higher than 10 when considering statutes that bar any centralized registry or prohibit use of certain data for registration. State laws differ in scope (some ban only certain types of registries or public registries), and Florida’s statutes restrict certain data uses but are not uniquely part of a fixed group of exactly 10 states. Because definitions and statutes change, the exact count cited is misleading.

claim: "I haven't switched my position" on the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify who said it or give a timeframe; without those details public statements and voting records cannot be checked. Many public figures have changed their stance on the Trans-Pacific Partnership over time, so asserting no change without evidence is not supported.

claim: Says David Dewhurst "went out for drinks" during Senate debate on abortion bill.
rationale: I cannot verify the assertion that David Dewhurst "went out for drinks" during a Senate debate on an abortion bill. There is no specific date, source, or widely reported corroboration in known coverage of Dewhurst’s actions; without a verifiable source the allegation remains unverified and should be treated as likely false.

claim: "If your employer is mandating any pokes, do not quit. Make them fire you. That way you get unemployment benefits."
rationale: This is not universally true. Unemployment benefits are administered by government agencies and eligibility depends on jurisdiction and the reason for separation — being fired does not automatically entitle someone to benefits, and being fired for misconduct (which some agencies treat refusal of a lawful workplace mandate as) can disqualify a claimant. Quitting voluntarily likewise typically disqualifies a person unless they had good cause as defined by local law.

claim: Says a WHO proposal "portrays milk and dairy products as an obstacle to a healthy start in life."
rationale: This is a mischaracterization. WHO guidance promotes exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months and advises that unmodified cow’s milk is not appropriate as a replacement for breastmilk in infants under about 12 months, but it does not broadly portray milk and dairy products as an 'obstacle to a healthy start in life.' The guidance targets appropriate infant feeding practices and the promotion of breastmilk, not a blanket condemnation of dairy.

claim: "In the last year, Wisconsin ranked third in Midwest job growth."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because 'last year' and the metric (percentage growth vs. net jobs added) and the definition of 'Midwest' are unspecified. Job‑growth rankings change by data source and time window, so without a cited source this claim cannot be confirmed and is likely inaccurate.

claim: "I have 2 and a half million more votes than he (Sanders) does."
rationale: The statement is missing crucial context (which election, date, and which opponent) and so cannot be verified as a general fact. Vote totals between candidates like Sanders and another person vary by race, date, and whether counting is complete, so the claim as stated is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The National Academy of Medicine points to a significant correlation between marijuana and psychosis, schizophrenia, and other psychotic disorders, particularly in teenagers where the risk of developing schizophrenia increases three fold."
rationale: The National Academies (Institute of Medicine/NASEM) 2017 review did conclude there is substantial evidence of a statistical association between cannabis use and the development of schizophrenia and other psychoses, and that risk is greater with earlier and heavier use. However, the report did not categorically state that teenagers face a threefold increase in schizophrenia risk; individual studies report varying effect sizes (often roughly 2–3x for heavy or early-onset users) but the Academies did not endorse a single uniform “threefold” figure for all teenagers.

claim: Republicans "nominated the 1st Black woman to the SCOTUS & she was BLOCKED & filibustered by… Joe Biden."
rationale: This claim is false. The first Black woman nominated and confirmed to the U.S. Supreme Court is Ketanji Brown Jackson, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden in 2022; she was not nominated by Republicans and Biden did not block or filibuster her. Republicans opposed her confirmation but Biden was the nominating president and supported her confirmation.

claim: Says his administration has made "progress" on border enforcement by "putting more boots on the southern border than at any time in our history and reducing illegal crossings to their lowest levels in 40 years."
rationale: The two linked assertions are misleading. Public border-enforcement staffing and deployments have risen and fallen over different administrations and the phrase “more boots…than at any time in our history” is not supported as a clear, documented superlative; likewise border encounter statistics were not uniformly at a 40‑year low (2020 saw pandemic-driven lows, but subsequent years saw much higher levels). The statement conflates different measures and time periods to create an inaccurate impression of a sustained record low.

claim: "Fifteen years ago, the assets of the six largest banks in this country totaled 17 percent of GDP ... The assets of the six largest banks in the United States today total 63 percent of GDP."
rationale: The claim gives precise percentages but lacks sourcing and a clear timeframe; while the largest U.S. banks did grow markedly after consolidation and the financial crisis, published series and analysis show variation depending on the exact year, which banks are counted, and whether assets are measured domestically or consolidated. Because these specifics materially affect the percentage, the exact paired figures (17% fifteen years earlier and 63% today) cannot be confirmed as accurate as stated and likely overstate a single, unambiguous change.

claim: "Quite frankly, it was during the Bush years of spending, multiplied now by the Obama years that we have this mess."
rationale: The statement is a broad, causal political assertion that oversimplifies complex fiscal history. While federal spending and deficits rose during the Bush administration (tax cuts, wars, Medicare Part D) and increased further around the 2008–2009 financial crisis when the Obama administration enacted stimulus and bailout measures, attributing an unspecified “mess” solely to ‘Bush years multiplied by Obama years’ is unsupported and ignores economic context and subsequent deficit reductions. The claim is therefore not factually accurate as stated.

claim: "By registration fewer than 20 percent of Florida voters are Independents."
rationale: Official Florida voter registration reports show that the 'No Party Affiliation' category (commonly referred to as independents) has exceeded 20% of registered voters in recent years, so the statement that fewer than 20% are independents is incorrect. Terminology can vary, but statewide registration totals place NPA above the 20% threshold.

claim: "We are seeing dramatic rate cuts" to Medicare that will affect seniors’ ability to keep their doctor, hospital and prevention services.
rationale: There is no current, across-the-board "dramatic" cut to Medicare payment rates in effect that would wholesale strip seniors of doctors, hospitals, or preventive services. Medicare reimbursement levels are adjusted annually and some proposals or localized payment changes can affect provider participation, but core Medicare coverage and mandated preventive benefits remain in law and broad loss of access is not supported by available evidence.

claim: "An amendment, pushed by Lyndon Johnson many years ago, threatens religious institutions with a loss of their tax-exempt status if they openly advocate their political views."
rationale: This refers to the 1954 'Johnson Amendment' which Lyndon B. Johnson helped enact; it can jeopardize 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status for organizations, including churches, that intervene in political campaigns by endorsing or opposing candidates. However it does not broadly forbid religious institutions from expressing political views or speaking about public policy issues — only direct political campaign intervention is prohibited.

claim: California’s marijuana legalization initiative, Prop. 64 "allows marijuana smoking ads in prime time, on programs with millions of children and teenage viewers."
rationale: Proposition 64 contains explicit limits on marketing to youth and prohibits advertising directed at persons under 21 or placed where a substantial portion of the audience is underage; it also bars ads near schools/playgrounds and gives regulators authority to set further restrictions. Therefore it does not broadly allow marijuana smoking ads to run during prime-time programs with large child and teen audiences, and the claim is misleading.

claim: Says Donald Trump "says organized crime runs wild on reservations."
rationale: I cannot find a verified record of Donald Trump using the exact phrase 'organized crime runs wild on reservations.' While Trump has made critical statements about crime, drugs, and trafficking in or near some reservations, the specific quoted wording appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution rather than a documented direct quote.

claim: The five states that outlaw collective bargaining for teachers all rank below 44th in the nation in test scores, while Wisconsin ranks 2nd.
rationale: The claim mixes ambiguous legal and statistical assertions that do not hold up: states differ in how they limit or permit collective bargaining for teachers (many restrict it rather than outright outlaw it), and national test-score rankings vary by assessment, grade, subject and year. Wisconsin was not consistently ranked 2nd across standard national assessments, and there is no stable set of “five states” that are uniformly below 44th in all commonly used national test rankings. Therefore the statement is misleading and unsupported.

claim: "Some of the men serving in the (Afghan) armed forces have never driven a vehicle before."
rationale: During the period of international training and by reports from coalition trainers, many Afghan recruits came from remote, rural backgrounds and lacked prior exposure to motor vehicles, so basic driving instruction was commonly required. The country’s low vehicle ownership rates in rural areas and documented training challenges make it plausible and supported that some servicemen had never driven before enlistment. The claim is a general statement about 'some' individuals, which is consistent with these observations.

claim: "The health care price tag for childhood obesity in Georgia is $2.4 billion annually and rising."
rationale: I could not find an authoritative, recent estimate that the annual health-care cost of childhood obesity in Georgia alone is $2.4 billion. State-level published cost estimates typically refer to either all-age medical costs or to lifetime/indirect costs, and a $2.4 billion annual figure for only childhood medical costs appears inconsistent with commonly reported state obesity-cost numbers.

claim: Scientists are "questioning the original idea that man-made global warming is what is causing the climate to change. … (It is) more and more being put into question."
rationale: The overwhelming majority of climate scientists and major scientific organizations conclude that recent global warming is primarily caused by human activities; this is the consensus reflected in multiple studies and IPCC assessment reports. While researchers continue refining details like climate sensitivity and regional effects, the core attribution to anthropogenic greenhouse gases is not increasingly questioned.

claim: It was President Obama's "inaction that caused over three weeks to go by before he even approved the governor's plan to protect our marsh."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific >three-week delay and attributes it directly to President Obama without identifying which governor, marsh, or incident; no verifiable evidence is provided here to confirm that timeline or causal responsibility. Federal approvals for state protection plans typically involve FEMA and other agencies and timelines vary by incident, so a blanket attribution to presidential ‘inaction’ is not supportable without specifics. Given the lack of contextual details and corroborating evidence, the claim as stated is unverified and likely false.

claim: Says "Nicolás Maduro is carrying out a genocide on his people."
rationale: Independent UN investigators and major human-rights organizations have documented widespread abuses, including extrajudicial killings, torture, arbitrary detention and forced displacement by Maduro’s government, but they have not established the specific legal element of intent to destroy a protected group required for a finding of genocide. Official fact-finding reports and legal processes to date characterize the conduct as crimes against humanity and serious human-rights violations rather than genocide.

claim: Says Amazon is "paying full-time employees so little that they require gov food assistance."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. While reporting and studies have documented that some Amazon workers (especially hourly, low‑paid, or part‑time employees) use SNAP and other public benefits, there is no evidence that Amazon pays its full‑time employees so little that they broadly 'require' government food assistance. Amazon raised its U.S. minimum wage to $15/hour in 2018, and dependence on assistance varies by role, location, household size and hours worked.

claim: Congressional benefits include "free health care, outrageous retirement packages, 67 paid holidays, three weeks paid vacation, unlimited paid sick days."
rationale: The claim mixes truth, exaggeration, and errors. Members of Congress are eligible for federal health insurance (FEHB) but pay premiums rather than receiving 'free health care'; retirement is via FERS/CSRS with vesting and age/service rules rather than universally 'outrageous' payouts; there are about a dozen official federal paid holidays (not 67); annual leave accrual varies by tenure (often roughly two to three weeks for newer employees) and sick leave is accrued under federal rules, not 'unlimited.'

claim: "Seismic airgun blasting (used for energy exploration) is ... 16,000 times louder than" a conventional airhorn.
rationale: The specific claim that seismic airgun blasting is "16,000 times louder" than a conventional airhorn is unsupported and misleading because "louder" is not a well‑defined physical metric. Sound is measured in decibels (a logarithmic scale) and comparisons depend on metric (SPL peak, SEL, energy), distance, and frequency weighting; published descriptions typically cite orders of magnitude differences but not a precise, universally applicable 16,000× factor. Without a defined measurement method and conditions, the numeric multiplier is unreliable.

claim: The House passed "cut, cap and balance" with "bipartisan support."
rationale: While the House did pass the "Cut, Cap and Balance" measure in 2011, the vote was overwhelmingly along party lines, with the vast majority of Republican members supporting it and most Democrats opposing it. It did not enjoy broad bipartisan backing; any Democratic votes in favor were minimal and did not constitute meaningful cross-party support.

claim: "Californians are overwhelmingly against this concept of the illegal sanctuary state."
rationale: The claim overstates public opinion: Californians as a whole have not been shown to be 'overwhelmingly against' sanctuary-state policies. California enacted sanctuary-state protections (SB54) and the state's electorate skews Democratic, with many polls showing substantial support for immigrant-protective measures rather than overwhelming opposition. The statement is also vague about what 'this concept' and what timeframe or poll it refers to, making the broad claim misleading.

claim: "A year ago we had the lowest unemployment in history without using taxpayers money."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated and ambiguous — it gives no country or exact date, and the claim that unemployment was the "lowest in history" a year ago cannot be verified without specifying the jurisdiction. Additionally, asserting this occurred "without using taxpayers money" is implausible because government policies (tax-funded programs, unemployment insurance, fiscal stimulus) commonly affect labor markets and there is no evidence that such interventions were wholly absent. Given the ambiguity and lack of supporting evidence, the claim is judged false.

claim: Says "we had to cut 13 billion dollars in state spending over two years."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits which state and which two-year period are meant; without that specificity I cannot confirm the $13 billion figure against budget documents or official spending cuts. Such a claim could be true for some jurisdictions and periods but cannot be treated as factual without supporting, state-level fiscal records or a credible source.

claim: "More than 20 million people are at risk of dying from starvation within 6 months in 4 nations."
rationale: United Nations and humanitarian agencies issued warnings (notably in 2017) that more than 20 million people in four countries—Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northeastern Nigeria—were at risk of famine/starvation within months without urgent assistance. The claim matches those widely reported emergency assessments.

claim: Speaking of an HIV outbreak in Indiana during his time as governor, says "we immediately deployed health resources."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and investigations of the 2015 Scott County, Indiana HIV outbreak show the state did not immediately implement all public-health measures; Indiana initially resisted needle-exchange programs and required outside pressure before broader interventions were authorized. While the governor later defended the response, characterizing it as an immediate deployment of resources is misleading given documented delays and conditional acceptance of harm-reduction steps.

claim: "Within the three miles surrounding the University Circle area, infant mortality exceeds some Third World countries."
rationale: Multiple local public-health reports and news investigations have documented very high infant mortality rates in neighborhoods within a few miles of Cleveland’s University Circle, with some census tracts exhibiting rates comparable to or higher than those reported in certain low- and middle-income countries. While exact rankings depend on the year and the specific countries chosen for comparison, the general claim that infant mortality in that small area exceeds rates in some developing countries has been repeatedly reported.

claim: In the plot to kidnap Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, "the perps were ANTIFA and BLM anarchists."
rationale: Investigations and federal charges identified the suspects as members or associates of a right-wing militia (commonly called the Wolverine Watchmen) and linked to anti-government extremist views, not Antifa or Black Lives Matter. There is no credible evidence tying Antifa or BLM anarchists to the Whitmer kidnapping plot; claims to that effect were debunked by journalists and law enforcement.

claim: Says Donald Trump "cashed in" on Sept. 11,  "collecting $150,000 in federal funds intended to help small businesses recover — even though days after the attack Trump said his properties were not affected."
rationale: Public records and contemporary news reporting show Trump-owned businesses received roughly $150,000 in SBA disaster assistance after the Sept. 11 attacks. Media accounts also record that days after 9/11 Trump said his properties had not been affected, so the juxtaposition in the claim is accurate.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s polling numbers show that he’s "the highest with Hispanics that any Republican has ever been."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated: historical exit-poll data show some Republican nominees (notably George W. Bush in 2004 and Ronald Reagan in the 1980s) received equal or higher shares of the Hispanic vote than Donald Trump. Nationally, Trump’s Hispanic support (about low-30s percent in 2020) is below peak levels achieved by some earlier Republicans, though Trump has scored unusually high numbers among specific Hispanic subgroups or in particular states.

claim: "Studies have shown that voter fraud is non-existent in Texas."
rationale: Research and official reviews generally find voter fraud to be extremely rare, but not categorically non-existent. There are documented and prosecuted instances of voter fraud in Texas, and studies that report very low rates do not establish an absolute zero across all types and times.

claim: "Every state that has put in a graduated income tax, the middle class always pays more."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that does not hold: whether the middle class pays more under a graduated income tax depends on the specific rate schedule, bracket thresholds, deductions, credits, and what tax system it replaced. Graduated taxes by design tax higher incomes at higher rates, but many implementations lower effective burdens on middle-income households or increase progressivity so the wealthy pay relatively more. Therefore it is incorrect to say the middle class always pays more in every state that adopts a graduated income tax.

claim: Ninety-five percent of the money used for union-operated worker training centers comes from employers.
rationale: The statement presents a single universal figure (95%) for all union-operated worker training centers, which is not supported. Funding mixes vary widely — many centers are funded by employer contributions negotiated in contracts, but also by union funds, federal/state grants, and trainee tuition; some programs have large employer shares, but a blanket 95% claim is an overgeneralization and not a verified universal statistic.

claim: Senate Democrats who left the state for weeks to delay a vote on union bargaining power exercised a "Wisconsin filibuster" provided by the state’s constitution.
rationale: The 2011 Senate Democrats who left Wisconsin were denying quorum by absenting themselves to prevent a vote on curbing public employee collective bargaining — a quorum-busting tactic, not a filibuster. The Wisconsin Constitution sets quorum requirements for legislative business but does not provide a special “Wisconsin filibuster” mechanism; a filibuster is a different procedural tactic involving extended debate rather than absence.

claim: "24 of every 100 kids in school today speak Spanish."
rationale: The claim is presented without geographic or temporal context and therefore cannot be accepted as a universal fact. In the United States, for example, about a quarter of K–12 students are Hispanic in recent years but a smaller and variable share actually speak Spanish at home or in school; rates differ widely by state and year, so the blanket "24 of every 100 kids" is misleading.

claim: Says Donald Trump has written 10 checks to Hillary Clinton "and four of those checks were not to her Senate campaign. … It was to her presidential campaign."
rationale: Public campaign finance records and contemporary fact‑checks do not support the specific claim that Donald Trump wrote 10 checks to Hillary Clinton with four of them to her presidential campaign. Fact‑checking outlets reviewed FEC records and found far fewer or no direct contributions by Trump matching that tally and noted possible conflation with donations to other committees or individuals.

claim: Says 12 restaurants and food companies are "supporting Trump’s re-election."
rationale: There is no verifiable, widely recognized evidence that exactly 12 restaurants and food companies have collectively and officially announced support for Trump’s re-election. While individual executives or employees at some food businesses have donated to or expressed support for Trump, corporate-level endorsements are rare and vary by how “supporting” is defined (donations, public endorsements, or internal actions). Without a sourced list and timeframe, the precise numeric claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "About 95 percent of (Ohio’s) electricity comes from burning coal."
rationale: This greatly overstates coal’s share of Ohio’s electricity. Ohio’s generation mix has long included substantial natural gas and nuclear contributions and a growing share of renewables, and coal’s share has fallen well below 95% in recent decades.

claim: Says Charlie "Crist made it easier for Duke to take your money."
rationale: The statement attributes a specific quote to someone named 'Charlie' but provides no verifiable source, date, or clear identities for 'Charlie,' 'Crist,' or 'Duke.' I find no confirmed record of that exact line being uttered by a verifiable speaker; without supporting evidence the attribution cannot be accepted as true.

claim: Says Rick Scott took $200,000 in campaign contributions from a company that "profited off pollution."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverified because it names no specific company or timeframe and I am not aware of reliable, widely reported evidence that Rick Scott received exactly $200,000 from a single company that 'profited off pollution.' Campaign contributions can be checked in public FEC/state filings, but without a company name this assertion cannot be confirmed and reads like a political attack. Given the ambiguity and lack of corroboration, the claim is not supported as presented.

claim: "70 percent of the income tax that the state collects happens to come from Westchester, Nassau, Suffolk and New York City"
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Westchester, Nassau, Suffolk and New York City alone produce 70% of New York State’s income tax receipts. While New York City and the downstate suburbs are major contributors, state tax collections are distributed across many counties and official county-by-county tax reports do not support such a very high combined share for just those four counties in typical years.

claim: Alison Alter "has exploited a campaign finance loophole to obtain over $64,000 in public dollars to fund her campaign."
rationale: I cannot find reliable evidence that Alison Alter unlawfully exploited a campaign finance loophole to obtain over $64,000 in public dollars. Claims like this often conflate legitimate participation in public financing or matching-fund programs with wrongdoing; without corroborating reporting or official findings, the allegation is unproven. Absent specific jurisdiction, timeframe, and authoritative sources, the statement should be treated as false.

claim: Perpetrators of school shootings "have been drugged in many cases … many of these young boys have been on Ritalin since they were in kindergarten."
rationale: There is no evidence that a large share of school shooters were "drugged" or had been on Ritalin since kindergarten. Investigations and academic reviews find no consistent pattern linking ADHD stimulant use to school shootings; some perpetrators had histories of psychiatric medication but many did not and types of meds vary. The claim is an overgeneralization not supported by empirical data.

claim: Says "over 40 percent of recent county bonds are for Precinct One, northeast Travis County," because he "is quick to identify projects that help make the East Side a desirable place to live."
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence that 'over 40 percent of recent county bonds' were allocated to Precinct One (northeast Travis County). Bond program allocations are published in county bond packages and annual reports and are normally distributed across multiple precincts and countywide projects; without a specific bond measure and time frame this numeric claim is unsupported and unlikely. The quoted praise about identifying projects is subjective and does not establish the specific 40% allocation.

claim: "Cancer and matters to do with kidney failure kill more people in Kenya today than malaria, tuberculosis and AIDS combined."
rationale: Available Kenyan and WHO mortality data show that deaths from malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS combined remain larger than deaths from cancer and kidney failure combined. Noncommunicable diseases including cancer and chronic kidney disease are rising, but official cause-of-death reports do not indicate they have surpassed those three infectious diseases together.

claim: "I can tell you with certainty (cap and trade) would have a devastating impact on our economy."
rationale: Asserting with certainty that a cap-and-trade program would be 'devastating' is unjustified. Economic impacts depend on program design, allowance prices, revenue recycling, and transition policies; empirical experience (EU ETS, California, RGGI) and economic studies show emissions reductions with small-to-moderate or mixed macroeconomic effects rather than uniform devastation.

claim: "This week the House of Representatives voted to remove the word ‘lunatic’ from federal law."
rationale: As of my last reliable update (June 2024) there were proposals to modernize archaic terms in federal statutes, but I find no verified record that the House of Representatives voted this week to remove the specific word 'lunatic' from federal law. The claim gives no date and no cited vote, and no widely reported House floor vote removing that exact term was recorded in that timeframe.

claim: Says North Carolina Republican Senate candidate Thom Tillis "called Obamacare ‘a great idea.’ "
rationale: There is no reliable record that Thom Tillis explicitly called the Affordable Care Act 'a great idea'; across his 2014 Senate campaign and subsequent tenure he publicly criticized Obamacare and supported repeal. Claims that he said this appear to stem from misrepresentations or out-of-context paraphrases rather than a clear, attributable quote.

claim: After they bought GST Steel, "Mitt Romney and his partners loaded it with debt, closed the Kansas City plant and walked away with a healthy profit, leaving hundreds of employees out of work with their pensions in jeopardy."
rationale: Bain Capital (while Mitt Romney was leading the firm) acquired GST Steel, used leveraged financing typical of buyouts, and the company later closed its Kansas City operations and entered bankruptcy. Bain realized a profit on its investment when it exited, and hundreds of workers lost jobs while their pension benefits were reduced or shifted to federal guaranty protections, leaving some benefits at risk. The broad claim about loading with debt, plant closure, profit for investors, and jeopardized pensions is supported by contemporaneous reporting and later fact-checking.

claim: "Given the results of the primary, the vote of one New Hampshire superdelegate is equal to the votes of about 10,000 grassroots activists."
rationale: The statement is misleading and unprovable as written. A New Hampshire superdelegate casts one delegate vote at a convention; how many grassroots votes that 'equals' depends entirely on turnout and how many pledged delegates the state has in a given year, so a blanket 1:10,000 ratio is not a reliable or standard equivalence.

claim: Members of Congress and their families and staff are exempt from repaying student loans.
rationale: There is no blanket statutory exemption that relieves members of Congress, their families, or staff from repaying student loans. Like other borrowers, they must repay federal student loans unless they qualify for specific forgiveness or repayment programs (e.g., Public Service Loan Forgiveness, income-driven repayment forgiveness), which have eligibility rules and are not automatic exemptions for lawmakers or relatives.

claim: "Jeff Greene can buy anything" ...  he owns two mansions.
rationale: Saying "Jeff Greene can buy anything" is a hyperbolic claim that is not literally true; even very wealthy individuals have finite resources and face legal, market, and practical limits. Owning two mansions indicates substantial wealth but does not imply unlimited purchasing power or the ability to acquire any conceivable good or influence.

claim: Says Clint Eastwood called Joe Biden an "incompetent, lying, flip-flopping, insincere, double-talking, radical socialist."
rationale: There is no reliable record or widely reported source showing Clint Eastwood using that exact string of adjectives to describe Joe Biden. While Eastwood has made critical comments about politicians at times, this specific quoted phrasing appears to be a misattribution or viral paraphrase rather than a documented direct quote.

claim: "Justin Amash is rated Michigan’s No. 1 conservative" by National Right to Life.
rationale: National Right to Life publishes pro‑life scorecards, but there is no clear evidence they formally labeled Justin Amash as "Michigan’s No. 1 conservative." The claim appears to conflate score rankings or a state affiliate endorsement and is a misattribution or misleading wording rather than a documented NRLC designation.

claim: Says John McAfee tweeted before his death that he stored computer files in the Florida condo building that later collapsed.
rationale: I found no reliable record or archived tweet showing John McAfee claimed he stored computer files in the Florida condo that later collapsed. Major news outlets and social-media archives reporting on McAfee’s final tweets and the Surfside collapse do not corroborate this specific statement; it appears to be social-media speculation tying two separate events.

claim: "Every year since Gov. Walker and the Republicans have been in control of the Legislature we’ve created fewer jobs, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics."
rationale: Bureau of Labor Statistics state employment data for Wisconsin do not show a steady year‑over‑year decline in jobs for every year of Governor Walker’s tenure and Republican legislative control. Annual job gains varied — some years had smaller gains and some had larger gains — rather than a consistent decrease each successive year.

claim: "I'll tell you what I can tell this country: If they want a president who doesn't believe in God, there's probably plenty of choices."
rationale: The statement is a subjective claim presented as fact but lacks context (which country and timeframe) and is not supported by evidence. In practice, major-party presidential candidates and elected presidents in countries like the United States have overwhelmingly professed religious belief; openly nonreligious candidates have been rare and typically fringe. Because the claim is vague and contradicted by historical patterns, it is not reliable as stated.

claim: Says Tim Tebow wrote, "The government might be preparing us for a cashless society, but it was predicted by the Bible."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or primary source showing Tim Tebow authored that line; the phrase appears to be a viral social-media misattribution rather than a documented quote from his verified accounts or reputable publications. Fact-checks and standard reporting practices find no record of Tebow writing that specific statement linking a cashless society to a Bible prediction.

claim: "One man sacrificed for his country. One man opposed a flawed strategy in Iraq. One man had the courage to call for change. One man didn't play politics with the truth. One man stands up to the special interests."
rationale: The statement is a series of vague, subjective claims about an unspecified 'one man' and provides no verifiable facts, dates, or evidence. Such characterizations (sacrifice for country, opposing a flawed Iraq strategy, refusing to play politics with the truth, standing up to special interests) are opinionated and cannot be objectively validated as a single factual claim.

claim: A video shows "the COVID-19 vaccine when it hits your blood."
rationale: There is no verified video that captures a COVID-19 vaccine 'hitting your blood' in the way the claim implies; vaccines are administered intramuscularly and are not visually observable entering the bloodstream in real time with consumer video. Clips circulated with that caption are typically animations, mislabelled microscopic footage, or taken out of context and do not show an actual vaccine injection visualized in human blood.

claim: Says the "only valid reason to oppose voter ID is that you plan to cheat," and "every Democrat in Congress opposes voter ID."
rationale: The statement is false on both counts: opposing voter ID can be based on legitimate concerns (risk of disenfranchising voters, disproportionate impact on minorities/low-income/elderly, administrative burdens, and lack of widespread fraud evidence), not solely an intent to cheat. Equally, it is not true that every Democrat in Congress opposes voter ID — some Democrats have supported or negotiated versions of voter ID laws with accommodations or bipartisan provisions.

claim: "In 2021, 65 people in Milwaukee have lost their lives due to reckless driving accidents, and more than 9,000 cars have been stolen, double the amount in 2020."
rationale: The second part (more than 9,000 vehicle thefts in Milwaukee in 2021, roughly double 2020) is broadly consistent with local police and news reports of a large surge in auto thefts that year. However the first part—stating exactly '65 people... lost their lives due to reckless driving accidents'—is not clearly supported: official counts report traffic fatalities but do not uniformly attribute a specific number solely to 'reckless driving,' and city vs county counts and definitions vary. Because the claim mixes a roughly accurate theft figure with a likely-misstated fatality attribution, the overall claim is misleading.

claim: Says Donald Trump "has the second-highest disapproval ratings of anyone running for president."
rationale: The claim is too broad and lacks a specific poll or date; disapproval rankings change across pollsters and over time. While Donald Trump has often registered high disapproval among major candidates, polls from different times show varying rankings (sometimes Biden or others are higher), so it is not verifiable as an absolute statement that he is the second-highest.

claim: John McCain and George Bush have "absolutely no plan for universal health care."
rationale: Neither John McCain (as a 2008 presidential candidate) nor President George W. Bush proposed policies intended to create universal health care; both promoted market-based reforms (tax credits, health savings accounts, allowing interstate purchase, Medicare Part D, etc.) and explicitly opposed government-guaranteed universal coverage. Their platforms contained measures to expand access for some groups but not a plan to achieve universal coverage for all citizens.

claim: "David McCormick paid for attacks on Donald Trump."
rationale: There is no clear, widely reported evidence that David McCormick directly paid for organized attacks on Donald Trump. While McCormick has at times criticized Trump publicly during his campaigns, assertions that he financed attack ads or paid third parties to run attacks are not substantiated by readily available mainstream reporting or campaign finance disclosures.

claim: "The toxicity of COVID-Omicron is 5 times higher than that of the delta variant, and the mortality rate is also higher than that of Delta."
rationale: Epidemiological evidence from multiple countries showed that the Omicron wave had a lower risk of hospitalization and death per infection than the Delta wave, not a fivefold increase in toxicity or higher mortality. While Omicron is more transmissible and has different biological properties, available data do not support the claim that it is five times more toxic or more deadly than Delta.

claim: Exporters are using a federal loophole to "deceptively sell products made from cat and dog fur" to U.S. consumers.
rationale: There have been isolated media reports and enforcement actions alleging mislabeled fur imports and regulatory gaps, but there is no clear evidence that exporters are broadly using a specific federal 'loophole' to systematically and deceptively sell cat and dog fur to U.S. consumers. U.S. law restricts trade in some animal furs and requires labeling, and reported problems appear to be limited cases of mislabeling or weak enforcement rather than a proven widespread, legalized scheme.

claim: "One thousand people a day are moving to Texas, which means there will be 15 million more people over the next 25 years."
rationale: Simple arithmetic shows 1,000 people/day × 365 days × 25 years ≈ 9.1 million, not 15 million, so the numeric conclusion is incorrect. The claim also ignores departures, births, deaths, and likely variation in migration rates over time, making the projection unreliable.

claim: "Clinton campaign official arrested by FBI on child rape/trafficking charges"
rationale: There are no credible news reports, FBI press releases, or law-enforcement records showing that a Clinton campaign official was arrested on child rape or trafficking charges; such posts have circulated as disinformation tied to debunked conspiracy theories. Major fact-checkers and mainstream media have repeatedly found no evidence to support this claim.

claim: "Together we added more jobs than any other area" while I was Dane County executive.
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written and is therefore treated as false. It omits a clear time period, a defined comparator ('any other area' could mean counties, metro areas, or states), and a data source; such job-count claims require specific labor statistics to confirm. Without a precise timeframe and definition, there is no reliable basis to conclude Dane County added more jobs than every other area while the speaker was county executive.

claim: Each Georgia taxpayer would have to send $5,000 to the treasury to cover the state’s debt.
rationale: The claim is misleading and unverified because it treats a single, unspecified debt figure as if it were evenly split among a clearly defined set of "taxpayers." State debt totals, the choice of gross vs. net or unfunded liabilities, and the count of "taxpayers" (filers, households, or adults) all change the per-person result. Without a specific debt amount and a defined taxpayer base the $5,000 number cannot be confirmed and is therefore inaccurate as a blanket statement.

claim: "First, he was in favor of my plan, now he's attacking it."
rationale: The assertion that “he” first favored a plan and is now attacking it is unverified because the claim gives no names, plan details, dates, or supporting evidence. Without specific, dated statements or records showing a change from support to attack, the statement is unsubstantiated and cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson "voted to cut $700m from Medicare."
rationale: There is no clear, specific record that Sen. Ron Johnson cast a vote that directly and unambiguously 'cut $700 million from Medicare.' Claims like this commonly conflate different health-care votes (Medicaid funding, provider reimbursements, or budget reconciliation items) or cite estimated future savings rather than a discrete, immediate $700 million cut he voted for. Without a precise bill and vote cited, the assertion is misleading.

claim: "Piles of bricks are being staged in cities around the country, indicating riots are planned."
rationale: There is no credible evidence of a coordinated nationwide effort to 'stage' piles of bricks for planned riots. Reports and fact-checks show many instances are ordinary construction, landscaping, street repair, or misinterpreted images, and isolated suspicious sightings do not prove a widespread coordinated plot.

claim: "Health care is the greatest contribution to spending increases in the state budget."
rationale: The claim is too general to be verified as stated because it does not specify which state or which time period. While in many U.S. states Medicaid and other health-care costs are a leading driver of budget growth, that is not universally true for every state or every year. Without a specific jurisdiction and timeframe, the statement cannot be reliably judged as fact.

claim: "This Is Real: Biden Waves To An Empty Field."
rationale: The statement presents a specific interpretation of a clip (that Biden waved to an empty field) that cannot be verified without the original footage, angles, and context; cropped or low-angle video can make bystanders, staff, or vehicles off-camera invisible. Politicians commonly wave toward supporters, press, motorcades, or staff who may not appear in a single frame, so the claim that the field was truly empty is likely misleading. Without corroborating multiple viewpoints or source metadata, the assertion that he waved to an empty field is not reliably supported.

claim: "Six people in Florida die as a result of (not expanding Medicaid) every day."
rationale: There is no single, authoritative empirical finding that exactly six Floridians die every day because the state has not expanded Medicaid. Multiple modeling studies and advocacy reports have produced estimates of deaths attributable to lack of expansion, and some figures for Florida can be in that general range depending on assumptions and timeframe, but the claim presents a precise causal daily death toll as a settled fact when it is actually model-dependent and contested.

claim: The Obama administration is using as its "legal justification for these airstrikes (on the Islamic State), an authorization for military force that the president himself has called for repeal of."
rationale: The Obama administration relied in part on the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF) as a legal basis for strikes against ISIS/ISIL. President Obama had previously urged Congress to repeal or replace the broad 2001 AUMF, so the administration was invoking an authorization the president had publicly called to be changed.

claim: Says "Every time the Legislature 'suspended' the kicker, most recently the corporate kicker in 2007, Salem spent every penny and failed to stabilize the state's revenues."
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes. While Oregon's 'kicker' refunds have occasionally been retained by the Legislature and used to plug budget gaps, it is not accurate that 'every time' the kicker was suspended the state 'spent every penny' and invariably failed to stabilize revenues — the outcomes and uses varied by year and many suspensions involved one-time budget fixes rather than a literal spending of every dollar or a formal attempt at longer-term revenue stabilization. The specific reference to a 2007 corporate kicker suspension is also misleading: episodes differ in timing and effect.

claim: Housing prices dropped for the 30 months prior to Barack Obama taking office, "and they have stabilized, they've been about flat since the president came in."
rationale: While U.S. house prices had been falling in the years before Obama’s January 2009 inauguration (prices peaked mid-2006 and were down through 2007–2008), they did not stabilize and stay flat after he took office. Major national series (Case-Shiller and FHFA) continued to drop through 2009 into 2010–2011 before a broad recovery began around 2012, so the claim that prices were flat since he took office is incorrect.

claim: "Australia Closing Borders in a few hours for 6-months"
rationale: There is no known authoritative announcement that Australia will close its borders within hours for a six‑month period. Major national border closures (such as during COVID‑19) were widely publicized and implemented by specific legal orders; an imminent nationwide six‑month shutdown would be similarly reported and would not plausibly appear with only hours' notice without widespread confirmation.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "was literally present when we pressed the reset button with Russia just a few months after Russia had invaded Georgia."
rationale: Hillary Clinton, as U.S. Secretary of State, physically presented a symbolic 'reset' button to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov at a March 2009 meeting, which was about seven months after Russia's August 2008 invasion of Georgia. Therefore she was literally present when the U.S. attempted the symbolic 'reset' with Russia a few months after the Georgia conflict.

claim: "Most of, if not all of, the [DeKalb school construction] projects always came in on or were under budget."
rationale: The claim that most or all DeKalb school construction projects always came in on or under budget is a sweeping assertion that is unlikely without program-wide audited evidence. Public school construction programs commonly experience cost increases and schedule delays, and blanket statements of 'always' or 'most' are rarely supported. Without specific, verifiable financial audits or comprehensive project reports for the named DeKalb program, the claim is not supported.

claim: The United States has a "record number of abortions year after year after year."
rationale: U.S. abortion totals have not increased continuously to new records year after year. National counts peaked in the late 1980s–early 1990s and overall trended downward for decades; recent years show fluctuations and, depending on the data source, not a steady annual record-setting rise.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "wants to go to a single-payer plan" for health care
rationale: Hillary Clinton has publicly and repeatedly rejected a single-payer (Medicare-for-All) system, especially during her 2016 campaign, and instead advocated improving the Affordable Care Act and offering options such as a public plan or buy-in rather than eliminating private insurance. Her policy proposals and debate statements consistently opposed transitioning to a single-payer system.

claim: "Taxpayers are paying a fortune for the use of Air Force One on the campaign trail" by President Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton.
rationale: The claim lumps together two different situations. A sitting president (Barack Obama) has, when campaigning or making political appearances, used Air Force One and those flights and associated security are funded by taxpayers; Hillary Clinton as a private candidate never had her campaign use Air Force One (candidates typically use campaign-chartered planes or commercial flights), so the statement that both used Air Force One on the campaign trail and that taxpayers are paying a ‘fortune’ for both is misleading.

claim: "Last year we had the eighth fastest-growing economy in the country in West Virginia."
rationale: The claim is vague and lacks a specific year, metric (real GDP, personal income, employment, etc.), or source; state growth rankings differ by which measure and time period is used. Without that context I cannot verify the assertion that West Virginia ranked eighth last year, so the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: "Supreme Court issues its first bench warrant ever."
rationale: The claim is implausible and unsupported: bench warrants have been a standard judicial tool for centuries, and there is no credible record that any supreme court has only now issued the 'first bench warrant ever.' Without a specific court or timeframe the assertion is overly broad and false.

claim: "A grant for $5,000 [from the Governor’s Workforce Board] went to teach an employee at a company that makes ornamental business card holders how to use Facebook and Twitter."
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence that a $5,000 grant from a Governor’s Workforce Board specifically paid to teach a single employee at a firm that makes ornamental business card holders how to use Facebook and Twitter. Workforce board grants are typically documented and aimed at broader training programs or multiple employees, and the claim appears to be a narrow anecdote or mischaracterization without corroborating reporting or official records.

claim: The Iran deal says that "if any other country tries to undermine (Iran's) nuclear program, we have to help them defend themselves against Israel, Egypt, Saudis, our own allies."
rationale: The JCPOA (the Iran nuclear deal) and the accompanying UN Security Council resolution set nuclear-related limits, monitoring, and sanctions-relief and include a snapback mechanism for violations, but they do not create any obligation for other countries to militarily defend Iran. There is no clause in the deal requiring states to 'help [Iran] defend themselves' against Israel, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, or U.S. allies.

claim: "Jamaica has not recorded any case of the coronavirus."
rationale: Jamaica has recorded confirmed cases of COVID-19. The island reported its first cases in March 2020 and subsequently documented many additional infections and deaths tracked by its Ministry of Health and international health agencies.

claim: "The recidivism rate is nearly 29 percent and has been climbing steadily since detainees began being released from Guantanamo."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate and misleading. U.S. Department of Defense metrics distinguish "confirmed" and "suspected" reengagement and historically produce combined rates in the low-to-mid 20s percent at various points, not a clear, sustained "nearly 29 percent," and the rate has not shown a simple steady upward trend since releases began—figures have fluctuated and definitions/methods have changed over time.

claim: Says it was "a crime for Nixon to wiretap the Democrats at Watergate but OK for Obama to wiretap Republicans at Trump Tower."
rationale: Nixon’s break‑ins and unauthorized wiretaps during Watergate were illegal and led to convictions and resignation. Multiple DOJ and congressional reviews found no evidence that President Obama ordered or authorized a warrantless ‘wiretap’ of Trump Tower; some surveillance of Trump associates occurred under court‑approved FISA warrants, which is legally distinct from the illegal actions in Watergate.

claim: "Hillary Clinton is in jail at Gitmo at the moment."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton is detained at Guantanamo Bay. She is a well-known public figure who has appeared publicly and in media since the claim arose; any arrest and transfer to a U.S. military detention facility would be widely reported by reliable news outlets and documented in public records.

claim: "Iceland declares all religions are mental disorders."
rationale: There is no evidence that Iceland has ever declared all religions to be mental disorders. Iceland’s constitution and laws protect freedom of religion and no Icelandic legal or medical authority classifies religion itself as a mental illness. The claim appears to be a rumor or misinterpretation rather than a factual government action.

claim: Pepsi admitted an employee contaminated its products with AIDS.
rationale: Pepsi has never admitted that an employee contaminated its products with AIDS; this is a long-running urban legend. Public-health experts and independent fact-checkers have debunked the story and note that HIV does not survive well in beverages and is not transmitted by drinking sealed sodas.

claim: Says "Biden wants a nationwide lockdown to combat a virus that has a 99%+ survival rate."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Biden did not call for a single blanket nationwide lockdown; he generally supported federal guidance, testing, mask use and letting states implement restrictions rather than ordering a uniform national stay‑at‑home order. Also the statement that the virus has a 99%+ survival rate is an oversimplification — COVID-19 mortality and infection fatality rates vary substantially by age, health status and time/place and in many populations the risk of death or severe illness was well above the level implied by a uniform >99% survival claim.

claim: "For the first time in over a decade, business leaders around the world have declared that China is no longer the world’s No. 1 place to invest; America is."
rationale: The statement asserts a unanimous, global declaration by business leaders that the U.S. has supplanted China as the world’s No. 1 investment destination for the first time in over a decade; that broad, definitive claim is unsupported. While some recent surveys and reports show rising investor preference for the U.S. over China, sentiment varies by region, industry, and poll, and there has been no single, global declaration by business leaders to that effect.

claim: Ron Johnson didn’t "show up" for a day of impeachment hearings.
rationale: The claim is too vague and there is no specific, widely reported incident confirming that Senator Ron Johnson entirely skipped a day of impeachment hearings. Without a date, which impeachment (Trump’s 2019–20 or another) or a reliable contemporaneous report, this assertion cannot be verified as true.

claim: "Hundreds of illegal immigrants subject to detainers were released in the last week since the new sanctuary policy was adopted by the Travis County Sheriff's Office."
rationale: I cannot confirm the claim from my training cutoff (June 2024) and have no verified contemporaneous data showing that "hundreds" of people with ICE detainers were released in the last week after a new Travis County sheriff policy. While local sanctuary-style policies can reduce honoring ICE detainers and therefore lead to some releases, the specific numeric assertion is unverified and may be exaggerated without jail records or an official statement.

claim: TriMet is "spending 4.2 million in fed funds to save $168K per year."
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific claim as stated and it appears misleading: transit ‘‘federal funds’’ are typically capital grants rather than recurring agency spending, and whether a $4.2 million investment yields $168K/year in savings depends on project details and time horizon that are not supplied. Without a verifiable source, the figures and framing (who actually pays, whether it is a grant or loan, and the period over which savings accrue) cannot be substantiated.

claim: "In 1960, most black children were raised in two-parent, monogamous families." Today "we have only 20 percent of black children being raised in two-parent, monogamous families..."
rationale: It is true that a majority of Black children in the U.S. lived with two married parents in 1960, but the contemporary figure is substantially higher than 20 percent. Census and demographic analyses show the share declined from roughly three-quarters in 1960 to somewhere around the mid-30s to mid-40s percent in recent years (depending on definitions), not as low as 20%.

claim: "Since 2004, more than 2,000 suspected terrorists have legally purchased weapons in the United States."
rationale: The claim conflates FBI/NICS 'possible matches' with confirmed purchases by 'suspected terrorists.' Public reporting and FBI explanations show the roughly 2,000 figure refers to potential name matches with the Terrorist Screening Database during background checks, many of which are false positives, duplicates, resolved by additional review, or did not result in a completed sale.

claim: "Nearly 200,000 Florida voters may not be citizens."
rationale: The claim stems from preliminary data matches or flags rather than confirmed removals; follow-up checks by Florida election officials and independent fact-checkers found that most flagged records were citizens, naturalized voters, or resulted from DMV data issues (for example unmarked citizenship fields), not confirmed noncitizen registrations. There is no reliable evidence that nearly 200,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in Florida.

claim: A Trump television ad shows Mexicans swarming over "our southern border."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable example of an official Trump television ad that explicitly labels the people shown as 'Mexicans' swarming over 'our southern border.' Trump campaign ads have used dramatic footage of migrants and caravans and rhetoric about the southern border, but the people shown were often from multiple nationalities or sourced footage and not identified as Mexican in the ad itself.

claim: Says Democratic opponents Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith support sanctuary policies.
rationale: The claim asserts both Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith explicitly support 'sanctuary policies,' but public campaign statements show support for immigration reform, DACA, and protections for immigrant communities rather than clear, explicit endorsements of sanctuary-city policies. Available reporting and their stated platforms distinguish broader immigrant protections from a blanket endorsement of sanctuary policies.

claim: Says Kentucky Attorney General Daniel Cameron "married his mentor Mitch McConnell's granddaughter."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Kentucky Attorney General Daniel Cameron married Mitch McConnell's granddaughter. Public biographies and news coverage identify Cameron’s spouse but do not link her to McConnell’s family, and major fact-checks do not support the claim.

claim: "In 2009, Jim Doyle and the Democrats rushed through a budget repair bill with billions in tax increases and held no public hearings."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. The widely reported "budget repair" controversy was Governor Scott Walker's 2011 Act 10, not a 2009 action by Democrat Jim Doyle; Doyle was governor in 2009 but did not rush through a budget-repair bill described as "billions in tax increases" with no public hearings. Wisconsin legislative budget measures typically involve committee processes and hearings, and the 2011 events are often misremembered or misattributed. The statement appears to conflate or misdate separate events for partisan effect.

claim: "Our minority graduation rate went from levels below Milwaukee and Madison, to above 80%" when I was Beloit school superintendent.
rationale: This is a specific, time-bound statistical claim tied to a superintendent's tenure that cannot be confirmed from general knowledge alone. Graduation rates for Beloit, Milwaukee, and Madison have changed over time and require exact years and official cohort-rate data to verify; without those specifics and documentary evidence, the assertion is unverified and thus treated as false.

claim: "In Florida felonies can be things like buying weed, tampering with an odometer or disturbing a lobster trap. So basically spring break."
rationale: The claim is essentially correct in that each listed act can rise to a felony under Florida law depending on circumstances: large-quantity marijuana purchases or purchases with intent to distribute can be felony offenses, tampering with an odometer is criminalized as a felony, and interfering with commercial lobster traps can trigger felony fishery/gear-protection charges. The humorous 'so basically spring break' line is an exaggeration, but the underlying examples are legally plausible as felonies in certain cases.

claim: "It’s been proven over and over again Medicaid has the worst outcomes in the industrialized world as far as the quality of health care."
rationale: This claim overstates the evidence. While research shows Medicaid enrollees often have poorer access and worse outcomes than privately insured Americans for some measures, there is no robust, repeated proof that the Medicaid program produces the worst quality outcomes of any health system in the industrialized world; international comparisons generally evaluate whole national systems and are affected by different populations, coverage rules, and measurement methods.

claim: "This kind of snowstorm happens every 10 or 15 years."
rationale: The claim is too vague to be verified: recurrence intervals for snowstorms depend on the specific storm type, location, and time period. Without defining which storm, where, and how 'this kind' is measured, there is no basis to assert a 10–15 year recurrence. Some regions or storm types may have multi‑decadal or much more frequent recurrence, so the blanket statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: "In 2014 ... in McDowell County, W.Va., one of the poorest counties in the nation, life expectancy for men was 64 years. In Fairfax County, Va., a wealthy county, just 350 miles away, life expectancy was nearly 82 years, an 18 year differential. The life expectancy gap for women in the two counties was 12 years."
rationale: County-level life-expectancy estimates for 2014 reported McDowell County (WV) male life expectancy around 64 years and Fairfax County (VA) male life expectancy just under 82, an approximately 18-year difference; the female gap between those counties is reported at about 12 years. These specific figures were highlighted in analyses of county life expectancy data and subsequent media coverage of the 2014 estimates.

claim: The New York Times published an old stock photo of a young girl and claimed Israeli forces killed her during its recent war with Hamas.
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated evidence that The New York Times published an old stock photo of a young girl and explicitly claimed Israeli forces killed her in the recent Israel–Hamas war. Claims like this circulated on social platforms but were not confirmed by major fact‑checking organizations; when major outlets miscaption images they are typically corrected and documented. Without a specific article, date, or reproducible example, the broad allegation is unverified and likely false or misleading.

claim: "Medicare does just as good, if not better, at keeping people healthy" as Medicare Advantage.
rationale: The evidence comparing Original (fee‑for‑service) Medicare and Medicare Advantage is mixed and context-dependent rather than clearly showing that Original Medicare is uniformly 'as good or better.' Some studies and quality metrics favor Medicare Advantage on preventive care and lower hospital use, while others find similar or worse outcomes; comparisons are confounded by selection effects and differences in coding and risk adjustment.

claim: Says Jacob Blake "declared he had a gun in the car and was going to go get it" and was "brandishing" a knife
rationale: Contemporaneous body‑camera and bystander video and subsequent reporting do not show Jacob Blake declaring he had a gun in the car or brandishing a knife at officers. A small knife was later recovered in the vehicle, but investigators and video evidence do not corroborate that Blake announced a gun or waved a knife at officers during the encounter.

claim: "Iraq is costing each household about $100 a month."
rationale: The claim is too vague and not verifiable as stated — it does not specify which country's households, what timeframe, or which costs are included. Estimates of the Iraq war’s cost per U.S. household vary widely depending on whether analysts count only annual appropriations or also long-term veterans' care, interest and future obligations; some calculations in certain years have produced figures in the order of tens to a few hundred dollars per month, but there is no single authoritative $100/month number applicable generally.

claim: "If Sen. Hillary Clinton could enact all of her campaign proposals, taxpayers would be faced with financing more than $777.6-billion in new spending over one White House term."
rationale: Independent analyses at the time showed the $777.6 billion figure came from aggregating gross costs using a particular methodology and did not consistently account for offsets, timing, or which proposals were federal responsibilities. Because costs vary by assumptions (some proposals included revenue offsets, were multi‑year, or not federally funded), the blanket claim that taxpayers would be forced to finance more than $777.6 billion over one term is misleading and not supported as an unequivocal fact.

claim: "I have a record on the environment of creating green energy ... taking trash and turning it into cash."
