claim: "This election actually was not unusually close."
rationale: The claim is unspecified — it does not identify which election or what metric of 'closeness' (popular vote margin, electoral college, seats) is meant. Without that context and comparative historical data, the assertion cannot be verified and is therefore treated as false as presented.

claim: "We haven't had any legislation which took away one gun in the past 20 years from anybody in this country--not one."
rationale: This is false. Over the past 20 years federal and state laws have authorized removal of firearms from individuals—examples include enforcement of prohibitions on possession by convicted felons, domestic-violence-related restraining orders that lead to firearm surrender, criminal forfeiture/seizure statutes, and the adoption and use of 'red flag' or extreme risk protection order (ERPO) laws in multiple states.

claim: David Perdue did not support the 2014 farm bill that U.S. Sens. Isakson and Chambliss did.
rationale: David Perdue was not a U.S. Senator in 2014 (he took office in January 2015) and therefore did not vote for or record Senate support for the Agricultural Act of 2014. Both Georgia Senators at the time, Johnny Isakson and Saxby Chambliss, did vote in favor of the 2014 farm bill. Thus Perdue did not support that specific congressional bill in the way Isakson and Chambliss did.

claim: Says U.S. Senate opponent Tommy Thompson "personally made over $3 million" from a federal contract granted to his healthcare company, but left  9/11 first responders "without the care they were promised."
rationale: I cannot find reliable, corroborated evidence that Tommy Thompson 'personally made over $3 million' from a federal contract to a healthcare company he owned or that he singularly 'left 9/11 first responders without the care they were promised.' This reads like an unsupported campaign attack combining a financial claim and a separate allegation about care; both would require specific contract, payment, and program records which are not documented here.

claim: Says that "the way to reach ‘herd immunity’ is for >70% of the population to get vaccinated."
rationale: Herd immunity thresholds are not a fixed >70% for all diseases; they depend on the pathogen’s basic reproduction number (R0) and on vaccine effectiveness/coverage. The theoretical threshold is roughly 1 - 1/R0 (and must be adjusted for imperfect vaccines and population heterogeneity), so some pathogens require well under 70% and others require well over 70%.

claim: ICE está en Uvalde, Texas, "entonces los padres indocumentados tienen que temer la deportación antes de verificar si sus hijos están vivos".
rationale: The claim combines two assertions that aren’t fully supported by public evidence. While some federal law‑enforcement personnel were reported in Uvalde after the shooting, credible reporting and official statements did not document ICE conducting deportation sweeps of grieving parents at the scene; there is no substantiated evidence that undocumented parents universally “have to fear” immediate deportation before confirming their children’s status. The broad causal claim is therefore unsupported.

claim: Says "11 straight years of no major hurricanes striking land" in the United States "bores a hole right through the whole climate change argument."
rationale: Even if there was an approximately 11‑year interval (roughly 2006–2016) without a Category 3+ hurricane making direct U.S. mainland landfall, that local, short-term lull does not invalidate the scientific evidence for anthropogenic climate change. Climate change is assessed from long‑term, global trends (temperature, sea surface heat content, precipitation patterns and storm intensity metrics) and natural variability can produce multiyear regional lulls in landfalls.

claim: "Seventy percent of the people living in abject poverty are women."
rationale: The specific claim that 70% of people in abject poverty are women is not supported by reliable global data. Independent fact-checks and reporting from international organizations find no evidence for a 70% global share; while women are often disproportionately affected by poverty in many places, the exact 70% figure is unsubstantiated and depends on definitions and measurements.

claim: "Every engine manufacturer in the United States is now in the state of Texas."
rationale: This is false. Many U.S. engine manufacturers remain headquartered or operate major plants outside Texas — for example Pratt & Whitney in Connecticut, Cummins in Indiana, Ford and GM engine operations in Michigan and Ohio, and Briggs & Stratton in Wisconsin. There has been no industry-wide relocation that places every U.S. engine manufacturer in Texas.

claim: "In a very real sense, (Oklahoma has) flattened the curve. ... The number of cases in Oklahoma — it's declined precipitously."
rationale: The statement is unverified and misleading because it lacks a specific timeframe; COVID-19 case counts in Oklahoma fluctuated with multiple waves rather than showing a single sustained, precipitous decline. While short-term drops occurred at various points, statewide data do not support an unqualified claim that Oklahoma definitively "flattened the curve" and saw a dramatic sustained decline without reference to dates or metrics.

claim: "George Floyd’s ‘murder’ filmed before COVID-19."
rationale: George Floyd was killed and the incident was filmed on May 25, 2020. The COVID-19 outbreak began in late 2019 and the World Health Organization declared a pandemic on March 11, 2020, so his death occurred after COVID-19 was already active and after the pandemic declaration.

claim: "101 utilities cut rates, credit GOP tax cuts."
rationale: After the 2017 GOP tax law (TCJA) took effect many U.S. electric and natural gas utilities publicly moved to reduce rates or return savings to customers and explicitly cited the tax cut as the reason; reports at the time counted roughly 100+ utilities taking such actions. The statement is a concise summary of that documented response by utilities following the tax change.

claim: "In eighth grade math, we’ve fallen to ninth place."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify because it doesn't say which country or which assessment/year it refers to. International and national math rankings (e.g., TIMSS, PISA, NAEP) change over time and do not uniformly show a drop to ninth place for a specific 'we'. Without a defined population and timeframe the claim cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "South Korea sprays rioters with dye so they can be identified & arrested later."
rationale: South Korean riot police have employed colored dye (often mixed into water cannon sprays) to mark protesters/rioters so they can be identified and potentially arrested later; this tactic has been documented in multiple news reports. It is not used in every policing situation, but it is an established crowd-control and identification method in South Korea.

claim: The White House "created a fake set for (President Joe) Biden to get his booster shot. The entire Biden presidency is one giant charade."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the White House built a 'fake set' to pretend Joe Biden received a booster; reporting and fact-checks indicate he received a booster in a medical setting and later participated in public photo/video coverage, which is standard. The broader claim that the 'entire Biden presidency is one giant charade' is a subjective opinion, not a factual assertion that can be proven true.

claim: Says last year "13 million (health insurance) rebates went out, in all 50 states. Another 8.5 (million) rebates are being sent out this summer, averaging around 100 bucks each."
rationale: The statement gives precise nationwide counts and an average rebate amount but does not cite a source and I cannot confirm those exact figures. While health insurers do issue Medical Loss Ratio (MLR) rebates and other refunds in various years, reported totals and state distribution have varied and publicly available MLR reports do not clearly support the specific numbers quoted. Without a specific program name and year, the claim is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: Says George LeMieux was one of two Republicans who voted for President Barack Obama's jobs bill.
rationale: George LeMieux served in the U.S. Senate from January 2009 to January 2011 and therefore was not among the senators who voted on President Obama's high‑profile 2011 "American Jobs Act." There is no authoritative roll‑call record identifying LeMieux as one of only two Republican senators who voted for a major Obama jobs bill while he was in office.

claim: "90 percent of fires in Arizona are human-caused."
rationale: State and federal wildfire data commonly report that roughly nine out of ten wildland fires in Arizona are caused by human activity (campfires, equipment use, debris burns, arson, escaped burns), so stating '90 percent' is a reasonable rounded characterization. The exact share varies by year and by whether one counts number of ignitions versus acreage burned, but the high human-caused proportion is well supported.

claim: The United States spent "2 trillion dollars to train and equip the Afghan military over the past 20 years. They fell in a week."
rationale: The claim conflates two different figures: roughly $2 trillion is a common estimate of the total long‑term U.S. cost of the Afghanistan war (including operations, reconstruction, veterans care, and interest), not the amount spent specifically to train and equip the Afghan military. Direct U.S. spending to train, equip, and sustain Afghan security forces over two decades was on the order of tens of billions of dollars (commonly cited around $80–90 billion), and the Afghan forces did collapse rapidly in August 2021 after U.S. withdrawal, with Kabul falling within about a week to ten days.

claim: Quotes Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as saying "I’m speaking with myself, number one, because I have a very good brain and I’ve said lots of things."
rationale: I could not corroborate a reliable primary-source transcript or reputable news report of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez using that exact wording; the line resembles a phrase more commonly associated with other public figures and appears in viral, often misattributed posts. Without a verifiable video or transcript, the claim is best treated as a likely misquote or fabrication.

claim: "Gene Green is the NRA’s favorite Democrat in Congress. ... "It’s no wonder the congressman has a lifetime A rating from the NRA."
rationale: Calling Gene Green the "NRA's favorite Democrat in Congress" is a subjective characterization and not an objectively verifiable label. The statement that he has a lifetime A rating from the NRA is plausible for some moderate Democrats but I cannot confirm a documented NRA lifetime A rating for Gene Green from authoritative records in my available knowledge, so the composite claim is not verifiable as stated.

claim: Originally "almost all models predicted" Dorian would hit Alabama.
rationale: Operational NHC forecasts and the bulk of model guidance at the time did not show Dorian making landfall in Alabama; most tracks had the storm near Florida's east coast or remaining offshore. Only a minority of outlier model runs suggested a westward shift toward the Gulf/Alabama, so saying 'almost all models predicted' Alabama is inaccurate.

claim: "Across the country, $174 billion of the Recovery Act have been committed in its first 130 days."
rationale: The precise claim that $174 billion of the Recovery Act was committed in its first 130 days is not supported by consistent official reporting; early ARRA reports used different metrics (committed, obligated, spent) and produced different totals. Because timing cutoffs and the meaning of "committed" vary, the single figure $174 billion for exactly the first 130 days is misleading and not reliably accurate.

claim: "We are spending more on affordable housing than we're spending on Dix Park right now."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because key terms—who 'we' refers to and what 'right now' means—are undefined and no spending figures are cited. Determining whether affordable housing spending exceeds spending on Dix Park requires specific, current budget numbers for the relevant jurisdiction and time period, which are not provided.

claim: "We actually have this critical race theory moved into all our schools in Virginia."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that formal critical race theory has been adopted or mandated across all public schools in Virginia. CRT is primarily an advanced academic legal and scholarly framework typically taught at the university level, and K–12 curricula and standards in Virginia are set locally and by the state — with recent public debate and some restrictions rather than a universal implementation.

claim: Says his proposed payroll tax cut "will mean an extra $1,500 in your pocket compared to if we do nothing."
rationale: The claim states a specific $1,500 gain but gives no details about the size of the cut, who it applies to, or the timeframe. Whether a payroll tax cut yields $1,500 in take-home pay depends on the cut percentage, the worker’s wages, and whether the employer share or employee share is reduced; without those parameters the blanket dollar figure is unverifiable and likely misleading. It could be true under specific assumptions but is not generally supportable as stated.

claim: I am the only U.S. Senate candidate who spoke out against bombing Syria, and who challenged Georgia’s governor and insurance commissioner over obstruction to the Affordable Care Act.
rationale: The claim asserts a unique status that is not verifiable and is unlikely: multiple U.S. Senate candidates publicly opposed bombing Syria during the high-profile Syria strike debates, and several candidates and advocacy groups have publicly challenged Georgia officials over actions related to the Affordable Care Act. Without specific names, dates, or evidence showing no other candidate took both positions, the exclusive claim cannot be supported.

claim: There were "$2 billion in earmarks in fiscal year 2012."
rationale: Congress imposed an earmark moratorium beginning in 2011 and official reporting and watchdogs show earmarks were effectively eliminated or reduced to only minimal amounts in FY2012, not $2 billion. Different definitions and one-off directed spending items can produce varying totals, but $2 billion is far higher than commonly reported figures for FY2012.

claim: "No Republicans voted for" recent hikes in the income tax, payroll tax, capital gains tax, dividend tax and estate tax. "These taxes were all passed under … Obamacare."
rationale: This claim mixes facts and inaccuracies. The Affordable Care Act did create an additional 0.9% Medicare payroll tax on high earners and a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax that affects capital gains and dividends, and Republicans overwhelmingly opposed the ACA vote; however, ACA did not raise ordinary income tax rates broadly nor enact estate-tax changes, and some later tax changes were enacted in other bipartisan laws. Saying "these taxes were all passed under Obamacare" and implying no Republican voted for all such hikes is therefore incorrect.

claim: "Since 1961 … our private economy has produced 66 million private-sector jobs. So what's the jobs score? Republicans 24 million, Democrats 42 (million)."
rationale: The statement presents precise totals without specifying the end date or method for attributing jobs to a president’s party. Official BLS payroll counts and independent fact-checks show that totals and the Republican/Democrat split vary substantially depending on the chosen start/end months, whether recessions are included, and whether jobs are measured as private nonfarm payrolls or another series, so the quoted 66M/24M/42M breakdown is not verifiably accurate as stated.

claim: "Bill Gates is behind the monkeypox outbreaks."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bill Gates caused or engineered the monkeypox outbreaks; public health investigations attribute outbreaks to natural human-to-human transmission and known animal reservoirs. Claims linking Gates to the outbreaks are unsubstantiated conspiracy theories that have been repeatedly debunked by health authorities.

claim: Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline in COVID infections"
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it gives no timeframe or data source; COVID-19 case trends are time-sensitive and vary by week and region. Without recent case counts, test-positivity, hospitalizations, or wastewater data from Wisconsin health authorities or the CDC, one cannot conclude Wisconsin is "clearly" experiencing a decline.

claim: "All the money the Department of Citrus has is paid for by the citrus growers. You don't save dollars by eliminating the Department of Citrus."
rationale: Departments of Citrus (e.g., Florida Department of Citrus) are funded primarily by grower assessments, but they also receive other revenue sources such as federal grants, fees, and sometimes state-allocated funds; therefore it is incorrect to say "all" funds come from growers. Likewise, whether eliminating the department saves taxpayer dollars depends on where costs and statutory assessments would be reallocated—costs could shift to state budgets or be absorbed elsewhere—so the blanket claim that you "don't save dollars" is not reliably true.

claim: "Since 2010, Republicans have won unaffiliated voters in every general election."
rationale: This is false for U.S. national general elections: unaffiliated/independent voters were carried by Democrats in multiple post-2010 cycles (notably 2012, 2018, and 2020 according to exit polls and post-election analyses), so Republicans did not win them in every general election since 2010.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that public school in the United States "will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law."
rationale: There is no U.S. Supreme Court ruling that literally states public schools 'will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law.' The Court's Establishment Clause decisions prohibit government endorsement or promotion of religion but permit neutral, academic instruction about religions. The claim misstates and overgeneralizes existing case law.

claim: As a Member of Congress, Chris Murphy "was raking in $1 million in salary."
rationale: As a Member of Congress Chris Murphy received the standard congressional salary (around $174,000 per year in recent years), not $1 million. Congressional leadership pay is only modestly higher and no senator's official salary approaches $1 million, so the claim that he was "raking in $1 million in salary" is incorrect.

claim: Sarah Palin "already has more executive experience" than Barack Obama and Joe Biden "combined."
rationale: As stated the claim is incorrect: Barack Obama served two terms as U.S. President (2009–2017) and Joe Biden served as Vice President (2009–2017) and has been President since 2021, so their combined federal executive service far exceeds Sarah Palin’s time as Wasilla mayor and Governor of Alaska. The statement appears to echo a 2008 talking point (when Obama and Biden had not yet held executive office), but without that explicit timeframe the claim is false.

claim: "President Obama himself attempted to filibuster Justice Alito, who now sits on the Supreme Court."
rationale: Barack Obama, then a U.S. senator, voted against Samuel Alito’s 2006 confirmation but did not personally filibuster him. Democrats debated a filibuster but did not block cloture; the Senate invoked cloture and confirmed Alito by a 58–42 vote.

claim: "Barack Obama will somehow manage to add more than $8 trillion to the national debt, which is more debt than the 43 presidents who held office before him compiled together."
rationale: While federal debt did rise by roughly $8–9 trillion over President Obama’s two terms, the claim that this was more than the 43 prior presidents combined is incorrect. Total U.S. federal debt at the start of Obama’s presidency was already on the order of $10+ trillion, so prior presidents collectively accounted for more than $8 trillion of accumulated debt.

claim: Says for otherwise healthy people "experiencing mild to moderate respiratory symptoms with or without a COVID-19 diagnosis … only high temperatures kill a virus, so let your fever run high," but not over 103 or 104 degrees.
rationale: It is incorrect to claim that only high temperatures kill viruses and that you should let a fever run high. Typical human fevers are far below temperatures needed to reliably inactivate viruses in the body, and while fever is part of the immune response it does not 'cook' pathogens; intentionally allowing fever to rise can cause harm (dehydration, organ stress, febrile seizures) and should be medically managed. Public-health guidance recommends treating high fevers and seeking care rather than deliberately permitting dangerously high body temperatures.

claim: "We’ve got an average of 5,600 soldiers committing suicide. That’s about 20 a day."
rationale: The numbers are inconsistent and do not match official data. 5,600 deaths per year corresponds to about 15 per day, not 20, and official U.S. figures show roughly 6,000 veteran suicides per year (~17/day) while active-duty military suicides are far lower, so the claim as stated is inaccurate.

claim: "98 percent of small businesses make less than $250,000" and would not see a tax increase under Barack Obama's plan.
rationale: The Obama campaign’s statement that about 98% of small businesses have net income under $250,000 is consistent with IRS data on pass-through filers; his tax proposals targeted individual income above $250,000, so most small-business owners whose business income is below that threshold would not face the proposed top-rate increase. However this ignores complexities (household income aggregation, C-corporations, payroll taxes or other changes) that can cause exceptions for some firms under $250,000.

claim: MSNBC’s Mika Brzezinski said, "Elon Musk is trying to control how people think. That’s our job."
rationale: There is no credible public record or verified clip of Mika Brzezinski saying the exact line "Elon Musk is trying to control how people think. That’s our job." While Brzezinski and other MSNBC hosts have criticized Musk's efforts to shape online discourse, the specific quotation appears to be a fabricated or misattributed statement rather than a documented remark.

claim: Says only about 250 Texans have been killed in action since 9/11.
rationale: State-by-state tallies of U.S. military fatalities from Department of Defense reports and independent casualty databases show that Texans killed in combat since the 9/11 attacks number well above 250. Given Texas’s large military population and documented lists of KIA from Iraq, Afghanistan, and other operations, the claim understates the total by a wide margin.

claim: "Less than 500 people a year killed by all rifles combined" and "4,000 a year killed by illegals."
rationale: The two-part claim mixes a partly-accurate statement about rifle-involved homicides with an unsupported claim about killings by undocumented immigrants. U.S. data from law-enforcement and public-health sources show homicides where a rifle is the known weapon are typically under 500 per year, but the assertion that 4,000 people per year are killed by “illegals” (undocumented immigrants) is not supported by DOJ/FBI/academic analyses, which find far fewer homicides attributable to unauthorized immigrants. Because the immigration-related figure is false and the phrasing is ambiguous, the overall claim is false.

claim: The Wisconsin Economic Development Corp. "cannot account for creating one single job."
rationale: Independent audits and reporting found that the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation had poor record-keeping and could not fully substantiate many claimed jobs, but investigators did not conclude that WEDC had literally created zero jobs. WEDC funded projects that reported job creation and it claimed job outcomes even though documentation for many of those claims was incomplete or missing.

claim: Quotes Albert Einstein as saying "I fear the day technology will surpass human interaction. The world will have a generation of idiots."
rationale: This quotation is not found in Einstein's writings, speeches, or the Einstein Archives and is widely identified by historians and fact-checkers as a modern internet fabrication. Reputable collections of Einstein quotes do not record it, and it appears to have originated from meme culture rather than any primary source.

claim: "Republicans are attempting to remove Barack Obama from Georgia’s Presidential Ballot in 2012."
rationale: The claim overstates and generalizes. While fringe activists and a few Republican-aligned individuals pursued birther lawsuits and ballot challenges against Obama in 2012 (including filings in some states), there was not a coordinated effort by the Republican Party as a whole to remove Barack Obama from Georgia’s 2012 ballot, and courts routinely rejected such challenges.

claim: Says Scott Walker "has taken money away from internet expansion in our state."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify as-is because it does not name the state, timeframe, or specific program; whether Scott Walker "took money away" depends on particular budget vetoes or program funding decisions. Scott Walker was governor of Wisconsin and his administration did make budget changes that affected some broadband-related programs, but that does not prove the generalized claim without more detail. On the available information the claim is unverified and therefore treated as false until supported with a specific program, state, and date.

claim: "Nancy Pelosi Removed From Benefit for ‘Being So Drunk She Couldn’t Stand Up’ "
rationale: There is no credible reporting or verifiable evidence that Nancy Pelosi was removed from a benefit for being 'so drunk she couldn't stand up.' The allegation appears to stem from partisan or satirical social posts and was not corroborated by reputable news organizations, which would have covered a high-profile incident like this.

claim: "An attack on a healthy 22-year-old homosexual man would be more protected under the law than an attack on an eight-year-old child."
rationale: Most legal systems treat attacks on children as especially serious (child abuse, statutory offenses, mandatory reporting and enhanced penalties), while hate-crime enhancements for sexual orientation apply to bias-motivated attacks but do not generally provide greater protection than the special criminal provisions for minors. Whether hate-crime laws apply can vary by jurisdiction, but that variation does not make an assault on an adult member of a protected class systematically 'more protected' than an assault on a child. In short, both categories can receive enhanced penalties in some places, but children routinely receive specific and often stronger legal protections.

claim: There are "many unanswered and obvious questions" about the 2001 death of a staff member of Joe Scarborough.
rationale: The 2001 death of Joe Scarborough staffer Lori Klausutis was investigated and an autopsy concluded she died after a cardiac arrhythmia led to a fall and fatal head injury, with investigators reporting no signs of foul play. Major news outlets and the medical examiner have treated the case as closed, so the assertion that there are 'many unanswered and obvious questions' is not supported by the available official findings.

claim: Wall Street megabanks that received bailouts in 2009 now get taxpayer-funded advantages not available to community banks in Ohio.
rationale: Large Wall Street banks that were rescued during the 2008–2009 crisis continue to enjoy advantages tied to government backstops and access to official liquidity that small community banks generally do not. Empirical studies and market behavior show these megabanks benefit from an implicit "too-big-to-fail" subsidy and easier access to Federal Reserve facilities and capital markets, lowering their funding costs relative to community banks in places like Ohio.

claim: The census "for years and years and years, decades, has asked, ‘Are you a citizen of the United States of America?’"
rationale: This statement is misleading. While the Census Bureau has asked about citizenship on sample questionnaires (the long form and, more recently, the American Community Survey) for many decades, the short-form decennial census sent to every household has not included a direct 'Are you a citizen…?' question for decades. The claim conflates long-form/sample practice with the full-count short-form.

claim: Says photo of beaten woman is Aracely Henriquez, a pregnant woman who George Floyd assaulted during an armed robbery.
rationale: Independent fact-checking and reporting found the circulated photo was misattributed and is not of Aracely Henriquez. While George Floyd had a prior conviction involving an armed robbery in which a woman was harmed, the specific image shared online does not show that victim and has been debunked as unrelated.

claim: Says Michelle Obama said Florida shooting "is clearly our president’s fault."
rationale: There is no credible record or major news reporting that Michelle Obama said the Florida shooting "is clearly our president’s fault." Her public statements and verified social media around the Parkland shooting did not contain that direct quote, so this appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase of others' criticisms.

claim: "I can send every qualified person to a four-year college in their state for $150 billion."
rationale: The statement is vague about who counts as a 'qualified person' and the timeframe, but under common U.S. interpretations it is unlikely $150 billion would cover sending every eligible student to a four‑year in‑state college. Using approximate figures (≈3.5–4.0 million high‑school graduates per year and average public in‑state tuition around $9k–11k/year), funding four years of tuition for a single cohort already approaches or exceeds $150 billion, and adding room, board, fees, or multiple cohorts raises the cost substantially. Therefore the claim as stated is not supportable.

claim: A person’s immune system "tanks" after their second COVID-19 vaccine dose.
rationale: There is no evidence that a person’s immune system "tanks" after a second COVID-19 vaccine dose. Clinical trials and immunology studies show the second dose usually boosts antibody and T‑cell responses (acting as a booster); typical post‑vaccine effects are short‑lived inflammatory reactions (fever, fatigue, soreness), not systemic immune collapse. Severe or persistent immune dysfunction is not an expected outcome of approved COVID‑19 vaccines.

claim: "Most young Americans right now, they’re not covered" by health insurance.
rationale: Surveys and government data since the Affordable Care Act show that a minority — not a majority — of young Americans lack health insurance. Uninsured rates for young adults are generally in the low-to-mid teens (and often lower), so the claim that "most" young Americans are not covered is incorrect.

claim: Obama "says he'll raise taxes on electricity."
rationale: There is no record of President Barack Obama directly saying “I'll raise taxes on electricity.” While Obama supported climate policies (and earlier signaled support for cap-and-trade and regulations that critics argued could raise energy prices), that is not the same as an explicit promise to levy a tax on electricity. The claim therefore misstates or omits context about policy proposals versus a direct statement.

claim: Says Mike DeWine "flip-flopped on the gun issue and has earned an F from the NRA."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record that Ohio Governor Mike DeWine was formally given an 'F' rating by the NRA; NRA candidate grades are public and DeWine has a mixed but not uniformly failing gun-voting record. The claim also relies on a subjective charge of 'flip-flopping' without specifying which votes or statements are meant, making the assertion unsubstantiated as stated.

claim: "Since that famous day in February where the governor campaigned with Barack Obama on behalf of the stimulus program, 211,000 Floridians have lost their jobs."
rationale: The claim is vague and presents a precise number without a defined time window or source; job counts are reported monthly and depend entirely on the start and end dates chosen. Without specifying which February day and which end date the 211,000 figure refers to, the statement cannot be verified and is therefore unreliable. Historical state employment data from official labor reports do not support taking an isolated unsourced number as fact.

claim: Says Marco Rubio took "three quarters of a million dollars from fossil fuel executives" during the 2016 Senate election.
rationale: There is no clear, reliable evidence that Marco Rubio received exactly $750,000 from “fossil fuel executives” during his 2016 Senate race. Public campaign finance databases show he did receive contributions from oil and gas interests (including PACs and industry donors) but totals and classifications differ, and the specific claim about three quarters of a million from fossil-fuel executives alone is not supported by those records.

claim: "In six years, (U.S. Rep. Gary) Peters introduced zero bills that became law."
rationale: The claim is unlikely to be true: members of the House typically sponsor at least some measures that become law over multiple terms, and available legislative records and fact-checking norms do not support a blanket zero for Peters’ six years. The statement is also ambiguous about which six-year period and whether cosponsored measures or amendments are counted.

claim: Rare is the president "who's passed more legislation, who's done more things than what we've done, between the executive orders and the job-killing regulations that have been terminated."
rationale: The claim is misleading and factually inaccurate: presidents do not "pass" legislation—Congress enacts laws—and the statement gives no clear comparator or metric for "more." While presidents can issue executive orders and support regulatory rollbacks, those actions are not equivalent to passing more legislation, and many presidents oversaw enactment of more statutory laws. Therefore the broad assertion as stated is false or unsupported.

claim: "CNN-NPR photojournalist Jade Sacker was embedded with antifa leader" during the U.S. Capitol attack.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a CNN/NPR photojournalist named Jade Sacker was "embedded with an antifa leader" during the U.S. Capitol attack. Fact-checking and news reports found no proof of antifa leadership or coordinated presence at the Capitol, and claims linking journalists to antifa were based on miscontextualized images and social media speculation.

claim: Says detained immigrant parents separated from their children at the border are being charged "as much as $8 a minute to call their children."
rationale: Multiple news investigations and immigrant-rights groups documented that detained parents separated from their children were sometimes billed very high per-minute rates for phone or video calls, with reported maximums around $8 per minute. While not every parent faced that exact rate, the $8/minute figure was reported as an upper-end charge by private telecom vendors used in detention and shelter settings.

claim: Says Leah Vukmir "wrote a letter seeking leniency for a fellow state legislator convicted of sexual assault."
rationale: I find no reliable reporting or public records indicating Leah Vukmir wrote a letter seeking leniency for a fellow state legislator convicted of sexual assault. Such an action would likely have been reported in major local and national news outlets and shown in court filing records, but I am not aware of any credible sources documenting it.

claim: Forty percent of union members voted Republican in 2008.
rationale: The precise claim that 40% of union members voted Republican in 2008 is not supported by a clear authoritative source. 2008 exit polls and surveys show union members/union households favored Obama by a substantial margin, with Republican support reported in the high-30s rather than an exact 40%, so the statement is an imprecise rounding that overstates certainty.

claim: "The minimum number of infrastructure (needs) in Atlanta is $900 million."
rationale: The claim gives a precise dollar figure without any source, timeframe, or definition of what counts as "infrastructure needs" for Atlanta; such estimates are produced by specific studies and vary widely by scope and year. Without a cited authoritative study or context, the assertion that the minimum is exactly $900 million cannot be verified and is therefore not factually supported.

claim: "The current (agriculture) commissioner allowed tainted beef to be sent to school cafeterias."
rationale: The claim is unspecified and I have no verifiable evidence that any current agriculture commissioner authorized sending tainted beef to school cafeterias. Food safety agencies and recall procedures ordinarily stop distribution of contaminated meat, and accusations of this severity require named officials and credible sources to confirm. Absent a named jurisdiction, time period, or supporting documentation, the allegation is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Nancy Pelosi said, "Employers cutting hours is a good thing. It then gives that person time to pursue their dreams and passions."
rationale: There is no credible record or reliable news reporting that Rep. Nancy Pelosi made that statement; fact-checkers who investigated the viral quote found it was fabricated or misattributed. Pelosi's public speeches and official transcripts do not contain that phrasing, and the quote circulated on social media without verifiable sourcing.

claim: Says Tom Barrett plans "to spend $100 million on a trolley that goes barely two miles on the east side of Milwaukee."
rationale: As Milwaukee mayor Tom Barrett supported the downtown streetcar (known as The Hop), the initial starter line runs about two miles downtown/east side and the project cost was in the roughly $100+ million range. Characterizing it as a plan to spend "$100 million on a trolley that goes barely two miles" is a broadly accurate summary, though the final reported cost was higher than $100 million.

claim: Gov. Scott Walker received a $7,300 pay raise.
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated evidence that Gov. Scott Walker personally received a discrete $7,300 pay raise; gubernatorial salaries and any adjustments are public and widely reported, and claims of a specific $7,300 increase lack sourcing. The statement is ambiguous about timing and whether it refers to an automatic statutory adjustment, pension change, or cumulative figure, and I could not confirm a one-time $7,300 raise paid to Walker.

claim: "After one year, Tennessee’s students made their biggest single-year jump in achievement ever recorded in the state."
rationale: The statement is unverified as an absolute claim. Tennessee has reported notable year-to-year gains on some assessments in certain years, but declaring a single-year gain as the largest "ever recorded" requires specifying the test, grade, subject and time period; because assessments and scoring systems have changed over time, such an unconditional claim is not supported without clear evidence.

claim: "Over 40 percent of small and mid-size banks that loan money to small businesses have been wiped out since Dodd-Frank has passed."
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes industry changes. While the number of small and mid‑size banks has fallen since the financial crisis era, careful counts and fact‑checks show declines are driven by failures during the 2008–2010 crisis, voluntary mergers and consolidation, not a direct effect that 'wiped out' over 40% solely because of Dodd‑Frank. No reliable data support the specific 'over 40 percent wiped out since Dodd‑Frank passed' assertion.

claim: "The Railroad Commission of Texas has nothing to do with railroads."
rationale: Despite its name, the Railroad Commission of Texas does not regulate railroads today. Created in 1891 to oversee railroads, its modern responsibilities focus on oil and gas regulation, pipelines, and surface mining, while railroad oversight is handled by other state agencies.

claim: "Oregon school districts are directing 24 percent of their food budgets to purchase local foods. That’s the highest percentage in the country."
rationale: I cannot verify that Oregon school districts are directing 24% of their food budgets to local foods or that this is the highest in the country. National data (e.g., USDA Farm to School surveys and state program reports) show wide variation by year, state, and how 'local' is defined, and no single widely cited source confirms the 24% figure or the nationwide ranking without additional context.

claim: Canadian-born Ted Cruz "has had a double passport."
rationale: Ted Cruz was born in Canada to an American mother and therefore held both Canadian and U.S. citizenship until he formally renounced his Canadian citizenship in 2014, meaning he was legally entitled to hold passports from both countries. Public reporting and Cruz’s own statements confirm he was a dual citizen prior to renunciation.

claim: Says Bubba Watson wrote a viral Facebook post about Black Lives Matter.
rationale: There is no well-documented, widely reported instance of Bubba Watson authoring a single viral Facebook post specifically about Black Lives Matter. While Watson has made public social-media posts and comments on social and political topics that drew attention, reliable sources do not corroborate the specific claim as stated.

claim: Rhode Island voters are moving away from the Democratic party to non-affiliation
rationale: Rhode Island voter-registration data and multiple news reports show a modest decline in Democratic enrollment in recent years coupled with growth in unaffiliated/independent (no-party) registrants, indicating a movement away from the Democratic Party toward non-affiliation. This is a trend rather than a wholesale realignment — Democrats often remain the largest single group, so the shift is gradual and varies by year and locality.

claim: Says the U.S. Department of Justice has "seen in the past" that police department "consent decrees don’t work, that there’s very little change, that oftentimes immediately after a consent decree goes into effect, crime actually goes up."
rationale: The U.S. Department of Justice has not taken a general, authoritative position that consent decrees “don’t work” or that they typically produce little change and immediate crime increases. DOJ has frequently used and defended consent decrees as a tool to remedy police misconduct and has reported improvements in many jurisdictions; academic studies show mixed outcomes and any observed post-decree crime changes are contested and not routinely attributed to the decrees by DOJ.

claim: "A family of four can make up to $88,000 a year and still get a subsidy for health insurance" under the new federal health care law.
rationale: The statement frames $88,000 as a fixed cutoff, but ACA subsidy eligibility is based on percentages of the federal poverty level (FPL) and varies by household size and year. Generally subsidies are available for households between about 100% and 400% of the FPL, and 400% of the FPL for a family of four is typically not exactly $88,000 and changes annually. Temporary program changes and state differences can also alter eligibility, so a single $88,000 figure is misleading.

claim: "I did very well with young people in Ohio, Massachusetts, California."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated: it asserts strong support among young voters in three states but gives no timeframe, election, or data. Without specific poll or exit-poll results tied to a particular candidate and election, the statement cannot be substantiated.

claim: The Keystone XL pipeline "doesn’t even have any oil for America."
rationale: The Keystone XL was designed to transport crude oil from Alberta to refineries on the U.S. Gulf Coast, so it would deliver oil into the U.S. refining system rather than "none for America." While some of the crude or refined products could be exported depending on market conditions, it is incorrect to claim the pipeline would carry no oil for the United States at all.

claim: "The richest 1 percent of America will get a bigger tax cut through this bill than the family income of the average family here in Central Texas."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it fails to identify which tax bill and which time period are meant, and "average family income here in Central Texas" is undefined and varies by county. While some federal tax bills have given the top 1% very large average dollar reductions that in some cases exceeded typical regional household incomes, without specifying the bill and the exact income benchmark this comparison is unsubstantiated. Therefore the statement as written is not supportable.

claim: "Toomey crossed party lines… to stop gun sales to suspects on the terror watch list."
rationale: In 2013 Republican Senator Pat Toomey joined Democratic Senator Joe Manchin in a bipartisan amendment that would have barred firearm sales to individuals on the federal terrorist watchlist, so he did cross party lines to support that restriction. The proposed measure was prominent after the Newtown shooting, though it ultimately failed to pass the Senate.

claim: Hillary Clinton "starts off with 47 percent of the country against her."
rationale: The claim gives a precise nationwide figure but lacks a timeframe and definition of "against her." While some polls in 2015–2016 showed Clinton's unfavorable ratings in the mid‑40s, poll results vary by question, sample and timing; there is no single authoritative measure that proves she "starts off with 47 percent of the country against her." The statement is therefore unsubstantiated as a general fact.

claim: The snow is government-generated or fake.
rationale: Snow is a natural meteorological phenomenon formed when atmospheric water vapor freezes into ice crystals; widespread snowfalls are not produced by governments. There are limited, localized practices—artificial snowmaking at ski resorts and occasional cloud-seeding experiments—that can create or enhance precipitation, but these are small-scale and do not make natural snow 'fake' on the broad scale implied by the claim.

claim: More private-sector jobs were created in the second year of the Obama administration than in the eight years of the Bush administration.
rationale: Contemporary BLS employment data and multiple fact-checks show that the net number of private-sector jobs added over the eight years of the George W. Bush presidency exceeds the private-sector job gains recorded in 2010 (Obama’s second calendar year). The claim misstates the comparative totals; the single-year 2010 private-sector gain was substantially smaller than the cumulative private-sector change across the Bush years.

claim: We live in "a time of historically low violent crime rates and historically high gun ownership rates nationally."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it bundles two different trends that depend on how you measure them. Violent crime rates in the U.S. are lower than their peaks in the late 20th century but rose in 2020–2021 and are not uniformly at historic lows by all measures; meanwhile the total number of firearms and gun purchases are near historic highs, but survey measures of household gun ownership are mixed and not clearly at an all-time high. Combining these ambiguous measures into a single definitive claim overstates the certainty.

claim: The U.S. has "over $62 trillion in unfunded liabilities."
rationale: The raw statement is misleading because “over $62 trillion in unfunded liabilities” depends entirely on definitions and methodology. Certain long‑horizon present‑value calculations of Social Security, Medicare, and other commitments can produce figures in that range, but official measures (federal debt, CBO metrics, Trustees’ 75‑year actuarial shortfalls) are reported differently and are much smaller. Without specifying which programs, time horizon, and discounting method the claim is unreliable.

claim: Says Mitt Romney opposes requiring employers to cover contraception and would eliminate funding for Planned Parenthood.
rationale: Mitt Romney has publicly opposed requiring employers to provide contraceptive coverage, arguing for employer and religious exemptions, and during his campaigns he said he would end federal funding for Planned Parenthood and redirect those dollars to other health providers. These positions were stated repeatedly during his 2012 presidential campaign and in subsequent public comments.

claim: "A portion of everything you pay A.A.R.P goes directly to the Democratic Party."
rationale: AARP membership dues are spent on member services and nonprofit advocacy, not automatically routed to the Democratic Party. Political contributions are made through a separate AARP Political Action Committee and voluntary donations, and while AARP/PAC spending has often favored Democrats, payments you make are not directly sent to the Democratic Party.

claim: Says she is a registered nurse.
rationale: The statement provides no named individual or evidence and is therefore unverifiable as presented. Professional registration as a nurse requires checking specific licensing records, so without identification or documentation the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "Florida ranks first in the nation for access to free prekindergarten."
rationale: The statement is too categorical without a year or metric. Florida does have a large, well-known Voluntary Prekindergarten (VPK) program and is among the national leaders in access and enrollment, but rankings for 'first in the nation' vary by year and by how access is measured, and other states (e.g., Oklahoma historically) have been ranked first on some measures.

claim: Says "Claire McCaskill receives the second-most contributions from insurance companies in the entire Senate."
rationale: The claim is presented without a timeframe or data source and cannot be confirmed as a standing fact. Industry contribution rankings (tracked by organizations like OpenSecrets) vary by election cycle and source; while Claire McCaskill was a notable recipient of insurance-industry money, available public data do not support a constant or unqualified statement that she received the second-most contributions in the entire Senate.

claim: "Thanks to President Trump and Republican leadership, the number of people collecting food stamps has declined by more than two million."
rationale: While SNAP (food stamp) enrollment did fall by several million in the years before the COVID-19 pandemic, attributing the decline solely to President Trump and Republican leadership is unsupported. SNAP caseloads reflect broader economic conditions, prior policy changes, and state-level administration, and they rose again during the pandemic after emergency measures. The claim mixes a plausible numeric trend (depending on the exact timeframe and measure) with an overstated causal attribution.

claim: Says an investigative report concluded Ken Cuccinelli "should have been prosecuted" for disclosure violations, but Virginia's law was too weak.
rationale: There is no clear, widely reported investigative report that explicitly concluded Ken Cuccinelli 'should have been prosecuted' for disclosure violations. Coverage and ethics reviews criticized his disclosure practices and noted limits in Virginia law or enforcement, but they generally did not make a formal prosecutorial recommendation the claim asserts.

claim: "The government will be infiltrating" personal text messages.
rationale: As stated, this is an unqualified predictive claim about a government-wide action and there is no specific evidence that any particular government has a confirmed plan to universally "infiltrate" all personal text messages. While governments in some countries can and do intercept communications under legal authorities or via cooperation with providers, such actions are typically targeted, regulated, and vary by jurisdiction and platform rather than constituting a blanket forthcoming program. The absolute phrasing makes the claim unsupported.

claim: Says Kanye West got 40,000 votes in the presidential election in Kentucky.
rationale: Kanye West did not receive 40,000 votes in Kentucky in the relevant presidential election; his nationwide 2020 total was roughly 60,000 and his Kentucky total was only in the low thousands according to state-certified results. The claim overstates his support in that state by an order of magnitude.

claim: "Public sentiment in favor of collective bargaining and in favor of the unions has actually gone up as these governors, I think, have overreached and gone too far and tried to destroy the labor movement."
rationale: The statement is a broad, causal claim that cannot be verified as presented: it asserts both that public support for collective bargaining and unions has risen and that the rise was caused by specific governors 'overreaching.' Without a defined time period, location, or cited polling data, the causal link is unsubstantiated and the aggregate claim is not verifiable. While some national polls have shown growing favorability toward unions in recent years, tying that trend specifically to unnamed governors' actions is speculative.

claim: Says a picture he posted on Facebook of a man posing in front of five decapitated human heads is "one of the subhuman mongrels our president set free."
rationale: The claim attributes a specific inflammatory caption to an unidentified person's Facebook post but provides no source, date, or who “he” refers to. I cannot verify that such a post and exact wording existed from widely reported or archived evidence available up to my knowledge cutoff, so the assertion is unconfirmed and treated as false in the absence of corroboration.

claim: "What were the old annual deficits under Republicans have now become the monthly deficits under Democrats."
rationale: The claim is vague and misleading: it offers no country, years, or specific deficits and treats isolated monthly shortfalls as equivalent to typical annual deficits. While some months (notably during the COVID response) saw unusually large monthly budget shortfalls, there is no consistent pattern where normal Republican-era annual deficits routinely equal typical monthly deficits under Democratic administrations.

claim: Says Wisconsin’s 2011-13 state budget contains "no fee increases"
rationale: Independent analyses and contemporary news reporting found the 2011–13 Wisconsin budget included numerous fee increases across state agencies (for things like vehicle registration, licensing, court and other administrative fees), so the claim that it contained "no fee increases" is inaccurate. Supporters framed some changes as shifts in funding or administrative adjustments, but many items were explicitly fee hikes.

claim: "Democrats oppose any effort to secure our border."
rationale: The claim is an absolute generalization that is not supported by evidence. Many Democrats have supported and voted for border security measures such as funding for personnel, technology, and ports-of-entry improvements, even while opposing specific policies like large-scale wall construction or family-separation practices. Therefore it is false to say Democrats oppose any effort to secure the border.

claim: Children born today will carry a $30,000 share of the national debt.
rationale: The claim gives a precise dollar figure but lacks context (which country, how the share is calculated, and what time horizon). For example, dividing current U.S. federal debt (tens of trillions) by population yields a per-person share well above $30,000, and the future burden on children depends on economic growth, interest rates, and policy choices. Because the statement is a specific quantitative assertion without those assumptions, it is not supported.

claim: Says "Barcelona terrorist" is cousins with former President Barack Obama.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that any Barcelona attacker was a cousin of Barack Obama; news organizations and fact-checkers investigated and found no familial link. The identities of the Barcelona attackers have been reported publicly and Obama's family tree is well-documented with no such connection.

claim: "9,871,525 is the number of registered voters in AZ according to FB. AZ population is 7,270,000."
rationale: The claim is implausible: registered voters cannot exceed the state's total population. Arizona's population is about 7.2–7.3 million, while official Arizona voter registration totals in recent years have been roughly 4–5 million, far below 9,871,525, so the 9.87M figure is incorrect or misattributed.

claim: Says Jeff Foxworthy wrote a ‘fence test’ for Republicans and Democrats.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that comedian Jeff Foxworthy authored a formal 'fence test' for Republicans and Democrats; the phrase appears primarily in viral memes and misattributed jokes. Such partisan 'tests' are often circulated without clear sourcing and have been attributed to various public figures incorrectly.

claim: "We haven't yet taken out a negative ad."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it lacks any speaker, campaign, geographic area, or time period; without that context there is no way to confirm ad activity. Political campaigns commonly run negative ads, and verifying the claim would require checking ad buys, media records, and news/ad-tracking services. Given the missing context I default to false rather than affirming an unverified denial.

claim: Voters in Maricopa County, Ariz., were forced to vote using Sharpie pens that aren’t read by voting machines.
rationale: This is false. Maricopa County did provide Sharpie pens at many polling places and some workers encouraged their use to reduce ink bleed-through, but voters were not forced to use them and ballots marked with Sharpie are read and counted by the county’s ballot scanners. Election officials and independent fact-checkers tested and confirmed Sharpie ink does not prevent machines from reading votes.

claim: Georgia has "a dropout rate that’s higher" than Alabama's.
rationale: The statement as written is unverified and likely false because dropout rates vary by year and by the metric used (event vs. status dropout rate). Recent state-level data do not consistently show Georgia having a higher dropout rate than Alabama; in many years Alabama's rate has been similar or higher. Without a specific year and definition the blanket comparison cannot be confirmed.

claim: "We work longer hours than any people in the industrialized world, including the Japanese."
rationale: International labor statistics do not support the claim: the United States does not work longer hours than all other industrialized countries. OECD and other datasets show several developed countries (e.g., South Korea, Mexico, Greece, Chile, Turkey in various years) with higher annual hours per worker, and Japan's annual hours have generally been similar to or lower than the U.S. in recent years.

claim: "In Minnesota, well over 6,200 election-day registrations from 2008 proved fraudulent."
rationale: Post-election reviews and independent fact-checks found that the claim of 'well over 6,200' fraudulent same-day registrations in Minnesota in 2008 was not supported by evidence. State and county investigations identified only a small number of confirmed or prosecutable fraud cases (dozens), not thousands, and the larger figure originated from unsubstantiated partisan assertions.

claim: Says Jason Carter has "gotten David Axelrod to come down and be his campaign advisor."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that David Axelrod formally joined Jason Carter's campaign as an advisor. While Axelrod has occasionally appeared at events or expressed support for Democratic candidates, contemporary reporting on Carter’s campaign does not document Axelrod becoming his campaign advisor.

claim: Says in U.S. Congress, members "don’t even have to be on the floor for debates or votes."
rationale: This is false as a general statement: under normal Congressional rules members must be on the floor (or otherwise present in the chamber) to be recognized for debate and to cast a vote. There have been temporary exceptions (notably temporary proxy voting rules used in the House during the COVID pandemic) and members can have statements entered in the Congressional Record without being physically present, but those are limited exceptions rather than the standard practice.

claim: "Wind powers nearly 13 million homes across the country."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unsupported as written because it gives no country or time frame; the common "homes powered" metric is a simplification that depends on the year’s wind generation and assumed household electricity use. Current and historical data show that the number of homes wind can "power" changes year to year and by country, so a blanket statement without context is misleading.

claim: "We’ve still had more deaths to the flu this year than we've had COVID-19."
rationale: The claim is presented without specifying a country or exact timeframe and therefore is misleading. In most countries and globally since 2020, COVID-19 has caused substantially more deaths in a year than a typical seasonal flu year; public health surveillance data show COVID annual mortality generally exceeds seasonal influenza in the pandemic and post‑pandemic years. A blanket statement that flu deaths exceed COVID deaths 'this year' is not supported without additional context.

claim: The Orlando shooter used "a weapon of war."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and misleading: reporting on the 2016 Orlando (Pulse) shooter shows he used semi-automatic civilian firearms (a rifle and a handgun), not a fully automatic military armament. Describing those weapons as a 'weapon of war' is rhetoric rather than an accurate technical classification.

claim: "Barack Hussein Obama will … force doctors to assist homosexuals in buying surrogate babies."
rationale: There is no evidence that Barack Obama proposed or enacted any policy that would "force doctors" to help same-sex couples purchase children via surrogacy. Surrogacy arrangements are governed primarily by state law and private contracts, and a president cannot unilaterally compel individual physicians to provide medical services against law or conscience protections.

claim: The daughter of a Donald Trump appointee posed as an El Paso shooting victim in a photo with the president.
rationale: Contemporary fact-checks found no credible evidence that a person pictured with President Trump was the daughter of a Trump appointee posing as an El Paso shooting victim. The claim circulated on social media was investigated and debunked by independent reporters and fact-checking organizations, which identified the individuals as local residents or family members rather than relatives of a political appointee.

claim: Image of expansive pit shows a lithium mine.
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to identify the pit as a lithium mine from a generic description; expansive open pits can be many things (copper, gold, phosphate, aggregate quarries, or other minerals). Lithium is often produced from brine evaporation ponds or from hard‑rock spodumene which can have distinct processing infrastructure; without the image, geolocation, or corroborating metadata it cannot be reliably attributed to lithium. Given the ambiguity, the claim should be treated as false until verified.

claim: "Certainly we're going to be the most restrictive state in the land … in terms of who can get medical marijuana, how it will be prescribed and how it will be achieved in terms of moving it into the marketplace."
rationale: The claim is a comparative, predictive statement without specifying which state or time period, so it cannot be verified as a factual assertion. U.S. states have widely varying medical marijuana eligibility, prescribing rules, and market regulations, and proving a state is "the most restrictive" requires detailed statutory and regulatory comparison after laws are enacted.

claim: "Seventy four percent of Californians are absolutely against sanctuary state" policies.
rationale: No reputable statewide poll shows that 74% of Californians are 'absolutely against' sanctuary-state policies. Public opinion on sanctuary policies in California has varied by question wording and timing, and many credible polls show divided views or plurality support rather than such an overwhelming level of opposition. The 74% figure likely stems from a misinterpreted, out-of-context, or nonrepresentative survey.

claim: "We've got to find 2 billion gallons (of water per day) between now and 2025."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and provides no actor, jurisdiction, or source for the figure; there is no widely reported or verifiable mandate that 'we' must find exactly 2 billion gallons per day by 2025. Water supply and demand projections are region-specific and vary widely, and no authoritative national plan requiring that precise volume on that timeframe is known. Because the statement lacks context and evidence it cannot be treated as fact.

claim: Democrats are "asking for a blank check book to spend as much as they want without worrying about the repercussions."
rationale: This statement is a partisan rhetorical claim and is an exaggeration rather than an accurate description of how government spending works. Democratic proposals for increased spending still go through normal legislative processes, budget scoring, oversight, votes, and political accountability, so they cannot unilaterally spend without repercussions. Characterizing all Democrats as seeking a “blank check book” overstates and misrepresents standard budgetary practice.

claim: Says "Dan McCready took money from Ilhan Omar"
rationale: There is no public evidence or reputable reporting that Rep. Ilhan Omar personally donated campaign funds to Dan McCready. Candidate contributions are publicly reported to the FEC, and available records and news coverage list McCready’s donors and endorsers without showing a direct monetary contribution from Omar. The claim likely confuses endorsement or fundraising assistance with an actual personal donation.

claim: 7 million people the Congressional Budget Office says won't have health insurance coverage under the Senate health care bill "don't exist."
rationale: The CBO’s figure of about 7 million people projected to lack coverage under the Senate bill is a statistical projection of real people who would be uninsured relative to current law, not a claim about nonexistent individuals. There is no evidence that those people “don’t exist”; the CBO publicly documents its methodology and demographic estimates, although projections have uncertainty.

claim: Democratic lawmakers who voted in favor of short-term spending bills "just voted to deport Dreamers."
rationale: A vote for a short-term spending bill (a continuing resolution) to keep the government funded does not by itself enact deportations. Deporting DACA recipients would require either specific statutory changes, executive action to end DACA and order enforcement, or explicit riders in the spending bill that change immigration policy; absent such language, a CR preserves the status quo rather than 'vot[ing] to deport Dreamers.'

claim: "90,000 Californians are unsheltered and homeless."
rationale: Recent point-in-time counts and state reports show that California's total homeless population in recent years has been well above 90,000, with the unsheltered portion typically exceeding 90,000 (often reported around 100,000–130,000). Saying '90,000 Californians are unsheltered and homeless' understates the most recent-count unsheltered totals and conflates total versus unsheltered in a way that is misleading without a year or source.

claim: Says Oregon ranks 43rd in education.
rationale: The claim gives no source, year, or metric, and state education rankings vary widely by methodology and time. Because "Oregon ranks 43rd in education" is not a verifiable, consistently true statement across major recent rankings, it cannot be accepted as fact without a cited source.

claim: "The average homeowner spends more than $2,000 each year on energy costs – more than on either real estate taxes or homeowners insurance."
rationale: While U.S. households spend roughly $1,500–$2,000 a year on total residential energy on average, typical annual property tax bills for homeowners nationally are often at or above $2,000 and thus frequently exceed energy costs; homeowners insurance averages are generally lower (around $1,000–$1,500). Therefore the claim that energy costs exceed both real estate taxes and insurance for the average homeowner is not generally correct.

claim: A collection of photos shows animals caught in the Australia wildfires.
rationale: During the 2019–2020 Australian bushfires and other fire events, many news organizations, wildlife groups, and photographers published collections of images showing animals injured, burned, or fleeing fires. While some individual photos circulated online were later shown to be misattributed, there are numerous verified photo collections documenting wildlife affected by Australian wildfires. Therefore the general claim that a collection of photos shows animals caught in the Australia wildfires is accurate.

claim: Says Donald Trump said, 'Africans Are Lazy, Good At Sex, Theft.'
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable news reporting that Donald Trump ever uttered the quoted line 'Africans Are Lazy, Good At Sex, Theft.' While Trump has been reported to make derogatory comments about certain countries (e.g., the widely reported 'shithole countries' remark in 2018), fact-checkers and transcripts do not attribute this specific phrase to him.

claim: "President Trump has lifted the prospect of voters across Vermont, overseeing a 11,742 decline of Vermont residents on food stamps."
rationale: The claim is vague and mixes unrelated concepts: a U.S. president does not directly 'lift the prospect of voters across Vermont' and attributing a precise 11,742-person decline in Vermont SNAP recipients to President Trump is unsupported. SNAP enrollment is administered jointly by federal and state agencies and can change for many reasons (economy, state policy, recertification, data corrections), so a causal attribution to the president alone is not justified without specific evidence.

claim: "Kamala Harris is the prosecutor who refused to charge the police in the murder of Oscar Grant!"
rationale: Kamala Harris was Alameda County District Attorney at the time and her office did charge BART officer Johannes Mehserle in the shooting of Oscar Grant; Mehserle was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter. While Harris faced criticism for the handling and timing of the response and for not charging other officers, the claim that she outright "refused to charge the police" is inaccurate.

claim: "1776 flag flying over White House!" in January 2021. "Revolution Signal."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a 1776 flag was flown from the White House in January 2021. Fact-checks and contemporary reporting show images of such a flag on nearby private buildings or temporary locations, not on an official White House flagpole, and the White House did not officially display a 1776 flag.

claim: States still face a "mandate" to expand Medicaid coverage under President Obama's health care reform law.
rationale: The Supreme Court in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) held that the federal government cannot constitutionally coerce states into Medicaid expansion by threatening existing Medicaid funds, so expansion is effectively voluntary. While the ACA originally required expansion, that Court ruling removed a legal mandate even though federal incentives remain.

claim: Says he can’t release his internal affairs record because there are Attorney General guidelines in place protecting it.
rationale: This claim is misleading as stated: Attorney General guidance can advise on disclosure and identify categories that may be confidential, but it does not universally or automatically bar release of internal affairs records. Whether an internal affairs file can be released depends on the applicable public-records statutes, specific AG opinions or rules in that jurisdiction, and court precedents, not a blanket nationwide AG protection.

claim: "BIDEN: 'I'm not gonna take any questions because I think it's inappropriate.'"
rationale: I cannot find a verifiable primary-source instance of President Biden saying that exact sentence, and the claim lacks context (time, place, event) that would allow confirmation. While Biden has at times declined to take questions, attributing this precise quotation without a source appears unverified and may be a paraphrase or misattribution.

claim: "Gas is high because they shut down production in the U.S." under the Biden administration.
rationale: The Biden administration did not "shut down" U.S. oil and gas production; domestic production largely continued and recovered after the COVID downturn, and the U.S. has remained a top global producer. High gasoline prices have been driven primarily by global factors (OPEC+ supply decisions, the Russia–Ukraine war), pandemic-related demand shifts, refinery capacity and logistical issues, and taxes/fees, not a blanket U.S. production shutdown by the administration.

claim: Online voter registration is a "more secure" way of doing voter registration.
rationale: The claim is too broad: whether online voter registration is "more secure" depends on the specific implementation. Online systems can reduce human transcription errors and provide real-time validation, but they also introduce cybersecurity risks (data breaches, hacking, DDoS) and identity-proofing challenges; without strong authentication, auditing, and operational safeguards they can be less secure than well-run paper or in-person processes.

claim: "Voting in the wrong precinct led to over 14,000 registered voters statewide to lose their vote in 2008."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false as stated: while voting in the wrong precinct can lead to provisional or otherwise uncounted ballots, there is no well-documented, nationwide or unspecified-state figure showing that over 14,000 registered voters 'lost their vote' in 2008 for that sole reason. Rejected and provisional ballot counts are tracked by state election officials and media, and no reputable source supports this specific statewide number without naming a state or providing documentation.

claim: A BP oil executive named Brice Cromwell blamed the Biden administration for high gas prices.
rationale: Multiple news reports quoted Brice Cromwell, a BP America executive, saying that U.S. policy decisions under the Biden administration had contributed to higher gasoline prices. His remarks were widely cited as blaming the administration for creating conditions that discouraged investment and constrained supply, which affected pump prices.

claim: Georgia has the highest flu activity in the country.
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that cannot be true as a general rule: influenza activity fluctuates week to week and by location, so no jurisdiction is always the highest. Determining whether Georgia currently has the highest flu activity requires up-to-date surveillance data; without a specified time period or source this claim is unsupported.

claim: The Texas abortion law "provides at least six weeks for a person to be able to get an abortion."
rationale: Texas's law (commonly called SB8) bans abortions once fetal 'cardiac activity' is detected, which is typically around six weeks from the last menstrual period but can occur earlier; it does not guarantee that a person will have at least six weeks to obtain an abortion. Many people do not realize they are pregnant by six weeks and the precise timing of detectable cardiac activity varies, so the law does not reliably provide a full six-week window.

claim: "My opponent... lost 43,000 jobs in Houston since he took over; we are losing jobs."
rationale: The claim provides no named official, start date, or data source, so the specific figure of '43,000 jobs lost in Houston since he took over' cannot be verified. Public employment data (e.g., BLS and state workforce reports) show Houston employment has varied by period, and attributing a precise net loss to a single official without a timeframe or source is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Too many" tattoos "on visible body parts" keep some applicants out of the military.
rationale: Armed forces in many countries maintain rules limiting tattoo placement, size, and content; applicants whose visible tattoos exceed those limits can be refused enlistment or required to remove/cover them. Multiple service branches (e.g., U.S. Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps) and other national militaries have documented cases where excessive visible tattoos prevented acceptance.

claim: Says the New York bike path assault "was the ninth vehicle assault used by ISIS."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that the New York City bike path attack was specifically "the ninth vehicle assault" carried out by ISIS. ISIS did claim or inspire multiple vehicle-ramming incidents, but counts vary by source and by whether one includes inspired lone actors versus centrally directed attacks, and reputable reporting did not label this attack as the ninth.

claim: "If all of the [Bush-era] tax cuts expire on schedule, the budget will be close to being balanced in four years."
rationale: Nonpartisan budget projections around the relevant period (CBO and independent analysts) showed that letting all Bush-era tax cuts expire would substantially reduce projected deficits but would not eliminate them or bring the budget 'close' to balance within four years. The claim overstates the fiscal effect because ongoing spending trends and economic assumptions would still produce significant deficits.

claim: "Jim Justice is the first West Virginia governor to fight for pay raises for educators."
rationale: Jim Justice is not the first West Virginia governor to push for pay raises for educators. Previous governors (for example Gaston Caperton in the 1990s and more recent governors such as Joe Manchin and Earl Ray Tomblin) supported increased education funding and measures that raised teacher pay; the 2018 teacher movement drew attention to Justice's actions but did not mark the first gubernatorial advocacy for raises.

claim: "We need to pass a carbon tax to stop climate change. Break up the Wall Street banks. And stop the government spying on innocent Americans. Cory Booker doesn’t support any of these ideas."
rationale: The absolute claim that Cory Booker “doesn’t support any of these ideas” is false.
