Booker has publicly backed strong climate action (including support for aggressive climate policies and carbon-pricing concepts), advocated tougher regulation of big banks and financial reform, and supported limits on bulk government surveillance and measures to protect privacy. He may disagree with particular policy designs, but he does not categorically oppose all three broad ideas.

claim: Says he and President Barack Obama have the same position on gay marriage.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because the antecedent 'he' is unspecified; without knowing which person is being compared to President Obama and at what time, you cannot confirm they share the same position. Additionally, Obama’s own position on same-sex marriage changed over time (he publicly endorsed same-sex marriage in May 2012 after earlier supporting civil unions), so timing matters. Given these gaps, the statement cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Amazing fact: Senate has already voted on more amendments in 2015 than Reid allowed ALL YEAR last year."
rationale: The statement is misleading and not supported by roll-call records; counts of amendment votes depend on definitions (e.g., any amendment votes, cloture-allowance votes, or recorded roll calls) and fact-checkers comparing 2014 to early 2015 concluded the claim exaggerated differences. When comparable measures are used, 2014 saw at least as many amendment or amendment-related roll calls as the early months of 2015, so it is not accurate to say 2015 had already surpassed all of last year under Reid.

claim: "Beginning in the early 1990s, we built barriers in 4 sectors at our southern border. Since each was built, those sectors have seen massive drops in apprehensions of people crossing the border illegally," including 90 percent to 95 percent decreases in the Tucson, Yuma, San Diego and El Paso sectors. ​
rationale: It is true that large enforcement operations and barrier construction in the early-to-mid 1990s (e.g., Operation Gatekeeper in San Diego, Hold-the-Line in El Paso) corresponded with very large drops in apprehensions in some sectors, particularly San Diego and El Paso. However the claim overgeneralizes: Tucson did not experience the same 90–95% decline at that time (it became a major crossing zone after enforcement in other sectors), and Yuma’s changes were smaller and more variable. The blanket causal claim that each sector saw 90–95% decreases 'since each was built' is therefore inaccurate and misleading without specifying years and accounting for displacement and other factors.

claim: "‘TrumpCare’ would allow insurance execs to personally make millions off your health care."
rationale: The claim is overstated and speculative: none of the major 'TrumpCare' proposals (e.g., the AHCA) contained provisions that directly paid insurance executives millions. Critics did warn that repealing the individual mandate, cutting Medicaid, and loosening regulations could increase insurers' profits, which might indirectly boost executive pay, but that is an indirect outcome and not a guaranteed or explicit allowance in the legislation.

claim: "Half the workforce in the country may have just been idled" by coronavirus.
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: it does not specify which country or timeframe, and empirical labor statistics from the COVID-19 pandemic show large but generally much smaller shares of workers temporarily idled or unemployed rather than half the workforce. Without a specific country, date, or authoritative source, the assertion that 'half the workforce... may have just been idled' is not substantiated.

claim: "Bill Gates talked about using vaccines to control population growth" in an "unedited 2010 TED Talk video"
rationale: In his 2010 TED Talk Bill Gates explicitly said that vaccines, health care and reproductive health services could help lower projected population growth by about 10–15 percent. He framed this as reducing child mortality and therefore reducing fertility, not as using vaccines to harm or forcibly reduce people. Portions of the talk were later clipped or misrepresented in edited videos, but the unedited 2010 TED Talk does include the quoted point.

claim: Democrats say Chafee wants to tax equipment that enables amputee veterans to drive
rationale: I can find no corroborating evidence that Democrats broadly accused any public figure named Chafee of proposing a tax specifically on adaptive driving equipment for amputee veterans. The claim is very specific but lacks supporting reporting or documented statements, and taxing assistive devices for veterans would be an unusual and widely reported policy move.

claim: "Ten percent of violent deaths in the U.S. each year are due to strangulation."
rationale: National vital statistics and law-enforcement homicide data show that firearms account for the majority of homicides in the U.S., while deaths by strangulation/asphyxiation comprise only a small minority of violent deaths. Available CDC/FBI cause-of-death breakdowns do not support strangulation causing roughly 10% of all violent deaths; the true proportion is much lower.

claim: "I have always been focused on reining in the deficit."
rationale: The statement is vague and lacks an identified speaker and timeframe, so it cannot be verified as universally true. Claims of always being focused on reining in the deficit require examination of concrete evidence (budgets, votes, policy actions) over the relevant period; without that, the assertion is unsubstantiated and often matches common political rhetoric rather than documented behavior.

claim: "We have cut taxes more than 40 times in four years."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable and likely misleading because it gives no jurisdiction or definition of what counts as a “tax cut.” Political claims that cite dozens of tax cuts over a multi-year period commonly include many small or technical changes (fee adjustments, credits, temporary measures) and inflations; without an itemized list tied to a specific government, the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "By fiscal year 2013, the state is expected to wipe through [HOPE scholarship] reserve funds."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and cannot be verified as stated because it does not identify which state or which official projection is being cited. While some reports around the early 2010s warned that Georgia’s HOPE scholarship reserves were strained and could be exhausted within a few years without revenue changes, different forecasts gave different depletion years and policy changes altered outcomes. Because the statement is presented as a definitive expectation for an unspecified jurisdiction and year, it is not reliably true as written.

claim: "A couple of debates ago, (Donald Trump) said if you don’t support socialized health care, you’re heartless."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Donald Trump saying the line “if you don’t support socialized health care, you’re heartless” in recent debates. Trump has consistently opposed so-called socialized medicine and would be unlikely to make that admonition; the phrasing more closely matches critics or Democratic opponents and appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase.

claim: Says Texas does not regulate the appearance of some kinds of imitation firearms sold in Texas.
rationale: Texas does not have comprehensive state law mandating the outward appearance or marking of all imitation firearms, and many realistic-looking devices such as airsoft and BB guns are sold in Texas without additional state-imposed appearance standards. Regulation of markings (for example, orange tips on toy guns) is primarily governed by federal rules and manufacturer practice rather than a broad Texas statute.

claim: "Paul Ryan has blocked all action to strengthen our gun laws."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement but is inaccurate: while Paul Ryan, as Speaker, used his agenda-setting powers and opposed many gun-control proposals, he did not single-handedly prevent every effort to address gun laws. Some firearms-related measures and hearings occurred in the House and other parts of Congress during his tenure, and the legislative process also involves the Senate and the President.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court decided in 1982 that non-citizen children must get free K-12 education.
rationale: In Plyler v. Doe (1982) the U.S. Supreme Court held that states may not deny free public elementary and secondary (K–12) education to children based on their undocumented immigration status. The Court ruled that such exclusion violated the Equal Protection Clause because the state failed to show a substantial justification for denying education to these children.

claim: A Texas police department bought an ad telling drug dealers, "We can take your competition off the streets for FREE."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official confirmation that any Texas police department purchased an ad with that exact wording; the claim appears to originate from a doctored/viral social media image and has been flagged by fact-checkers. While some departments have used provocative billboards targeting drug activity, authorities generally do not run ads promising to remove 'competition' and available evidence shows this specific ad is fabricated or misattributed.

claim: "Thanks to Washington, nearly everyone will pay more in taxes in 2013. Somehow people think it's just the wealthy. It's not."
rationale: At the start of 2013 the temporary 2 percentage-point payroll-tax cut expired, meaning most wage earners saw higher payroll tax withholding and thus higher taxes that year. While some income-tax rate increases were aimed at high earners, the payroll-tax increase applied broadly, so it was not limited to the wealthy. There are exceptions (unemployed, some retirees or non-wage income recipients) and later legislation addressed some cliff issues.

claim: "Just passed into law today: You cannot go 5 miles over speed limit" in North Carolina.
rationale: There is no authoritative record that North Carolina passed a law today specifically barring driving 5 mph over the posted speed limit. North Carolina traffic statutes already make driving above the speed limit unlawful, but enforcement tolerances are discretionary and not changed by a single "5 mph" prohibition reported today. Social posts often mischaracterize proposed bills or local enforcement guidance as new statewide law.
cited_knowledge: General knowledge of how traffic statutes and enforcement discretion work in the U.S., lack of corroborating legislative or news reports of a new NC law explicitly banning going 5 mph over the limit.
safety_notes: This is time-sensitive and could refer to a proposed bill, local ordinance, or temporary enforcement campaign; check the North Carolina General Assembly or state DOT for the current, official text and effective date.

claim: Say video "shows massive alligator strolling across Florida golf course."
rationale: There is no provided video link, metadata, date, or independent reporting to verify the specific clip described. While Florida alligators on golf courses are plausible and genuine examples exist, without the original footage or corroboration this particular claim cannot be confirmed and may be miscaptioned or edited.

claim: "Trump wins the award Obama never could."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and gives no specific award to verify; there is no known, documented award that Donald Trump uniquely won that Barack Obama was categorically unable to receive. Without naming the award and providing evidence, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: Officials "recommend that women who get one of these (COVID-19) shots should absolutely not get pregnant for at least the first two months after they’ve been injected."
rationale: Major public-health agencies did not issue a blanket recommendation that women must avoid pregnancy for two months after COVID-19 vaccination. Agencies including the WHO, CDC, and EMA have stated there is no evidence vaccines cause infertility and people do not need to delay pregnancy; clinical trial protocols sometimes required contraception during the study period, which is not the same as a public health recommendation.

claim: "Greenland's ice sheet isn't shrinking any more rapidly today than it was 80 years ago."
rationale: Multiple independent lines of evidence show Greenland’s ice sheet is losing mass much more rapidly now than about 80 years ago. Satellite gravimetry (GRACE), altimetry and field studies, supported by IPCC assessments, document a marked acceleration of ice mass loss and increased surface melt and ice discharge since the late 20th century.

claim: "Trump revokes Barack Obama’s security clearance."
rationale: While President Trump revoked the security clearances of several former intelligence officials in 2018 (notably John Brennan and others), Barack Obama was not among those whose clearances were revoked. Moreover, former presidents typically do not hold a routine personal security clearance in the same way as agency officials; they may receive classified briefings on request, which is a different administrative arrangement.

claim: "I was the deciding vote on abolishing the death penalty in the state of Illinois."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated and is unlikely: Illinois abolished the death penalty through legislative votes in 2011 followed by the governor's signature, not by a single "deciding" individual casting one pivotal vote. Public records and contemporary reporting attribute the change to majority votes in both chambers and the governor's action rather than to a lone tie-breaking vote.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "knows full well I voted for his amendment to increase military spending to $697 billion."
rationale: I cannot verify the quoted statement as presented: there is no clear, attributable source or widely reported record showing someone saying that “Marco Rubio knows full well I voted for his amendment to increase military spending to $697 billion,” nor a documented Rubio amendment explicitly setting military spending at $697 billion tied to such an exchange. Congressional amendments and floor statements are recorded and would be citable if this exact claim were true, but no such clear record is evident from available summaries of defense spending votes.

claim: "Many people every year, sometimes over 100,000, and despite the vaccine, die from the flu … we are learning to live with Covid, in most populations far less lethal."
rationale: The first part is correct that seasonal influenza causes many deaths worldwide and can exceed 100,000 in some years, and vaccines do not prevent all flu deaths. The second part — that COVID-19 is now "in most populations far less lethal" — is misleading: while vaccination, prior infection, treatments, and some variants (e.g., Omicron) have reduced severity, COVID-19 generally still carries higher infection fatality risk and has caused far greater excess mortality than a typical flu season, especially for older and vulnerable groups.

claim: "The nine-day deer hunt contributes more than $1.3 billion in revenue to the state of Wisconsin."
rationale: Independent studies and state reporting typically describe the nine-day deer hunt as generating roughly $1.3 billion in total economic activity for Wisconsin, but that is not the same as 'revenue to the state' (i.e., government receipts). The exact figure varies by study and year, and most sources frame it as economic impact or spending by hunters, not state tax or budget revenue exceeding $1.3 billion.

claim: "Obama’s daughters caught on camera burning US flag at DC protest."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Sasha or Malia Obama were filmed burning a U.S. flag in Washington, D.C.; the claim circulated from misattributed or manipulated images and has been debunked by fact-checkers. Major news outlets and verification organizations found the footage/photos unverified and inconsistent with known facts about the individuals and events.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton won "health care for 8 million children."
rationale: Attributing 'winning health care for 8 million children' solely to Hillary Clinton is misleading. The State Children’s Health Insurance Program (SCHIP/CHIP) that covered millions of children was created by Congress and signed into law in 1997 during Bill Clinton’s presidency; Hillary Clinton advocated for health reforms but did not single-handedly 'win' that program or the coverage number.

claim: A "majority of our students are trapped in" underperforming schools.
rationale: The claim is underspecified — it does not define who 'our students' are, what counts as 'underperforming', or a timeframe. Without those definitions and supporting local data, the assertion that a majority are 'trapped' cannot be verified. While some districts may have most students in low-performing schools, that cannot be generalized to an unspecified population.

claim: Says President Barack Obama released a statement on the "death of brother Robin Williams before ... a statement on brother Michael Brown."
rationale: Robin Williams died on August 11, 2014 and the White House/President Obama released a statement mourning his death that day. Obama's more substantive public statement addressing the death of Michael Brown and the unrest in Ferguson came later in mid‑August 2014, so the obituary statement for Williams preceded a presidential statement on Michael Brown.

claim: Says recent studies indicate that nationally, only 8 percent of white voting-age citizens but 25 percent of African-American voting-age citizens lack government-issued photo IDs.
rationale: National survey research (most prominently the Brennan Center’s 'Citizens Without Proof' analysis) has reported that about 8% of white voting-age adults and roughly 25% of African‑American voting‑age adults lack a government-issued photo ID. Those numbers have been widely cited in analyses of voter ID laws and derive from representative survey estimates of ID possession.

claim: "Maxine Waters Is Getting Criminally Charged!"
rationale: There were no credible public reports or a Department of Justice indictment charging Representative Maxine Waters as of mid‑2024. Claims that she is being criminally charged have circulated on social media but have not been substantiated by official filings or mainstream news outlets.

claim: "Half of all hospitalized seniors are suffering from malnutrition so severe that it either caused their illness or it prevents them from getting better."
rationale: The claim overstates the evidence. While malnutrition or risk of malnutrition is common among hospitalized older adults and is linked to poorer outcomes, prevalence estimates vary widely (roughly 20–60% depending on setting and screening tool) and there is no consensus that half of all hospitalized seniors are so severely malnourished that it caused their illness or definitively prevents recovery.

claim: Says "we are overcharging students . . . to help pay for the health care law."
rationale: The claim that "we are overcharging students ... to help pay for the health care law" is unsupported as a general statement. Student health fees and insurance premiums are set by institutions and insurers based on coverage costs and risk pools, not by a uniform per-student surcharge mandated by federal health legislation. Without specific evidence identifying the institution, amounts, and a direct link to a particular law, the assertion is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: There are nanoparticles in the COVID-19 vaccine that will help people "locate you" via 5G networks.
rationale: There is no evidence COVID-19 vaccines contain nanoparticles that enable locating people via 5G. mRNA vaccines use lipid nanoparticles as a biochemical delivery vehicle for mRNA, not electronic transmitters, and 5G radio networks cannot detect or communicate with inert microscopic particles inside the body. Manufacturers, regulatory agencies, and physicists have found no mechanism by which injected particles could act as 5G-based tracking devices.

claim: "One in 19 Americans today get SSDI or SSI. That's one in 19 Americans (who) are disabled."
rationale: The claim overstates the prevalence. Social Security records show roughly 9 million SSDI beneficiaries and several million SSI recipients, but because some people receive both and SSI includes aged as well as disabled recipients, the unique count of people receiving either program is closer to about 13–14 million — roughly 1 in 24–25 Americans, not 1 in 19 (~1 in 19 would be about 17–18 million).

claim: Says Jeb Bush tweeted "Ok boomer" at Donald Trump.
rationale: There is no credible record or media reporting that former Florida Governor Jeb Bush tweeted the phrase "Ok boomer" directly at Donald Trump. Such a notable exchange would have been widely covered, and Jeb Bush is not known to have publicly tweeted that phrase at Trump.

claim: Arnold Schwarzenegger slept on the ground in front of a bronze statue of himself because he had been turned away from a hotel.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Schwarzenegger slept in front of a bronze statue of himself after being turned away from a hotel. Bronze statues honoring him were erected only after he became famous, whereas the anecdote describes an early-career episode; sources and his memoirs document hardships but do not corroborate this specific story.

claim: "There are hit squads being trained all over this country" to violently oppose a second term for President Donald Trump.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that organized ‘hit squads’ are being trained nationwide to violently oppose a second Trump term. Major news outlets, independent fact-checkers, and law-enforcement statements have found such claims originate from unverified social-media posts and conspiracy narratives rather than verified investigations. A coordinated, nationwide campaign of violent training would likely have produced arrests, official warnings, or investigative reporting, none of which exists.

claim: "When I became mayor of Los Angeles, we had a 44 percent (high school) graduation rate. I said that was unacceptable. I challenged that notion. I said the mayor needs to be involved with our schools. We need to partner together. As I left, after a number of reforms, we grew our graduation rate from 44 percent to 72."
rationale: The statement is misleading: while graduation rates in Los Angeles did improve in the 2000s, the commonly quoted jump from 44% to 72% mixes different metrics, timeframes, and geographies and overstates a single mayor's direct effect. The mayor does not control the independently run LAUSD, and fact-checkers have found the specific 44→72 point claim conflates on-time four‑year cohort rates with other adjusted or extended measures rather than a single, attributable increase during one mayoral tenure.

claim: Says of El Paso that some years, "in a city of almost 700,000, we had five murders the entire year. Our average over the last 10 years is 18 (murders per year). We exceeded that average just on one day" after a gunman opened fire at a Walmart in the city.
rationale: El Paso has had unusually low annual homicide counts for a city of its size, including some years with single-digit murders, and its 10-year average homicide total has been reported in the high-teens. The August 3, 2019 Walmart mass shooting in El Paso killed 22 people, which exceeded that multi-year annual average in a single day. These points match widely reported crime statistics and contemporary news coverage of the incident.

claim: In "the past four or five" presidential elections, "people who poll high at the beginning are not the people who end up being the nominees."
rationale: This sweeping claim is not supported by the recent nomination record. In several of the last five competitive cycles early poll leaders did win their nominations (for example Al Gore in 2000, Mitt Romney in 2012, and Joe Biden in 2020), while in others early front‑runners lost (for example Hillary Clinton was an early leader in 2008 and did not win the nomination; Jeb Bush polled high in 2016 but lost). The pattern is mixed, so the generalization is false.

claim: Says Joe Biden was asleep and snoring during a TV interview.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Biden actually fell asleep and snored during a televised interview; widely circulated clips making that claim have been debunked or shown to be misinterpreted (briefly closing his eyes) or manipulated. Fact-checks and video/audio analysis from reputable outlets found no on-air sleeping or audible snoring in verified footage.

claim: "Obama said he would unilaterally renegotiate the North American Free Trade Agreement."
rationale: Barack Obama did not say he would unilaterally renegotiate NAFTA; renegotiating a multilateral agreement requires agreement from the other signatories (Canada and Mexico). Public records show Obama criticized aspects of NAFTA at times and discussed modernizing trade rules, but he did not claim the power to unilaterally renegotiate the treaty.

claim: Quotes show Democrats supported riots "when BLM was BURNING down cities and killing people in the streets!"
rationale: The claim over-generalizes and is inaccurate: while some 2020 protests saw riots, arson, and deaths, mainstream Democratic leaders and the national Black Lives Matter movement largely condemned violence and advocated nonviolent protest. Assertions that “Democrats supported” burning cities or endorsed killing people rely on cherry-picked or out-of-context quotes from isolated individuals rather than broad, documented party support.

claim: An app called Talking Angela asks children personal questions and takes their photo.
rationale: Talking Angela is a virtual-pet/chat app that includes conversational prompts which can ask users personal-style questions (name, age, location) and it has a camera/selfie feature that can take pictures if the user grants permission. Claims that it secretly transmits photos to strangers were widely debunked by the developer, but the app does indeed ask questions and can take photos with device permission.

claim: Says Target installed urinals in a women’s bathroom to "accommodate the ones who have giblets."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Target announced installing urinals in a women’s bathroom or made the quoted remark about “giblets.” Target has discussed gender-inclusive restroom policies and single-stall restrooms, but fact-checks and news reporting found the specific quote and claim to be fabricated or satirical. The claim appears to be a mocking rumor rather than an actual corporate statement or documented installation policy.

claim: Republicans are "trying to create a fake unemployment insurance crisis."
rationale: The claim asserts a coordinated intent by ‘Republicans’ to fabricate a crisis, which is a strong factual assertion about motive and coordination that lacks clear, verifiable evidence. While some Republican politicians and commentators have publicly emphasized or exaggerated unemployment-insurance fraud and pushed policy changes, that does not prove a unified, deliberate effort to create a wholly fake crisis across the party.

claim: Says Gen. David H. Berger, commandant of the U.S. Marine Corps., refused Nancy Pelosi’s request to use the Marines for inauguration security, telling her "we don’t work for you."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official record that Gen. David H. Berger told Nancy Pelosi “we don’t work for you” or outright refused a request to use Marines for inauguration security. Fact-checks and contemporary news found the quoted retort is unverified and originated on social media; it appears to be fabricated. While military support decisions follow DOD/chain-of-command procedures rather than congressional direction, that does not validate the attributed quote.

claim: "Clinton's former pastor convicted of child molestation."
rationale: There is no credible, documented evidence that a pastor identified as ‘Clinton’s former pastor’ was convicted of child molestation. Major news outlets and public records do not link either Bill or Hillary Clinton to a pastor who was later convicted of such crimes. The claim is vague about which Clinton and which pastor, and no well-sourced instances match that description up to mid-2024.

claim: "More people have watched ‘Morning Joe’ than CNN and HLN 5 years in a row."
rationale: The claim is unsupported and ambiguous: television ratings typically compare programs to programs or networks to networks, and available Nielsen data do not show that the single program Morning Joe has consistently outdrawn the entire CNN network for five consecutive years. Morning Joe has sometimes outperformed low-rated networks or time slots (including HLN) but it is not accurate to assert it has beaten CNN (a full network) five years running without a specified metric or timeframe.

claim: Says state Rep. Jim Keffer, a GOP lieutenant to House Speaker Joe Straus, "did mail pieces for Democrat Mark Strama to help him defeat" a Republican.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Texas state Rep. Jim Keffer personally mailed campaign pieces on behalf of Democrat Mark Strama to help defeat a Republican. Keffer is a Republican and an ally of House Speaker Joe Straus, and such a notable cross-party action would likely have been documented; the claim appears to be a misattribution or unverified assertion.

claim: Pennsylvania rejected 372,000 mail-in ballots
rationale: There is no evidence that Pennsylvania rejected 372,000 mail-in ballots in any recent election; official Pennsylvania Department of State and media fact-checks report far smaller numbers of rejected mail/absentee ballots (generally in the tens of thousands or fewer depending on the year). The 372,000 figure appears to conflate different categories (e.g., unreturned applications, undeliverable mail, or total mail ballot requests) rather than actual rejected ballots counted by the state.

claim: "Six justices" on the U.S. Supreme Court have been "confirmed in presidential election years since 1912."
rationale: At least seven justices — Louis Brandeis (1916), Benjamin Cardozo (1932), William Brennan (1956), Lewis Powell (1972), William Rehnquist (1972), Anthony Kennedy (1988), and Amy Coney Barrett (2020) — were confirmed in presidential election years since 1912, so the claim that only six were confirmed is incorrect. Historical confirmation dates show multiple confirmations have occurred in election years.

claim: State "school funding per pupil is down 16 percent compared to 2009, after adjusting for inflation."
rationale: The claim is incomplete and unverifiable as written because it does not name which state or cite a data source and inflation index. Per-pupil funding trends since 2009 vary widely by state and by how inflation is adjusted; some states experienced large declines while others saw increases or smaller declines. Without a specific state and methodology, the blanket 16% figure cannot be confirmed.

claim: Democratic Party candidates for the state Assembly "actually received 200,000 more votes statewide" than their Republican counterparts in the 2012 election
rationale: The claim is ambiguous because it does not name which state's Assembly is meant, and I cannot verify a precise statewide vote margin of 200,000 for 2012 without that context. Vote totals for state legislative races vary widely by state and by whether uncontested seats and cross-filed races are included, so the specific numeric assertion is unconfirmed and therefore treated as false.

claim: "45.6 million people watched (the State of the Union), the highest number in history. @FoxNews beat every other Network, for the first time ever, with 11.7 million people tuning in."
rationale: Historical Nielsen and media reports for State of the Union viewership do not support the absolutes in this claim: the 45.6 million number is not clearly the highest ever and Fox News has previously topped other networks for SOTU broadcasts, so the statements 'highest in history' and 'for the first time ever' are inaccurate. The claim appears to conflate particular measurement windows and network/cable subtotals to make exaggerated superlative claims.

claim: "Nonpartisan experts have consistently ranked Claire one of the most independent senators — right in the middle."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as written because it fails to identify which “Claire” is meant and gives no timeframe or source for the alleged rankings. While nonpartisan metrics of bipartisanship and ideology exist (e.g., GovTrack’s Bipartisan Index, FiveThirtyEight metrics, DW-NOMINATE), I am not aware of any consistent, expert rankings that describe a senator named Claire as simultaneously “one of the most independent” and “right in the middle.” Without a specific name, time period, or cited ranking, the assertion cannot be supported.

claim: "Granite Staters who hold individual policies from Anthem...can indeed renew their policies and keep their current doctors and hospitals" in 2014.
rationale: In 2013–2014 many individual, pre-ACA Anthem policies were being cancelled because they did not meet new ACA standards. Although the federal transitional policy allowed one-year renewals in some cases, insurers and states varied; Anthem did not universally permit all Granite Staters to keep their prior plans or networks for 2014. Thus the blanket claim that Anthem individual policyholders in New Hampshire could renew and keep the same doctors in 2014 is not accurate.

claim: Fifty-three percent of graduates from liberal arts colleges these days can’t find jobs.
rationale: No reputable labor statistics or higher-education outcome reports show that 53% of liberal arts college graduates are unable to find jobs. Typical unemployment rates for recent college graduates are far lower, and while measures of underemployment or job-field mismatch can be notable, they do not equate to a majority being jobless.

claim: "The cost of living is going up, but paychecks aren't keeping up."
rationale: In many countries in recent years consumer prices (inflation) rose faster than wage growth, so real (inflation-adjusted) pay declined for large numbers of workers. Economic data and reporting from 2021–2023 show wages rising in nominal terms but failing to keep pace with spikes in housing, energy, and food costs, leaving household purchasing power reduced.

claim: "U.N. official John Ashe set to testify against the Clintons may not have died by accident."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that John Ashe was "set to testify" against the Clintons; his 2016 indictment concerned alleged bribery involving a Chinese businessman and reporting/federal filings do not show he was preparing testimony about the Clintons. The New York City medical examiner ruled Ashe's death accidental (asphyxiation with contributing drugs) and investigators did not produce evidence of homicide, so claims he "may not have died by accident" are speculative and unsupported.

claim: "Our jobless rate, our unemployment rate, is the lowest of all of the big cities in New Jersey."
rationale: The claim lacks a specific city and timeframe, so it cannot be verified as stated. Unemployment rates vary across municipalities and over time and must be compared using a defined period and official labor statistics; without that information the blanket assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: The United States' southern border is "basically open" and is "a super spreader event."
rationale: Characterizing the U.S. southern border as "basically open" is inaccurate: U.S. law enforcement continues to control ports of entry, detain or expel many undocumented arrivals, and process asylum claims, even though encounters have risen. There is also no strong evidence that crossings at the border have acted as a major "super spreader" event for COVID-19; most transmission has been driven by domestic community spread and public-health agencies did not identify border crossings as a primary driver of national surges. High encounter counts do not by themselves prove an uncontrolled border or that those encounters caused widespread disease transmission.

claim: Israel has seen a "90 percent reduction in terrorist attacks" that it attributes to building a 500-mile fence.
rationale: While Israeli officials have claimed large reductions (often cited as around 90%) in suicide bombings after parts of the West Bank barrier were built, independent analyses attribute the overall drop in attacks to a mix of factors—barrier sections, increased security measures, intelligence operations, and Palestinian security actions—so the simple claim that Israel saw a 90% reduction in terrorist attacks solely attributable to a 500-mile fence is misleading. The quoted percentage and the single-cause attribution overstate and oversimplify the evidence.

claim: Democratic candidate Jeff Greene "ran for Congress as a California Republican."
rationale: Jeff Greene, the Florida real-estate investor often described as a Democratic candidate, is known for running for U.S. Senate and governor in Florida as a Democrat and for donating to candidates of both parties. There is no credible record that he ever ran for Congress in California as a Republican; the claim appears to conflate him with someone else or confuse party affiliation and location.

claim: "Michigan just refused to certify the election results!"
rationale: There is no general, credible evidence that Michigan 'just refused to certify' statewide election results. Michigan's statewide results have been certified in past federal elections (including a temporary 2020 board deadlock that was later resolved and the state ultimately certified electors), and claims that the state recently refused to certify are misleading without a specific date and authoritative source.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s "Make America Great Again" hats were made in China.
rationale: Multiple media investigations and campaign sourcing records showed that large batches of Donald Trump’s original 'Make America Great Again' hats were manufactured in China during the 2015–2016 campaign. The campaign later stated some merchandise was produced in the U.S., but the initial bulk came from Chinese factories.

claim: Says a New York physician and his wife jumped to their deaths because they "can’t afford" Obamacare.
rationale: Contemporary reporting and fact-checking found no evidence that a New York physician and his wife killed themselves because they "couldn’t afford" the Affordable Care Act; the allegation appears to have originated from unverified social posts and was not supported by coroner statements or reputable news coverage. Reputable fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked similar viral claims that attribute suicides to inability to pay for Obamacare without documentary evidence.

claim: Says "Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated and confirmed 43 days before an election."
rationale: Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated by President Bill Clinton on June 14, 1993 and confirmed by the Senate on August 3, 1993. Those dates are neither 43 days before a U.S. presidential or the next general election (the next major general election was November 1994), and the time between nomination and confirmation was about 50 days, not 43.

claim: "A million people … could get health insurance right away" if Texas expanded Medicaid under Obamacare.
rationale: Multiple nonpartisan analyses estimate roughly one to 1.4 million low‑income Texans are in the Medicaid 'coverage gap' and would become eligible for Medicaid if Texas expanded under the ACA. That means on the order of a million people could gain health insurance relatively quickly once expansion took effect, though actual enrollment would depend on administrative steps.

claim: "I've been here almost every day."
rationale: This is a first-person statement about attendance that cannot be verified from the claim alone. Without timestamps, logs, witnesses, or other corroborating evidence, there is no basis to confirm the truth of 'I've been here almost every day.'

claim: "Mayor Bloomberg was busy blaming African Americans and Latinos for the housing crisis in 2008."
rationale: There is no substantial evidence that Mayor Michael Bloomberg publicly blamed African Americans and Latinos for the 2008 housing crisis. Contemporary reporting and his public remarks attributed the crisis to systemic factors—predatory lending, lax regulation, securitization and Wall Street practices—and while he sometimes criticized irresponsible borrowing in general, he did not single out racial groups as the cause.

claim: "$360 million of our tax dollars went straight to ... the Taliban."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that $360 million of U.S. taxpayer money was handed directly to the Taliban. Reporting and independent fact-checks show the figures cited in similar claims usually refer to Afghan central-bank assets held abroad, humanitarian-managed transfers, or cash moved during the chaotic withdrawal — none of which were an unrestricted payment of U.S. tax dollars straight to the Taliban.

claim: "White people control almost 90 percent of the nation's wealth."
rationale: Available data on U.S. household wealth show non-Hispanic white households hold a majority but far less than 90% of total national wealth (typically around 60–75% depending on year and definitions). The claim overstates the share and ignores differences in definitions of 'white' and 'wealth.'

claim: Political activists are "being paid" to protest members of Congress.
rationale: The claim is a broad, unqualified assertion without supporting evidence. While there are documented instances where paid organizers, staff, or reimbursed attendees participate in protests, reputable fact-checks and reporting do not support a widespread, systematic practice of activists generally being paid to protest members of Congress.

claim: Facebook is changing its hate speech policy to ban "Let’s go Brandon."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Facebook/Meta has announced a policy change that categorically bans the phrase "Let’s go Brandon." Meta’s hate speech rules target protected characteristics (race, religion, etc.), and political slogans or insults directed at public figures are generally not classified as hate speech; content moderation actions depend on context rather than an outright ban of that phrase.

claim: Says award-winning Milwaukee Public Schools teacher Megan Sampson was laid off because Gov. Scott Walker cut state aid to education.
rationale: I could not find authoritative evidence establishing that award‑winning Milwaukee teacher Megan Sampson was laid off specifically because Gov. Scott Walker cut state aid. Teacher layoffs are typically determined by district budget choices, enrollment, seniority rules, or position eliminations; while reductions in state aid can contribute to district shortfalls, a direct causal link requires contemporaneous district records or reliable reporting.

claim: A defense bill "includes language that would require military hospitals to provide abortions on demand."
rationale: Reported versions of recent U.S. defense bills (NDAA amendments) expanded access to abortion-related care for service members — including travel and reimbursement protections and authorization for services consistent with law — but did not contain an unconditional requirement that military hospitals provide abortions 'on demand.' The provisions were limited by existing law, medical exceptions, and conscience/contracting rules, so the claim overstates what the text mandates.

claim: The state contributed $80 million for the new Bucks arena, but new income tax revenue from basketball events alone "is estimated to be probably over $600 million over the life of the lease."
rationale: While Wisconsin did provide an $80 million state contribution toward the new Bucks arena, the specific claim that new income tax revenue from basketball events alone would be "probably over $600 million over the life of the lease" is unsupported and highly likely inflated. Publicly available independent analyses and typical economic-impact methods show much smaller and more qualified fiscal benefits than the large headline figure often cited by team-commissioned studies. The $600M figure appears to be an optimistic projection or marketing number rather than a reliably measured revenue outcome.

claim: Figures for September 2014’s job growth in Wisconsin mark the "largest private-sector job creation we've had in the month of September in more than a decade"
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific claim with available data here; whether September 2014 was the largest private‑sector September gain depends on which series (seasonally adjusted vs unadjusted, establishment survey vs state payroll counts) and the chosen comparison window. Without the precise data source, the statement is ambiguous and therefore cannot be verified as a factual absolute. Claims like this have historically depended on narrow definitions and selective timeframes.

claim: "After every major conflict ... what happened was that we ultimately hollowed out the force, largely by doing deep, across-the-board cuts."
rationale: The statement presents a universal pattern that does not hold across history. While some major conflicts (e.g., WWI demobilization, Vietnam-era drawdowns and the 1970s 'hollow force') led to significant cuts and readiness problems, other postwar periods (notably after WWII with the Cold War build-up) saw rapid re-expansion or selective changes rather than uniform deep, across-the-board cuts. Thus it is inaccurate to claim this happened after every major conflict.

claim: "I’m one of two members of Congress out of 535 that takes no corporate cash, no political action committee money."
rationale: The claim that only two of 535 members of Congress take no corporate cash or PAC money is inaccurate. Numerous members of both the House and Senate have publicly refused corporate PAC contributions or all PAC money at various times, and multiple reporting and campaign finance records show far more than two members follow that practice.

claim: Says a Twitter account for "Scarsdale NY Antifa" tweeted that "chapters of Antifa around Oregon have collaborated to ignite fires around the state."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a verified or otherwise credible account called "Scarsdale NY Antifa" posted a claim that Antifa chapters in Oregon collaborated to ignite fires. Multiple independent fact-checks and news reports found no corroboration for claims that Antifa organized statewide arson in Oregon and such attributions have been traced to unverified or parody social-media posts.

claim: "The KKK was formed by the Democratic Party."
rationale: The Ku Klux Klan was founded in 1865 in Pulaski, Tennessee by a small group of former Confederate officers and other local whites as a white supremacist vigilante organization, not as an official creation of the Democratic Party. While many early Klan members in the Reconstruction-era South were Democrats and the Klan later found support among segments of Southern Democratic politics, it was never an organization formally formed by the Democratic Party.

claim: Says he "raised graduation rates to nearly 90 percent."
rationale: The statement lacks a named subject, institution, cohort, baseline, and timeframe, so it is unverifiable as presented. Claims about raising graduation rates require specific, published data and context; without those details this assertion cannot be confirmed and should be treated as false.

claim: Says the National Labor Relations Board told Boeing that it couldn’t build a factory in South Carolina because South Carolina is a right-to-work state.
rationale: The NLRB did not tell Boeing it could not build a factory in South Carolina because it is a right-to-work state. The NLRB filed a complaint in 2011 alleging Boeing illegally moved work from Washington to punish pro-union employees and sought remedies, but it does not have authority to bar a company from locating a plant simply because a state is right-to-work. The complaint focused on alleged anti-union motivation for the site choice, not a categorical prohibition tied to right-to-work status.

claim: "They found 60 votes in the Senate in 2006 and 2013" for immigration legislation, and "each time the House Republican majority refused to take it up."
rationale: The Senate passed comprehensive immigration bills with well over 60 votes in both years (the 2006 bill passed the Senate by roughly 62 votes, and the 2013 bill passed 68-32). In both cases the Republican-controlled House leadership declined to bring the Senate-passed bipartisan measures to the floor for a vote. Thus the claim that the Senate reached about 60 votes and the House GOP refused to take them up is accurate.

claim: "The State of Texas is funding … women’s health services at historically high levels; they just increased their level another $50 million for the next two years."
rationale: The claim is imprecise about which program and timeframe it refers to, and there is no clear, verifiable record that Texas has just enacted a $50 million increase specifically for 'women’s health services' that brings funding to historically high levels. Texas budget appropriations for health and family-planning have varied by program and biennium, and claims about a single $50 million boost require a specific legislative appropriation or announcement to confirm. Without a cited source or program name, the statement is not verifiable as presented.

claim: "We have over 300,000,000 weapons, firearms in this country. That’s almost as big as the population."
rationale: Reliable estimates of civilian-held firearms in the United States are well over 300 million (commonly cited around 390–400 million in recent years), so the claim that there are over 300,000,000 firearms is accurate. Saying that figure is "almost as big as the population" is reasonable because U.S. population is roughly 330 million, making the quantity of firearms comparable to the population size.

claim: "If you are a hard-working law-abiding citizen who earns $80,000, you don’t get a stimulus check. But if you are a convicted murderer or rapist sitting in jail, you do."
rationale: This claim is false. Under the CARES Act and later federal stimulus payments, individuals with AGI of $80,000 were generally eligible for at least a partial payment because payments phased out above $75,000 and did not cut off entirely until higher thresholds; conversely, being incarcerated does not automatically guarantee or bar receipt — incarcerated people who meet IRS eligibility (valid SSN, income thresholds, not claimed as dependents) could receive payments, and in some cases payments could be intercepted for debts or restitution.

claim: As state Commerce secretary, Mary Burke drafted, sponsored and promoted "budgets that raised taxes by billions, created high structural deficits and raided funds to finance huge spending hikes."
rationale: Mary Burke served as Wisconsin Commerce Secretary in the Doyle administration, but state budgets are drafted and formally proposed by the governor and enacted by the legislature; there is no clear evidence that Burke personally 'drafted, sponsored and promoted' budgets that raised taxes by billions, created large structural deficits, or 'raided funds' for huge spending hikes. The claim attributes primary budget-making authority and specific fiscal outcomes to a cabinet official whose role did not include sponsoring state budgets.

claim: "We've seen 115,000 jobs created in the American auto industry since GM and Chrysler emerged from bankruptcy."
rationale: The raw figure is misleading because whether 115,000 jobs were created depends entirely on which BLS categories and which end date are used. Different measures (motor-vehicle manufacturing only, motor-vehicle-and-parts, or the broader auto-related supply and dealer sectors) yield different job-change totals since GM and Chrysler exited bankruptcy in mid-2009, so the claim as stated is not reliably verifiable without that context.

claim: "Private prison systems are calculating how many new beds (they will need) based on the ... number of third graders."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that private prison companies systematically determine future bed needs solely by counting current third‑graders. While research has shown correlations between early reading scores and later incarceration risk, and corrections planners and some firms use demographic and risk models to forecast demand, the claim overstates and mischaracterizes how bed projections are made.

claim: "In America, there is a father who is holding down two jobs and paying more taxes than the richest 400 families in America."
rationale: The claim is implausible and unsupported: the combined tax liabilities of the richest 400 families in the U.S. are far larger than what a single individual working two jobs would pay. No credible data or reporting documents an individual payer surpassing the aggregate taxes of the top 400 families.

claim: "The House has never failed to pass a budget in the modern era."
rationale: The U.S. House of Representatives has at times failed to enact a full budget or the necessary appropriations in recent decades, contributing to multiple federal government funding lapses and shutdowns (for example in 1995–1996, 2013, and 2018–2019). Additionally, Congress frequently uses continuing resolutions when regular appropriations or a concurrent budget resolution are not completed, so the statement that the House has 'never failed' is incorrect.

claim: Says Mitt Romney’s investments created zero jobs.
rationale: The statement is incorrect: Romney’s investments via Bain Capital were linked to both job creation and job losses across different portfolio companies, and independent fact-checkers have documented examples of Bain-backed firms that expanded and hired workers. It is therefore inaccurate to claim they created “zero” jobs as an absolute.

claim: "Kansas City Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes has left training camp and says he will ‘not play another down in the NFL’ until the team changes their name."
rationale: This claim is false. There are no credible reports or verified statements from Patrick Mahomes, the Kansas City Chiefs, or major sports outlets that he left training camp or said he would refuse to play until the team changes its name; Mahomes has continued to participate in team activities and made no public declaration like that. The story appears to be a fabricated social-media claim or misattribution rather than a documented fact.

claim: In Afghanistan, "over 100 billion dollars spent on military contracts."
rationale: The claim is presented without a timeframe, source, or definition of what counts as 'military contracts,' so it cannot be verified as stated. While some analyses of U.S. war-related contracting tied to Afghanistan across multiple years report totals in the tens of billions and occasionally near or above $100 billion depending on scope and period, the broad, context-free assertion is misleading and unsubstantiated.

claim: Says "I've authored the first bipartisan tax reform bill in a quarter-century."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits the jurisdiction, the author, and the precise bill being referenced; without that context it cannot be confirmed. Many legislatures have passed bipartisan tax legislation in the past 25 years, so claiming to be the "first" bipartisan tax reform in a quarter-century is unlikely and requires specific evidence.

claim: There are "360,000 (deaths) a year from swimming pools. But we don’t shut the country down for that."
rationale: The figure of roughly 360,000 per year is similar to older global counts of total drowning deaths, but not deaths specifically in swimming pools. Data from WHO and national health agencies show that drownings in swimming pools are only a small fraction of total drowning deaths, so claiming 360,000 deaths annually 'from swimming pools' is incorrect.

claim: "The amount of money that we put into running our own state legislature is nearly as much as we put into the University of Rhode Island."
rationale: State legislative operating budgets are typically modest (covering member pay, small staff, and facility costs) while public universities like the University of Rhode Island have large operating budgets covering faculty, staff, campuses, and student services. Without specific fiscal-year figures, the general pattern of public finance makes it very unlikely the legislature’s budget is 'nearly as much' as the university’s.

claim: "Almost 1 million children ... have no health insurance in this state."
rationale: The claim as written omits which state and the time period, so it is not verifiable. Without a specific state and date, the assertion that 'almost 1 million children' lack health insurance is unsupported and potentially misleading; such a large number would only be plausible for the most populous states and must be checked against state-level survey data.

claim: Says North Carolina gives taxpayer dollars to private schools, but "we really don’t know what these schools are doing or how they are performing."
rationale: North Carolina operates state-funded voucher programs (notably the Opportunity Scholarship Program) that send taxpayer dollars to private schools. Those private schools are generally subject to weaker accountability and transparency requirements than public schools, so comprehensive, comparable information on their overall performance is limited.

claim: "Since February 2009, the private sector has lost millions of jobs while the federal government has grown by hundreds of thousands of workers."
rationale: This claim is incorrect: after the February 2009 trough in the recession, the private sector overall went on to add millions of jobs over the subsequent recovery years rather than lose them. Federal civilian employment showed only modest net change over that period (with temporary spikes for Census hiring), not a sustained growth of hundreds of thousands of permanent workers.

claim: "Kids are less likely to get it (COVID-19). You know, they’re less likely to spread. So I think there’s some pretty good data out there that will help alleviate some of the concerns."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. Early in the pandemic some studies found lower reported infections and reduced transmission from children for original strains, but later evidence — especially with Delta and Omicron — showed children can be infected and transmit SARS-CoV-2 at rates similar to adults depending on age and setting. Whether children are "less likely" therefore depends on variant, age group, detection practices, and mitigation measures.

claim: A Georgia law has not "criminalized giving people bottles of water." It pertains to political organizations.
rationale: Georgia’s 2021 election law (SB 202) contains provisions that restrict non-election officials and third parties from giving “anything of value” to voters in or near polling places, a provision critics and fact-checkers said could be read to include handing out bottled water. The law is not solely about political organizations, and although there have been clarifications and exemptions, its text and guidance do place limits on who can distribute items to voters.

claim: Georgia has some of the best maintained roads in America.
rationale: The statement is vague and not supported by consistent, objective measures: national infrastructure assessments and state-by-state pavement condition studies typically rate Georgia as average or mixed rather than clearly among the top U.S. states for road maintenance. Claiming it has 'some of the best maintained roads' overstates the available evidence.

claim: "If we pass immigration reform, it will make wages go up on average $250 for the average household."
rationale: The statement is a specific, quantitative prediction without defining what 'immigration reform' means, the time period, or the methodology for averaging across households. Empirical research and government analyses show that wages effects of immigration policy depend heavily on the reform design and time horizon, and are typically small and heterogeneous rather than a uniform $250 gain per household. Therefore the blanket numeric claim is unsupported as presented.

claim: Says Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s "wealth has surged while in public office."
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated evidence that Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s personal wealth has experienced a dramatic surge while holding public office. Public financial-disclosure records for members of Congress show year-to-year variation and modest increases tied to investments and spouse income for many senators, but reputable reporting does not document a notable, sudden wealth surge attributed to her tenure.

claim: "That’s 5,615 projected coal-powered plants in just 8 countries. The USA has 15 - building 0 more."
rationale: The claim that there are 5,615 projected coal-fired plants in just 8 countries and that the U.S. has 15 with none more being built is not supported by reputable trackers. Global data sources that track coal plants (projects and units) show far fewer planned or under-construction coal plants worldwide, and the U.S. currently has very few new coal plants proposed or being built — most recent trends are retirements and conversions rather than large new coal builds.

claim: "Now, 50% of all of America, more than any other country, is fully vaccinated."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unlikely to be correct. If interpreted as the United States having 50% of its population fully vaccinated and that being higher than any other country, that is false—many countries and territories (e.g., several in Europe, the UAE, Chile, etc.) have had higher fully vaccinated shares. If interpreted as "all of America" meaning the continents, the phrase "more than any other country" is nonsensical.

claim: "BREAKING: Pennsylvania initiated a FULL audit of the RIGGED ELECTION"
rationale: There was no statewide ‘‘full audit’’ of Pennsylvania’s election initiated by state authorities; after the 2020 election Pennsylvania completed certification, some counties conducted audits or recounts, and multiple court challenges alleging widespread fraud were dismissed. The claim’s framing as a breaking announcement that Pennsylvania initiated a full audit of a 'rigged election' is unsupported and conflates isolated county actions and political rhetoric with an official statewide audit.

claim: "If we ban the practice of earmarks, we could save the American taxpayer anywhere between $15 (billion) to $20 billion dollars a year in pork-barrel spending."
rationale: The claimed $15–$20 billion annual savings is misleading: annual totals labeled as 'earmarks' vary widely by year and by definition, and some watchdogs have reported figures in that range for certain years but independent analyses (CBO/CRS/GAO) produce different totals. Moreover, banning earmarks does not automatically equal that level of taxpayer savings because appropriated funds can be redistributed into other programs or continue through formulaic spending, so the net savings are uncertain.

claim: "FBI uncovers evidence that 62 million Trump voters are all Russian agents!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public FBI announcement that 62 million Trump voters are Russian agents. The FBI conducts targeted investigations and would not validly or legally label an entire voting bloc as foreign agents without individual evidence, charges, or reputable reporting supporting such an extraordinary claim.

claim: "New Jersey today has fewer employees in state government than it had when Christie Whitman left office in January of 2001, and I think that’s good. And we did it without any layoffs. We did it through attrition."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because it omits the date of “today” and the exact employment measure (payroll headcount, full‑time equivalents, state‑level only vs. all public employees). Historical New Jersey payroll data have fluctuated since 2001 and outcomes differ by the metric chosen; some reductions were achieved via attrition but counts relative to January 2001 are not uniformly lower across common measures. Because the claim is specific and lacks those key definitions, it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: Says Chris Christie was "behind" in the polls against Jon Corzine during the 2009 governor's race.
rationale: The statement is misleading: while some early polls at points in 2009 had Jon Corzine ahead, polling shifted during the campaign and by the fall Christie was leading and went on to win the November election. Saying Christie was (generally) “behind” during the 2009 race without a specific timeframe is therefore inaccurate.

claim: The poorest counties in the U.S. are in Appalachia and "happen to be more than 90 percent white."
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes: Appalachia does contain many high-poverty counties and some of those are overwhelmingly white, but the poorest counties in the U.S. are not all in Appalachia nor are they all >90% white. Nationwide poverty and lowest-income lists also include majority-Black Mississippi Delta counties, Native American-majority counties in the Southwest and Plains, and very poor Hispanic-border counties.

claim: "Today, it is more difficult to enlist in the U.S. military than it is to enroll in college."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. Enlistment in the U.S. military requires meeting specific age, medical, physical, moral, and aptitude (ASVAB) standards and has seen recruiting difficulty, but college admission varies widely — many community colleges have open enrollment while elite colleges are highly selective. Because difficulty depends on which branch of the military and which type of college are being compared, the blanket claim is not supportable.

claim: One-third of the economic stimulus package was tax cuts.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous because it does not identify which country or which specific stimulus package is meant; different stimulus bills allocate very different shares to tax cuts, so a blanket statement that "one-third" was tax cuts cannot be verified and is likely incorrect. To evaluate the claim requires the exact package and a line-item breakdown showing the share devoted to tax measures.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar vowed "to remove senior’s ‘entitlements,’ Social Security/Medicare."
rationale: There is no credible record of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Ilhan Omar vowing to eliminate Social Security or Medicare for seniors. Both lawmakers have publicly supported protecting or expanding social insurance (including backing versions of Medicare-for-All or strengthening Social Security) and opposed cuts or privatization. The claim appears to be a misattribution or distortion of opponents’ rhetoric.

claim: Says Luke Messer and Todd Rokita "voted to fast-track Obama’s trade deals."
rationale: The statement implies both Luke Messer and Todd Rokita voted to fast-track President Obama’s trade deals, but they did not vote the same way. In the 2015 House votes on Trade Promotion Authority (fast-track), Luke Messer voted in favor while Todd Rokita voted against, so saying both voted to fast-track is inaccurate.

claim: If Florida expanded Medicaid, "some studies indicate it would create about 120,000 jobs."
rationale: Multiple economic and policy analyses have produced estimates that Medicaid expansion in Florida would create on the order of tens to a few hundred thousand jobs, and several such reports produced figures near 120,000 jobs. While the precise number varies by model and assumptions, the statement accurately reflects that some studies project about 120,000 jobs.

claim: In the federal government, "there’s $16 billion in duplicate programs" that can be cut.
rationale: There is no authoritative, universally accepted audit showing a standalone $16 billion figure for 'duplicate programs' across the entire federal government; estimates of duplication and overlap vary by report and depend on definitional and methodological choices. Agencies and the GAO have identified overlapping programs and potential savings in different years and categories, but the specific claim of a single $16 billion of duplicative programs that 'can be cut' is unsubstantiated without a cited source and is subjective.

claim: In New York, "Average college debt - $30,000 per student."
rationale: The claim is presented as a precise current fact but is too imprecise and likely misleading: average student loan debt in New York varies by year, by whether you measure mean or median, and by whether graduate debt is included. Depending on the source and cohort the figure can be near $30,000 but is not a single fixed, universally reported 'average $30,000 per student' for New York.

claim: Says Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie made a late-night visit to Kinko’s to forge President Barack Obama’s birth certificate two days before Obama unveiled it to the media.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie visited a Kinko’s to forge President Obama’s birth certificate. The allegation is part of the debunked “birther” conspiracy narrative; Hawaii officials and news investigations have found no proof of such a forgery and confirmed the state holds vital records. Abercrombie did say he had seen the original Hawaii birth record, but that is not evidence of any Kinko’s forgery.

claim: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has "no congressional oversight."
rationale: The CFPB is not free of congressional oversight. It was created by Congress (Dodd-Frank), its director is Senate-confirmed, and Congress routinely exercises oversight through hearings, subpoenas, reporting requirements and the power to change the agency’s statute and funding. While the bureau has an independent funding mechanism and some statutory protections that limit direct appropriations control, that does not equate to ‘no congressional oversight.’

claim: President Barack Obama’s latest executive order "mandates the apprehension and detention of Americans who merely show signs of ‘respiratory illness.’ "
rationale: There is no known Obama executive order that broadly mandates the apprehension and detention of Americans who merely show signs of 'respiratory illness.' Public health authorities do have limited quarantine and isolation powers for contagious diseases, but such actions are governed by statutes, public-health regulations, and constitutional due-process protections rather than a blanket executive order that permits mass detention based on mere symptoms. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or viral misinformation conflating routine public-health measures with an alleged sweeping detention mandate.

claim: When Mitt Romney was governor, Massachusetts lost 40,000 manufacturing jobs, a rate twice the national average, and fell to 47th in job creation, fourth from the bottom.
rationale: The statement mixes facts and misleading context. Massachusetts did lose a substantial number of manufacturing jobs during the early 2000s, but the timing of those losses spans before and after Romney’s term, the rate was not clearly twice the national average once baseline years are accounted for, and the "47th in job creation" ranking depends on a narrowly chosen timeframe and metric rather than a standard multi-year comparison.

claim: Say Apple’s Tim Cook "will not do business with Indiana."
rationale: There is no public evidence that Tim Cook declared he "will not do business with Indiana." While Cook and Apple publicly criticized Indiana's 2015 religious freedom law and opposed discrimination, Apple did not announce a blanket refusal to conduct business there and continued normal commercial activities. The claim appears to misattribute or exaggerate criticism into an absolute business boycott statement.

claim: "Eighty-five percent of every dollar donated to the Clinton Foundation ended up either with the Clintons or with their staff to pay for travel, salaries, and benefits. Fifteen cents of every dollar actually went to some charitable beneficiary."
rationale: The claim that 85% of every dollar went to the Clintons or staff and only 15 cents to beneficiaries is demonstrably incorrect. Independent analysis of the Clinton Foundation's IRS Form 990s and third‑party charity ratings show the foundation historically spent the majority of its budget on program services and grants, with administrative and fundraising costs substantially lower than 85%. The 85% figure stems from a misreading and misclassification of line items and does not reflect how nonprofit accounting reports program versus administrative spending.

claim: "The Doherty Campaign, unlike the Cicilline Campaign, is funded mostly by individual donors -- not the big PACs that Cicilline relies on."
rationale: The statement is an unsupported, oversimplified comparison: campaign funding mixes vary by election cycle and candidate, and I have no specific FEC or OpenSecrets data showing that a particular 'Doherty' campaign is funded mostly by individuals while Cicilline 'relies on' big PACs. Without specifying which Doherty and which election year, available public finance records are needed to substantiate the claim. Given typical patterns, both individual contributions and PAC money commonly fund Congressional campaigns, so the categorical contrast is likely incorrect.

claim: Goldman Sachs was Barack Obama's "No. 1 private contributor."
rationale: This is misleading. While many Goldman Sachs employees were significant individual donors to Barack Obama’s campaigns, the firm itself (its corporate PAC) was not the single largest private contributor. Campaign finance analyses distinguish employee/individual donations from corporate PAC giving and do not support Goldman Sachs being his No. 1 private donor as an entity.

claim: Georgia has had the nation’s busiest Court of Appeals for a decade or more.
rationale: The statement is too categorical and lacks a defined metric or timeframe. While Georgia’s Court of Appeals has frequently ranked among the busiest intermediate appellate courts, national rankings vary by year and by measure (total filings, dispositions, cases per judge), and there is no consistent evidence that it has been the single busiest Court of Appeals in the nation for more than a decade.

claim: "Already, the Affordable Care Act is helping to slow the growth of (Medicare’s) health care costs."
rationale: Multiple authoritative analyses (Congressional Budget Office, Medicare Trustees, independent researchers) found that ACA provisions—such as reduced Medicare Advantage payments, payment-rate changes, and delivery-system reforms—have lowered Medicare spending relative to prior projections and contributed to slower Medicare cost growth in the early 2010s. However, the overall slowdown in health spending also reflects other factors, so the ACA is a contributing cause rather than the sole cause.

claim: "I’m running the second-largest county district attorney’s office … at 1985 staffing levels."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and provides no verifiable data or named office; without specifying which county or presenting staffing records it cannot be accepted. General public records and reporting of large county prosecutor offices show staffing has changed since 1985 in line with population and caseload growth, so the unqualified assertion is not supported.

claim: Says Donald Trump's first 17 Cabinet appointments "have a net worth of more than a third of America."
rationale: This claim is misleading and incorrect. Public estimates put the combined net worth of Trump’s early Cabinet members in the tens of billions, which is far smaller than the combined net worth held by one-third of U.S. households or one-third of the population (which runs into hundreds of billions or trillions). The claim conflates different baselines and overstates the Cabinet’s share of national wealth.

claim: "According to the most recent report, Wisconsin’s high school graduation rates are also up again -- to third best in the country."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and likely incorrect: U.S. high-school graduation rankings vary by data source and year, and there is no consistent, authoritative "most recent report" that places Wisconsin third nationally. Wisconsin has relatively high graduation rates, but national rankings in the latest federal and independent datasets do not reliably show it as third-best without a specific year and source.

claim: Says Jimmy Carter was the last "U.S. president to say flat out those (Israeli) settlements are illegal."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: multiple U.S. administrations after Carter have publicly criticized Israeli settlements and senior officials have described them as illegitimate or inconsistent with international law, so Carter was not uniquely the last president to call them illegal. U.S. policy has varied by administration (and some later administrations explicitly reversed or softened earlier language).

claim: "A Gallup report recently said that nearly 50 percent of small business owners aren't hiring because of what they call ‘regulatory uncertainty.’"
rationale: I can’t find a verifiable Gallup report stating that nearly 50% of small business owners are not hiring specifically because of 'regulatory uncertainty.' Gallup has polled small-business owners on barriers to hiring, but reported shares attributing hiring weakness to regulation are substantially lower or framed differently; this claim appears to conflate or misstate survey results.

claim: "Newgard owed more than $13,000 for unpaid taxes on his $1 million Milwaukie apartment complex."
rationale: I cannot confirm this specific claim from available knowledge and there is no widely reported or verifiable record I can find tying a person named Newgard to a $1 million Milwaukie apartment complex with more than $13,000 in unpaid taxes. Property tax delinquencies and amounts are public records in county tax/assessor databases and would need to be checked to substantiate the claim. Because the claim is unverified and lacks sourcing, I judge it false for now pending primary-record confirmation.

claim: Says he and Mitt Romney "always said that we agree with the 2014 deadline" for leaving Afghanistan.
rationale: The statement claims someone said that he and Mitt Romney “always said that we agree with the 2014 deadline,” but publicly Romney opposed rigid withdrawal deadlines during the 2012 campaign and criticized setting a firm 2014 deadline. Without a clear source or speaker, there is no corroborated evidence that Romney consistently said he agreed with a 2014 exit date, so the claim is not supported.

claim: Says the Wisconsin Republican Party tweeted "Happy International Women's Day! You ladies should get paid less and not be able to make health care decisions."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the official Wisconsin Republican Party account tweeted this statement; no reputable news or fact-check outlets documented such an inflammatory post and the wording matches common fabricated or parody screenshots that circulate online.
